title: English, Class 10
subject: English
description: NCERT Grade 10 English, chapter by chapter.

chapters.title: A Letter to God
chapters.summary: In this chapter: before you read and money order activity; lencho's field, rain, and hailstorm; a single hope and the letter to god; the postmaster answers.

lessons.title: Before You Read and Money Order Activity

activities.prompt: What would you do if your only hope was to write a letter to God?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Faith and a Letter to God
activities.body: Faith means believing in something even when you cannot see it. People say faith can move mountains. In this lesson you will meet Lencho, a farmer whose crops are ruined. He writes a letter to God and asks for a hundred pesos. As you read, think: should the letter reach God? Should God send him money?
keyPoints: Faith means believing even when you cannot see.
Lencho is a farmer whose crops are ruined.
He asks God for a hundred pesos.
activities.explanation: Keep these questions in your mind as you read the lesson.

activities.prompt: Your family's crop dies. You have no money. Who should you ask for help, and why?
steps: People say faith can move mountains, so faith gives people hope when life is hard.
Lencho loses his crops, so he puts his faith in God and writes a letter.
But money is sent by people at the post office, so a real person may answer the letter.
So the real question is not if we have faith, but who or what we should put our faith in.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Sending Money by Post
activities.body: One cheap way to send money is through the post office. You fill in a money order form. It has three parts: the Money Order form, a part for official use, and the Acknowledgement. The form has six sections. You may send money for a magazine subscription, or to a relative or friend. You can be the sender, and your partner the receiver. You will also learn words like counter and counterfoil.
keyPoints: The post office is a cheap way to send money.
The form has three parts and six sections.
You are the sender; your partner is the receiver.
activities.explanation: Now you know how a money order form is arranged.

activities.prompt: What work does Lencho do?
options: He is a farmer.
He is a teacher.
He is a doctor.
activities.explanation: Well done! Lencho is a farmer, and his crops are ruined.

activities.prompt: Lencho asks God for a hundred pesos.
activities.explanation: Yes! In his letter, Lencho asks God for a hundred pesos.

activities.prompt: Which is one cheap way to send money?
options: A gold shop
A taxi ride
The post office
activities.explanation: Right! The post office is one cheap way to send money.

activities.prompt: The money order form has ______ sections.
activities.hint: It is one more than five.
activities.explanation: Yes, the form has six sections. You will fill them one by one.

activities.prompt: Match each one to its partner.
pairs: You fill the form as the
A cheap way to send money is the
activities.explanation: Great matching! You remember who does what in this lesson.

activities.prompt: Put the three parts of the money order form in order.
items: Money Order form
Part for official use
Acknowledgement
activities.explanation: The form begins with the Money Order form, then comes the official use part, and it ends with the Acknowledgement.

activities.prompt: Lencho is a farmer. His crops are ruined. He has no money now. He writes a letter to God. Why does he write to God?
options: He believes God will listen and help him.
He wants to learn how to write letters.
He is angry with God for the rain.
He wants to sell his letter for money.

Wrong: thinks writing a letter is a school skill, not a prayer.
Wrong: confuses asking for help with being angry.
Wrong: thinks a letter is a thing to sell, not a way to ask.

activities.explanation: Right: he has faith, so he asks God for help.

activities.prompt: Lencho's crops are gone. He asks God for a hundred pesos. Why does he ask for money?
options: He needs money to live and farm again.
He wants to buy a big new house.
He wants to pay the postman a gift.
He wants to buy a ticket to a city.

Wrong: thinks of a big wish, not his real need.
Wrong: mixes the post office into his need for money.
Wrong: thinks he wants to run away, not to farm again.

activities.explanation: Right: money is what he lost with his crops.

activities.prompt: The chapter asks if Lencho's letter reaches God. It also asks if God sends him money. What does this make you think?
options: The answers may be strange and surprising.
The story is only about a post office.
Lencho will find a new job soon.
The letter will be lost and never read.

Wrong: thinks the place matters more than the big question.
Wrong: adds a new idea that the story never asks about.
Wrong: jumps to one ending without thinking about the question.

activities.explanation: Right: a letter to God cannot be answered in a normal way.

activities.prompt: You fill a money order form at the post office. You keep one small part of the form. That part is called the counterfoil. Why do you keep it?
options: It is your proof that you sent money.
It is a gift for your friend far away.
It is paper for writing a new letter.
It is the fee you pay the postman.

Wrong: thinks the form part is a present, not a record.
Wrong: thinks all paper is for writing letters.
Wrong: mixes up money you pay with paper you keep.

activities.explanation: Right: keeping a part of the form shows what you did.

activities.prompt: The money order form has three parts. One part is the Acknowledgement. The receiver signs this part. What happens to it then?
options: It goes back to show the sender it arrived.
It stays with the receiver in a drawer.
It is torn up and thrown in a bin.
It is kept by the clerk as a gift.

Wrong: thinks signing is the end, so nothing more happens.
Wrong: thinks a signed paper has no use after signing.
Wrong: thinks the clerk keeps it for himself, not for the sender.

activities.explanation: Right: an acknowledgement tells the sender the money came.

lessons.title: Lencho's Field, Rain, and Hailstorm

activities.prompt: Why did Lencho call the falling raindrops 'new coins'?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Lencho's Home and the Coming Rain
activities.body: Lencho's house stood alone on the crest of a low hill. It was the only house in the whole valley. From up there, Lencho could see the river and his field of ripe corn. The earth needed a good shower. One evening, big raindrops began to fall during the meal. Lencho was happy, for he knew his fields well. But soon very large hailstones fell with the rain, and the hail rained for an hour.
keyPoints: The house was alone on the crest of a low hill, the only one in the valley.
From the house one could see the river and the field of ripe corn.
Rain began during the meal, but large hailstones fell with it for an hour.
activities.explanation: The lesson begins with hope, as rain brings joy, and then trouble, as hail destroys that joy.

activities.prompt: Lencho is eating with his family. He keeps looking out of the window at the sky. Why is he watching the sky so carefully during his meal?
steps: The corn in the field is ripe, so the plants have grown fully and are ready.
Ripe corn still needs water, because the earth needed a downpour or at least a shower.
Lencho knows his fields very well, so he can tell what his plants need just by looking.
So when huge clouds come near, he watches closely, because rain now means food for his family later.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where did Lencho's house sit?
options: Beside the river
On the crest of a low hill
In the middle of the corn field
At the foot of a tall mountain
activities.explanation: The house sat on the crest of a low hill, high enough to look over the land.

activities.prompt: Lencho looked at the falling rain and said the raindrops were new ______.
activities.hint: Shiny round money pieces.
activities.explanation: Lencho called the raindrops new coins, because rain meant a good crop for him.

activities.prompt: Match each thing from the lesson with how it is described.
activities.explanation: The lesson uses lovely pictures: coins for rain, pearls for hail, mountains for clouds.

activities.prompt: Why did the earth need a downpour or at least a shower?
options: The river had gone dry
The ripe corn field needed water
The boys wanted to play in rain
The clouds were too heavy
activities.explanation: Lencho's field of ripe corn needed rain, so a good shower would help his crop grow.

activities.prompt: Put these events from the lesson in the order they happened.
items: Huge mountains of clouds were seen approaching
Big drops of rain began to fall during the meal
Very large hailstones began to fall with the rain
The boys ran out to collect the frozen pearls
activities.explanation: First the clouds came, then the rain fell, then the hail, and last the boys ran out to gather the icy pearls.

activities.prompt: Lencho knew his fields intimately. What would happen to his joy if the rain had fallen as soft rain with no hail?
options: He would be sad, as rain spoils ripe corn
He would be happy, as rain helps his crop like coins
He would be angry, as clouds block the river view
He would be worried, as boys collect frozen pearls
activities.explanation: Lencho called the raindrops new coins, so gentle rain would make his crop, and his joy, grow.

activities.prompt: Lencho's house is the only one in the whole valley. It stands alone on a low hill. From the window he can see the river and the ripe corn. One evening he looks at the sky again and again. What does this tell us about him?
options: He is bored and has nothing else to do.
He cares deeply about his field and his crop.
He is afraid of living alone in the valley.
He wants to move his house down the hill.

This thinks boredom is the same as watching carefully; he looks with hope, not boredom.
why.He is afraid of living alone in the vall: This mixes watching the sky with fear of people; the story gives no sign of fear.
why.He wants to move his house down the hill: This thinks he dislikes the hill, but he chose to watch the sky, not to leave.

activities.explanation: Right: the ripe corn is his crop, and he watches the sky because rain decides his harvest.

activities.prompt: The earth is dry and needs a downpour or at least a shower. Lencho looks at his field every day. One evening he sees huge mountains of clouds coming near. How does he most likely feel at that moment?
options: Sad, because clouds always bring him bad luck.
Scared, because dark clouds mean a storm is coming.
Happy and hopeful, because rain is coming at last.
Angry, because the clouds block his view of the river.

why.Sad, because clouds always bring him bad: This thinks all clouds are bad; but his land was waiting for rain.
why.Scared, because dark clouds mean a storm: This confuses clouds with the hailstorm that comes later; at this moment rain is good news.
why.Angry, because the clouds block his view: This thinks he cares about the view; a farmer cares about water for his crop.

activities.explanation: Right: the earth needed rain, so clouds coming near feel like a gift to a farmer.

activities.prompt: Big drops of rain begin to fall while the family is eating. Lencho calls the raindrops new coins. He says this with joy in his voice. Why does he compare rain to coins?
options: He found real money lying in the wet field.
He thinks coins fall from clouds in heavy rain.
He believes rain will grow into money in the soil.
Rain will help the crop grow, and the crop brings money.

why.He found real money lying in the wet fie: This takes the words too literally; he is comparing, not reporting real coins.
why.He thinks coins fall from clouds in heav: This thinks he really believes coins fall; he is speaking with joy, not telling a fact.
why.He believes rain will grow into money in: This mixes the picture with magic; rain helps the crop, it does not turn into money.

activities.explanation: Right: rain feeds the ripe corn, a good harvest means money, so drops feel like coins.

activities.prompt: Very large hailstones begin to fall along with the rain. The boys run out of the house. They gather the frozen pearls in their hands. What do the boys most likely feel while doing this?
options: Bored, because they were told to come inside.
Curious and excited, because the stones look strange and new.
Sad, because they already know the crop is dying.
Angry, because the stones are falling on their heads.

why.Bored, because they were told to come in: This thinks running out means being forced; they run out on their own.
why.Sad, because they already know the crop: This thinks children understand farming loss at once; the story shows them playing instead.
why.Angry, because the stones are falling on: This confuses the hail with being hurt; they are picking the stones up happily.

activities.explanation: Right: they call them pearls and collect them, which shows wonder and play, not worry.

activities.prompt: The hail keeps falling on the house for a whole hour. Lencho stands watching his field through it. The boys first played with the stones, but the hail does not stop. How do the boys most likely feel after a long time?
options: Proud, because they collected so many frozen pearls.
Excited, because the hail is still falling harder.
Worried, because the fun has lasted far too long.
Sleepy, because the hour of hail made them tired.

why.Proud, because they collected so many fr: This keeps the first happy feeling; an hour of hail changes joy into worry.
why.Excited, because the hail is still falli: This thinks more hail means more fun; a long storm stops being a game.
why.Sleepy, because the hour of hail made th: This adds a feeling the story does not point to; the change shown is from joy to worry.

activities.explanation: Right: hail for an hour is not play any more; the boys start to sense something is wrong.

lessons.title: A Single Hope and the Letter to God

activities.prompt: What hope made a farmer write a letter to God himself?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: One Hope in the House
activities.body: The hailstone ruined the crop, but the family kept one single hope in their hearts. They told each other that no one dies of hunger. All through the night, Lencho thought only of that one hope. He believed God's eyes see everything. So on Sunday at daybreak, he wrote a letter to God. He asked for a hundred pesos to sow his field again.
keyPoints: The family had one single hope: help from God.
Lencho believed God's eyes see everything.
He wrote a letter asking for a hundred pesos.
activities.explanation: Lencho's faith was strong, so he turned straight to God for help.

activities.prompt: Lencho's house is alone. The family is hungry and worried. Why does Lencho write a letter instead of just waiting?
steps: The family has one hope, so they all believe things will get better.
They say no one dies of hunger, so they trust help will come.
Lencho thinks all night about this one hope, so it fills his mind.
He believes God sees everything, so he feels God knows his trouble and will answer. So writing to God is his way of asking for that help.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Thinking All Night
activities.prompt: Lencho thought about many different things all through the night.
activities.explanation: He thought only of his one hope, nothing else. Keep going!

activities.title: A Strong Man
activities.prompt: Lencho was an ______ of a man, strong and hard-working.
activities.hint: A big, strong farm animal.
activities.explanation: The lesson calls Lencho an ox of a man, meaning very strong.

activities.title: On the Envelope
activities.prompt: What did Lencho write on the envelope?
options: His own name
The post office address
To God
Help needed
activities.explanation: He wrote 'To God' on the envelope before posting it.

activities.title: Match the Letter Facts
activities.prompt: Match each thing with what the lesson says about it.
activities.explanation: Each part of the story fits neatly with its pair. Great memory!

activities.title: How Much Money?
activities.prompt: Lencho asked God for fifty pesos in his letter.
activities.explanation: He asked for a hundred pesos, not fifty. You are thinking carefully!

activities.title: Lencho's Steps
activities.prompt: Put the things Lencho did in the correct order.
items: He thought of his one hope all through the night.
On Sunday at daybreak, he began to write a letter.
He wrote 'To God' on the envelope.
He placed a stamp on the letter.
He dropped the letter into the mailbox.
activities.explanation: First the hope, then the writing, then the envelope, stamp and post. Perfect order!

activities.prompt: Ravi's kite is stuck in a tall tree. He cannot climb. He knows his uncle is kind. Ravi writes a note and gives it to his uncle. Why does Ravi write the note?
options: He wants his uncle to know his problem and help him.
He wants to show his uncle that he can write well.
He wants his uncle to feel sad about the broken kite.
He wants his uncle to buy him a new tall ladder.

why.He wants to show his uncle that he can w: Wrong. He is asking for help, not showing off his writing skill.
why.He wants his uncle to feel sad about the: Wrong. He wants help, not just to make his uncle feel sad.
why.He wants his uncle to buy him a new tall: Wrong. He asks for help with the kite, not for a new ladder.

activities.explanation: Right. He asks for help because he trusts his uncle will answer, like Lencho trusted God.

activities.prompt: Meena's garden died in a storm. Her family has no seeds. Meena says, 'We will plant again. Someone will help us.' What does Meena's words show about her?
options: She still has one hope in her heart.
She is angry at the storm and the rain.
She wants to move to a new big city.
She thinks gardens can never grow again.

Wrong. Her words show trust, not anger at the storm.
Wrong. She wants to plant again, not leave her home.
Wrong. She says she will plant again, so she believes it can grow.

activities.explanation: Right. Like Lencho's family, she holds one hope even in trouble.

activities.prompt: Lencho was an ox of a man. He worked hard all day in his field. Why does the story call him an ox of a man?
options: He was strong and worked like a big animal.
He was slow and could not think for himself.
He was angry and often fought with other farmers.
He looked like an ox and made animal sounds.

why.He was slow and could not think for hims: Wrong. The words praise his strength, not say he cannot think.
why.He was angry and often fought with other: Wrong. Nothing says he was angry or fought with anyone.
why.He looked like an ox and made animal sou: Wrong. It is about his hard work, not his looks or sounds.

activities.explanation: Right. An ox is strong and works hard, like Lencho in his field.

activities.prompt: Amit finds an old envelope. On it is written 'To God'. There is a stamp on it. Amit wonders who wrote it. What can Amit guess about the writer?
options: The writer believed a letter could reach God.
The writer forgot to write a friend's real name.
The writer was playing a joke on the postman.
The writer wanted to send the letter back home.

why.The writer forgot to write a friend's re: Wrong. The name was written on purpose, not forgotten.
why.The writer was playing a joke on the pos: Wrong. The careful stamp shows a serious letter, not a joke.
why.The writer wanted to send the letter bac: Wrong. 'To God' shows where it should go, not back home.

activities.explanation: Right. Like Lencho, the writer truly believed the letter could reach God.

activities.prompt: Sara needs money to buy seeds for her field. She knows how to write. On Sunday morning she starts writing a letter. What will Sara most likely do next?
options: She will ask for the money she needs in the letter.
She will tear the letter because she feels too shy.
She will read the letter to her friends at school.
She will draw pictures of seeds instead of words.

why.She will tear the letter because she fee: Wrong. She started the letter on purpose, so she will not tear it.
why.She will read the letter to her friends: Wrong. The letter is for asking help, not for showing friends.
why.She will draw pictures of seeds instead: Wrong. She knows how to write, so she will use words.

activities.explanation: Right. Like Lencho, she writes to ask for the money she needs.

activities.prompt: Lencho wrote 'To God' on the envelope. He put a stamp on it. Then he dropped it into the mailbox. Why did he put a stamp on the letter?
options: So the letter could really travel through the post.
So God would know the letter came from Lencho.
So the letter would look pretty and colourful.
So the postman would keep the letter for himself.

why.So God would know the letter came from L: Wrong. The stamp is for the post, not to show his name.
why.So the letter would look pretty and colo: Wrong. The stamp is needed for posting, not for beauty.
why.So the postman would keep the letter for: Wrong. The stamp helps the letter go, not stay with the postman.

activities.explanation: Right. A stamp makes the letter real post, so it can travel.

lessons.title: The Postmaster Answers

activities.prompt: What would you do if a letter arrived addressed to God?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Letter Nobody Knew
activities.body: A postman saw a strange letter and showed it to his boss. The postmaster laughed at first, but soon he felt serious. The letter writer had deep faith. The postmaster wished he had such faith too. So he decided to write a reply, so the writer's faith would not be shaken.
keyPoints: The postman showed the letter to his boss.
The postmaster laughed, then became serious.
He answered the letter to protect the writer's faith.
activities.explanation: A kind heart can turn a joke into a gift of hope.

activities.prompt: A man promises to send a friend one hundred pesos. He gives part of his salary and asks his friends to help. He can only collect a little more than half. What should he do?
steps: He cannot send the full amount, because no one has more money to give.
He could send nothing, but that would break his kind promise.
He sends the half he has, because some help is better than none.
So he keeps his promise as best he can, even though it is not perfect.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who showed the strange letter to the boss?
options: The postman
The letter writer
A friend of the boss
The postmaster's clerk
activities.explanation: Well done! The postman took the letter to his boss.

activities.prompt: How did the postmaster feel after he laughed at the letter?
options: He became serious
He became angry
He forgot the letter
He tore it up
activities.explanation: Yes! His laughter soon turned into a serious, caring mood.

activities.prompt: The postmaster signed the letter with one single word: ______.
activities.hint: Think of who the letter writer believed in.
activities.explanation: Great! He signed it with the single word God.

activities.prompt: Match each person to what they did.
pairs: Showed the letter to his boss
activities.explanation: Many hands came together to help answer one letter.

activities.prompt: Why did the postmaster decide to answer the letter?
options: So the writer's faith would not shake
So the postman would get a reward
So the office could sell stamps
So the letter could travel faster
activities.explanation: Well thought! He wanted to protect the writer's precious faith.

activities.prompt: Put the events of the story in the right order.
items: The postman shows the letter to his boss
The postmaster laughs but becomes serious
He decides to answer the letter
He asks his employees for money
He sends a little more than half
activities.explanation: Perfect order! You remembered the story step by step.

activities.prompt: A postman has walked every street for many years. One letter has an address he has never seen. He takes the letter to his boss first. Why does he show it to his boss?
options: He wants his boss to write the address again.
The address is strange, so he wants help with it.
He thinks his boss should deliver all the letters.
He is tired and does not want to walk today.

why.He wants his boss to write the address a: This thinks the problem is bad handwriting, not a strange address.
why.He thinks his boss should deliver all th: This thinks the postman is passing his own work to someone else.
why.He is tired and does not want to walk to: This thinks the postman is lazy, but the real reason is the strange address.

activities.explanation: Right: he never knew this address, so the letter is strange and he needs help.

activities.prompt: A teacher laughs at a silly question in class. Then she sees the shy boy really wants to learn. Her face becomes serious. Why does her face change?
options: She is angry that the boy asked at all.
She now feels care for the boy's real wish.
She wants the other students to stop laughing too.
She forgot her joke and cannot remember the answer.

This thinks anger came first, but her laugh came first, not anger.
why.She wants the other students to stop lau: This thinks she is only managing the class, not feeling something inside.
why.She forgot her joke and cannot remember: This thinks she is confused, but her face changed from a feeling.

activities.explanation: Right: like the postmaster, she laughs first, then feels serious care.

activities.prompt: Meera believes her old tree grants wishes. Her uncle does not believe this. But he says, 'I wish I believed like Meera.' What does he really mean?
options: He wants a strong belief like Meera's.
He wants Meera to stop believing the tree.
He wants to cut the old tree down.
He wants Meera to teach him about trees.

why.He wants Meera to stop believing the tre: This thinks he wants to end her belief, but he wants it for himself.
This thinks he hates the tree, but he is talking about belief.
This thinks he wants tree facts, but he wants her kind of faith.

activities.explanation: Right: like the postmaster, he wishes he had the writer's strong faith.

activities.prompt: Ravi's friend believes a lucky stone keeps him safe. Ravi knows it is only a stone. Still he says, 'Keep it in your pocket.' Why does Ravi say this?
options: He wants to keep the friend's belief safe.
He wants to borrow the stone for himself.
He also thinks the stone has real magic.
He wants the friend to buy another stone.

why.He wants to borrow the stone for himself: This thinks Ravi wants the stone, but he is thinking of his friend.
This thinks Ravi believes too, but he knows it is only a stone.
why.He wants the friend to buy another stone: This thinks Ravi wants a sale, but he is protecting a belief.

activities.explanation: Right: like the postmaster, he answers kindly so the faith is not shaken.

activities.prompt: A gift appears on your desk. The note has only one word: 'God'. Your family secretly bought the gift. Why did they write that one word?
options: They want you to think the gift came from God.
They forgot to write their names on the note.
They want you to give the gift back to them.
They think God will bring you more gifts soon.

why.They forgot to write their names on the: This thinks it is a mistake, but the single word was chosen on purpose.
why.They want you to give the gift back to t: This thinks they want it back, but they gave it for you to keep.
why.They think God will bring you more gifts: This thinks it is about future gifts, but the word hides the real givers.

activities.explanation: Right: like the postmaster's signature, the word keeps your faith alive.

lessons.title: Lencho's Second Letter

activities.prompt: What will Lencho do when he opens his letter from God?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Lencho Comes Back
activities.body: On Sunday, Lencho came to the post office earlier than usual. He asked if there was a letter for him. The postman handed him the letter with money inside. Lencho was not surprised to see the money. But when he counted it, he grew angry. He felt some money was missing. So he wrote a second letter to God.
keyPoints: Lencho came to the post office earlier than usual on Sunday.
He was not surprised by the money, but he was angry when he counted it.
He wrote a second letter because he thought some money was missing.
activities.explanation: Lencho trusted God fully, so he never doubted the money would come.

activities.prompt: Lencho got money from God. Why did he get angry instead of happy?
steps: Lencho asked God for money, so he was sure God would send it all.
He believed God never makes a mistake, so the missing money was not God's fault.
So someone between God and him must have taken the money.
That is why he got angry and called the post office workers crooks.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: When did Lencho come to the post office?
options: Later than usual on Sunday
Earlier than usual on Sunday
On a weekday morning
Late on Saturday night
activities.explanation: The lesson says Lencho came earlier than usual that Sunday.

activities.prompt: The postman ______ the letter to Lencho.
activities.hint: Think of what the postman did with the letter.
activities.explanation: Well done! The postman handed him the letter.

activities.prompt: Lencho was surprised when he saw the money.
activities.explanation: Lencho showed no surprise at all. His faith in God was that strong.

activities.prompt: What made Lencho angry?
options: Counting the money he got
Seeing rain on his crops
Waiting for the postman
Reading the postmaster's note
activities.explanation: He became angry when he counted the money, as it seemed less than he asked for.

activities.prompt: Match each person or thing with what happened.
pairs: felt happy about a good deed
activities.explanation: Each one played a part in this part of the story. Great matching!

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: Lencho came to the post office earlier than usual
The postman handed him the letter
Lencho counted the money and grew angry
He wrote the letter with much wrinkling of his brow
He stuck a stamp on it with a blow of his fist
activities.explanation: First the letter came, then the anger, then the writing and the stamp. You got the story's order right!

activities.prompt: Ravi studies hard and is sure he will score full marks. He sees his score is less. He does not blame himself. He thinks the teacher made an error. What does Ravi feel like Lencho?
options: He feels sure that someone else caused the loss.
He feels sorry that he did not study more.
He feels happy that he still got some marks.
He feels shy to ask the teacher about it.

why.He feels sorry that he did not study mor: This is wrong because he is sure he studied well, like Lencho trusted God.
why.He feels happy that he still got some ma: This is wrong because anger, not happiness, comes when you feel cheated.
why.He feels shy to ask the teacher about it: This is wrong because he is bold and sure, not shy, like Lencho.

activities.explanation: Right. Like Lencho, he trusts one side fully, so he blames the other side.

activities.prompt: Lencho saw the money and did not even smile. He just counted it at once. What does this show about him?
options: He expected the money, so he only checked the amount.
He was too scared to take money from anyone.
He did not know how money looked or worked.
He wanted to hide the money from other people.

why.He was too scared to take money from any: This is wrong because fear would show on his face, but nothing did.
why.He did not know how money looked or work: This is wrong because he counts money well, so he knows money.
why.He wanted to hide the money from other p: This is wrong because hiding is not shown; counting is what he does.

activities.explanation: Right. He was sure God would send it, so no surprise, only a check.

activities.prompt: Lencho wrote his new letter with a wrinkled brow. His forehead was folded tight. What was he feeling while writing?
options: He was thinking hard and feeling angry inside.
He was feeling sleepy after his long day.
He was feeling afraid to write to God.
He was feeling bored with writing letters.

why.He was feeling sleepy after his long day: This is wrong because sleep makes eyes close, not the brow wrinkle.
This is wrong because he trusts God, so he is not afraid of God.
why.He was feeling bored with writing letter: This is wrong because boredom looks loose and lazy, not tight and wrinkled.

activities.explanation: Right. A wrinkled brow shows hard thinking, and his words show anger.

activities.prompt: Lencho stuck the stamp with a hard blow of his fist. What does this small act tell us?
options: His anger came out even in a small act.
His hand was weak and needed much force.
He was in a hurry to catch a bus.
He did not know how stamps usually work.

This is wrong because the blow shows feeling, not a weak hand.
This is wrong because no bus or hurry is part of this story.
This is wrong because he had posted a letter before, so he knows stamps.

activities.explanation: Right. A hard blow shows the anger burning inside him.

activities.prompt: The postman gave Lencho the letter. The postmaster felt happy inside. He had done a good deed. What can we guess the postmaster did before this?
options: He helped collect money and put it in the letter.
He wrote a funny story and mailed it to Lencho.
He kept all the letters safe in a big drawer.
He told Lencho that no letter had come for him.

why.He wrote a funny story and mailed it to: This is wrong because a funny story is not a good deed for a poor farmer.
why.He kept all the letters safe in a big dr: This is wrong because keeping letters safe helps no one in need.
why.He told Lencho that no letter had come f: This is wrong because hiding the letter would be a bad deed, not good.

activities.explanation: Right. A good deed with a letter for Lencho means he filled it with help.

activities.prompt: Lencho wrote that only seventy pesos reached him. He called the post office workers crooks. Who did he NOT blame, and why?
options: God, because he believed God cannot make a mistake.
The rain, because it had ruined his whole crop.
His own family, because they counted the money badly.
The stamp, because it was stuck with a hard blow.

why.The rain, because it had ruined his whol: This is wrong because the rain came before, not after, the money arrived.
why.His own family, because they counted the: This is wrong because he counted the money himself, not his family.
why.The stamp, because it was stuck with a h: This is wrong because the stamp only carried the letter, not the money.

activities.explanation: Right. His deep faith in God made him blame only the people in between.

lessons.title: Dust of Snow and Fire and Ice

activities.prompt: Can a tiny snowfall change your whole day?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Short Poems, Two Big Ideas
activities.body: In 'Dust of Snow', a crow shakes snow from a hemlock tree onto the poet. This small moment changes his mood and saves part of a day he had rued. In 'Fire and Ice', some say the world will end in fire, some say in ice. The poet links fire with desire and ice with hate, and says both are strong enough to destroy.
keyPoints: A crow shook dust of snow from a hemlock tree onto the poet.
The snow changed the poet's mood and saved part of a day he had rued.
Fire stands for desire; ice stands for hate. The poet says both could end the world.
activities.explanation: Two tiny poems, one about a happy surprise and one about how the world might end.

activities.prompt: Riya is having a bad day. She spilled ink on her homework and got scolded. On her way home, a bird on a branch shakes some leaves and drops water on her head. She laughs. Why did a small wet surprise change her whole mood?
steps: Riya was sad, so her mind was stuck on bad things, because one bad moment can colour the whole day.
The water drop was small and harmless, so it did not hurt her, because it was just a playful splash from nature.
The surprise made her laugh, so her sad thoughts broke for a moment, because you cannot laugh and feel gloomy at the same time.
So a tiny act of nature can change a mood, because it stops the sad chain and saves the rest of the day.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: In 'Dust of Snow', which bird shook down the dust of snow on the poet?
options: A sparrow
A crow
An owl
A pigeon
activities.explanation: Well done! The poem says a crow shook down the dust of snow.

activities.prompt: The falling snow gave the poet's heart a change of ______.
activities.hint: How you feel inside is your ______.
activities.explanation: Great! The snow changed the poet's mood for the better.

activities.prompt: In 'Fire and Ice', what are the two things some people say will end the world?
options: Fire and ice
Wind and rain
Sun and moon
Day and night
activities.explanation: Correct! Some say fire, and some say ice, will end the world.

activities.prompt: Match each word from the poems with what it stands for.
activities.explanation: Lovely! Fire goes with desire and ice goes with hate in the poem.

activities.prompt: Put these things in the order they happen in 'Dust of Snow'.
items: A crow shakes the hemlock tree
Dust of snow falls on the poet
The poet's mood changes
Part of the day he had rued is saved
activities.explanation: Perfect order! The crow shakes the tree, snow falls, the mood changes, and the day is saved.

activities.prompt: Why does the poet say ice would also be enough to end the world?
options: Because he knows enough of hate
Because ice is very cold
Because ice melts quickly
Because he loves winter
activities.explanation: Well thought! If the world perished twice, the poet knows enough of hate, so ice would do the job.

activities.prompt: Aman feels angry all morning. A crow shakes snow off a hemlock tree. The cold dust falls on him. He smiles. What most likely happened to his mood?
options: It changed from bad to better.
It changed from good to bad.
It stayed exactly the same.
It became worse than before.

He thinks any surprise must be bad, but the smile shows the opposite.
He thinks small events cannot change feelings, but the poem says they can.
He links snow with more sadness, missing that Aman smiled.

activities.explanation: Right. The snow changed his mood, and his smile shows it turned better.

activities.prompt: The snow fell from a hemlock tree, not from a merry tree. The poet still felt better. What does this suggest?
options: A sad-looking thing can bring joy.
Only happy trees can help people.
The poet did not notice the tree.
Snow feels the same on everyone.

He thinks the tree type must be cheerful, but the poem shows otherwise.
He thinks the poet ignored the tree, but the poet names it clearly.
He talks about people in general, not what this moment suggests.

activities.explanation: Right. The hemlock is a gloomy tree, yet it lifted his mood.

activities.prompt: Meera rued wasting her whole Sunday. By evening, one kind message saved part of the day for her. What does 'saved part of the day' mean here?
options: Some of the day turned good.
She stored the day in a box.
She got one extra free day.
She forgot the day completely.

She takes the word 'saved' in its money-and-things sense.
She thinks 'saved' means gaining more time, which is not the idea.
She thinks saving means erasing, but the day was partly repaired.

activities.explanation: Right. Part of the day stopped being wasted and became good.

activities.prompt: Two friends argue about how a story world ends. One says fire, one says ice. Both feel very sure. What does this argument show about people?
options: People hold different strong beliefs.
People always agree about endings.
People never think about endings.
People only care about real fires.

He thinks agreement is normal, but the poem shows two sides.
He thinks nobody thinks about it, but both friends clearly do.
He takes the word 'fire' too literally, missing the bigger idea.

activities.explanation: Right. Each friend favours one idea, just like people favour fire or ice.

activities.prompt: The poet tasted desire, so he sides with fire. What does 'tasted desire' suggest about him?
options: He has felt strong wanting himself.
He has eaten food cooked on fire.
He has never felt any emotion.
He has watched fire burn a house.

He takes 'tasted' and 'fire' as real food and real flames.
He thinks the poet is cold, but he clearly knows desire inside.
He brings in a fire accident, which is not the point at all.

activities.explanation: Right. He speaks from his own experience of wanting things badly.

activities.prompt: The poet knows enough of hate, so ice would also be enough to destroy. Why does he say ice is 'great' too?
options: Cold hate can destroy just like fire.
Ice is great for cooling hot drinks.
Hate makes people feel warm inside.
Ice is stronger than any real fire.

He thinks of ice in the kitchen, missing its meaning of hate.
He mixes up the two ideas, since hate matches cold, not warmth.
He compares the powers literally, but the poet means both are enough.

activities.explanation: Right. Hate, like ice, is cold, and it can destroy just as well.

activities.context: Ramesh, a farmer like Lencho in the story, loses his crops and decides to write a letter asking for help, just as Lencho wrote to God asking for a hundred pesos. His friend tells him that faith can move mountains, but Ramesh wonders what he should really put his faith in. His cousin, who lives in another town, promises to send him money through the post office, which is one cheap way to send money.
activities.prompt: Ramesh's cousin goes to the post office to send the money. What will most likely happen next at the counter?
options: The counter clerk will give him a form to fill in before the money can be sent
The counter clerk will hand over the money directly to Ramesh in his village
The post office will refuse to send money because crops were ruined
The cousin will have to write a letter to God before sending anything

why.The counter clerk will hand over the mon: Wrong: the post office sends money to the receiver, it cannot hand cash to someone in another village
why.The post office will refuse to send mone: Wrong: a ruined crop does not stop the post office from sending money
why.The cousin will have to write a letter t: Wrong: writing to God is what Lencho did in the story, not a step in sending money

activities.explanation: Correct: at the counter the clerk provides the money order form, which must be filled in before sending

activities.context: Ramesh, a farmer like Lencho in the story, loses his crops and decides to write a letter asking for help, just as Lencho wrote to God asking for a hundred pesos. His friend tells him that faith can move mountains, but Ramesh wonders what he should really put his faith in. His cousin, who lives in another town, promises to send him money through the post office, which is one cheap way to send money.
activities.prompt: If Ramesh's cousin fills the money order form carelessly and leaves out the receiver's details, what is the most likely result?
options: The money will still reach Ramesh because the sender's part is complete
The official use part of the form will be filled by Ramesh himself
The money may not reach Ramesh, and the acknowledgement may not be returned properly
The post office will send the money only to God instead

why.The money will still reach Ramesh becaus: Wrong: the receiver's details are essential; the sender's part alone cannot deliver the money
why.The official use part of the form will b: Wrong: the official use part is meant for the post office staff, not for the receiver
why.The post office will send the money only: Wrong: the post office delivers to people, and the story only asks whether Lencho's letter reaches God

activities.explanation: Correct: without correct receiver details the money order cannot be delivered and the acknowledgement cannot come back properly

activities.context: Ramesh, a farmer like Lencho in the story, loses his crops and decides to write a letter asking for help, just as Lencho wrote to God asking for a hundred pesos. His friend tells him that faith can move mountains, but Ramesh wonders what he should really put his faith in. His cousin, who lives in another town, promises to send him money through the post office, which is one cheap way to send money.
activities.prompt: Ramesh's cousin wants to send money for a magazine subscription and also to a friend. Why is the post office a sensible choice in this case?
options: Because faith can move mountains faster than any post office
Because it is one cheap way to send money to a relative or a friend
Because the counterfoil proves that God has received the money
Because the acknowledgement section asks whether Lencho's letter reached God

why.Because faith can move mountains faster: Wrong: faith moving mountains is an idea from the story, not a reason for choosing the post office
why.Because the counterfoil proves that God: Wrong: the counterfoil is the sender's receipt, not proof that God received anything
why.Because the acknowledgement section asks: Wrong: the acknowledgement is a part of the form, not a question about Lencho's letter

activities.explanation: Correct: the post office is a cheap way to send money, which suits sending it for a subscription or to a friend

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Lencho writes a letter to God when his crops are ruined.
Reason (R): Lencho asks God for a hundred pesos because his crops are ruined.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the request for a hundred pesos is directly linked to his ruined crops.

activities.prompt: Explain why the story of Lencho begins with the idea that faith can move mountains, and what question the chapter asks about his letter.
activities.answer: The story begins with the saying that faith can move mountains because it wants us to think about what we should put our faith in. Lencho is a farmer whose crops are ruined, and in his faith he writes a letter to God asking for a hundred pesos. The chapter then asks two important questions: whether Lencho's letter actually reaches God, and whether God sends him the money. These questions make readers think about faith in real life.
points: Mentions the saying that faith can move mountains
States the chapter asks what we should put our faith in
Says Lencho is a farmer whose crops are ruined and he asks for a hundred pesos
Gives both questions: does the letter reach God, and does God send money
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Lencho's house stood alone on the crest of a low hill, the only one in the entire valley. From that height he could see the river and his field of ripe corn, which he knew intimately. The earth needed a downpour, or at least a shower. During the meal, big drops of rain began to fall, and huge mountains of clouds could be seen approaching. Lencho called the raindrops new coins, but very large hailstones began to fall with the rain. The boys ran out to collect the frozen pearls while the hail rained for an hour on the house.
activities.prompt: Why did Lencho think of the falling raindrops as 'new coins'?
options: Because he expected the rain to make his ripe corn yield a good harvest, which would bring him money
Because he believed coins were falling from the clouds along with the rain
Because he was being paid in silver for letting the clouds pass over his field
Because he wanted to save the rainwater and sell it like treasure

why.Because he believed coins were falling f: Wrong: he was using a comparison about value, not literally describing coins falling
why.Because he was being paid in silver for: Wrong: nothing in the situation suggests any payment or deal connected to the clouds
why.Because he wanted to save the rainwater: Wrong: his concern was the growing corn, not storing or selling water

activities.explanation: Correct: for a farmer whose corn was ripe and whose land needed rain, rain directly meant a good crop and income

activities.context: Lencho's house stood alone on the crest of a low hill, the only one in the entire valley. From that height he could see the river and his field of ripe corn, which he knew intimately. The earth needed a downpour, or at least a shower. During the meal, big drops of rain began to fall, and huge mountains of clouds could be seen approaching. Lencho called the raindrops new coins, but very large hailstones began to fall with the rain. The boys ran out to collect the frozen pearls while the hail rained for an hour on the house.
activities.prompt: After an hour of very large hailstones falling on the valley, what would most likely happen to the field of ripe corn?
options: The corn would ripen faster because hailstones add coolness to the crop
The corn would be badly damaged, since large hail falling for so long strikes the plants again and again
The corn would remain untouched because the house on the hill shielded the whole valley
The corn would be washed away by the river rather than harmed by the hail

why.The corn would ripen faster because hail: Wrong: hail is ice striking the plants; it does not help crops ripen
why.The corn would remain untouched because: Wrong: the house sits on the hill; it cannot cover an entire open valley
why.The corn would be washed away by the riv: Wrong: the danger described is the hail from above, not the river flooding the field

activities.explanation: Correct: large hailstones falling steadily for an hour would batter and destroy standing ripe corn

activities.context: Lencho's house stood alone on the crest of a low hill, the only one in the entire valley. From that height he could see the river and his field of ripe corn, which he knew intimately. The earth needed a downpour, or at least a shower. During the meal, big drops of rain began to fall, and huge mountains of clouds could be seen approaching. Lencho called the raindrops new coins, but very large hailstones began to fall with the rain. The boys ran out to collect the frozen pearls while the hail rained for an hour on the house.
activities.prompt: The hail went on raining for a full hour on the house. What was the wisest thing for the boys to do once the hailstones grew very large?
options: Keep collecting the frozen pearls quickly before they melted
Run inside and stay under shelter until the hail stopped
Climb to the crest of the hill to watch the clouds more closely
Walk down to the river to see if the water was rising

why.Keep collecting the frozen pearls quickl: Wrong: staying outside under large falling hailstones is dangerous, however interesting the ice looks
why.Climb to the crest of the hill to watch: Wrong: an open hilltop is the worst place to stand under falling ice
why.Walk down to the river to see if the wat: Wrong: the river is not the danger here; the falling hailstones are

activities.explanation: Correct: with very large hailstones falling for an hour, safety means going indoors and waiting

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The hailstorm could destroy Lencho's field of ripe corn.
Reason (R): Very large hailstones fell with the rain, and the hail rained for an hour on the house.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Large hailstones falling for a whole hour would batter the ripe corn, so the reason correctly explains the assertion.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The earth in the valley needed water at that time.
Reason (R): The river flowing below the hill gave the corn all the water it needed.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true because the earth needed a downpour or at least a shower, but the reason is false since the need for rain shows the river was not enough.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between the rain Lencho welcomed during the meal and the hail that followed, in terms of what each meant for his field?
activities.answer: The rain that began during the meal was what the earth needed, a downpour or at least a shower, and it fell from the huge mountains of clouds approaching the valley. For Lencho, who knew his fields intimately and grew ripe corn, this rain was welcome and promising, like new coins. The hail was different in kind, not just amount: very large hailstones fell with the rain, the boys ran out to collect the frozen pearls, and the hail rained for an hour on the house. Instead of feeding the crop, such hail strikes and breaks it, so it threatened the very harvest the rain had promised.
points: Rain matched the earth's need for a downpour or at least a shower
Rain was welcomed as promising, like new coins, for the ripe corn
Hail was very large, fell with the rain, and lasted an hour on the house
Hail damages the standing crop instead of nourishing it
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In the solitary house on the hill, every heart held a single hope after the crops were ruined. All through the night Lencho, an ox of a man, thought only of that one hope. He believed God's eyes see everything, and he knew how to write. At daybreak on Sunday he began to write a letter to God, asking for a hundred pesos because he needed the money to sow his field again. He wrote 'To God' on the envelope, placed a stamp, and dropped the letter into the mailbox.
activities.prompt: Lencho addressed the envelope to God and posted it himself. What is the most likely reason he did not ask a neighbour to deliver it instead?
options: He believed that God's eyes see everything, so a letter was a direct way to reach Him
He was too lazy to walk to his neighbour's house that Sunday morning
He wanted the neighbour to read the letter before sending it on
He did not know how to write, so he needed the neighbour's help

why.He was too lazy to walk to his neighbour: Wrong: nothing suggests laziness; he rose at daybreak to write, showing effort, not idleness.
why.He wanted the neighbour to read the lett: Wrong: he trusted God alone with his need; letting a neighbour read it would go against that trust.
why.He did not know how to write, so he need: Wrong: the facts clearly say he knew how to write, so help with writing was not needed.

activities.explanation: Correct: his faith that God sees everything made a letter to God seem the natural, direct solution.

activities.context: In the solitary house on the hill, every heart held a single hope after the crops were ruined. All through the night Lencho, an ox of a man, thought only of that one hope. He believed God's eyes see everything, and he knew how to write. At daybreak on Sunday he began to write a letter to God, asking for a hundred pesos because he needed the money to sow his field again. He wrote 'To God' on the envelope, placed a stamp, and dropped the letter into the mailbox.
activities.prompt: Suppose Lencho had believed that no one dies of hunger, yet had lost all hope during the night. What would most likely have happened the next morning?
options: He would still have written the letter, since hope was what drove him to act
He would probably not have written the letter, because the single hope was what kept the plan alive all night
He would have written a longer letter asking for more than a hundred pesos
He would have asked his family to write the letter for him instead

why.He would still have written the letter,: Wrong: without hope he would have no reason to act; the belief alone would not push him to write.
why.He would have written a longer letter as: Wrong: the amount he asked for came from his need to sow the field again, which would not change just because hope was lost.
why.He would have asked his family to write: Wrong: he knew how to write himself, so there was no need for anyone else to write it.

activities.explanation: Correct: it was the one hope he thought of all through the night that led directly to the letter at daybreak.

activities.context: In the solitary house on the hill, every heart held a single hope after the crops were ruined. All through the night Lencho, an ox of a man, thought only of that one hope. He believed God's eyes see everything, and he knew how to write. At daybreak on Sunday he began to write a letter to God, asking for a hundred pesos because he needed the money to sow his field again. He wrote 'To God' on the envelope, placed a stamp, and dropped the letter into the mailbox.
activities.prompt: Lencho asked for a hundred pesos. If his only need had been food for the family to eat, rather than sowing the field again, how would his letter most likely have been different?
options: He would not have written to God at all, since God only helps with farming
He would have asked for a different amount, because the hundred pesos was tied to his need to sow his field again
He would have written the letter on a weekday instead of Sunday at daybreak
He would have left the envelope unaddressed, since the purpose had changed

why.He would not have written to God at all,: Wrong: his faith in God was not limited to farming; he believed God's eyes see everything.
why.He would have written the letter on a we: Wrong: the timing came from his habit of writing at daybreak on Sunday, not from the purpose of the money.
why.He would have left the envelope unaddres: Wrong: he wrote 'To God' on the envelope because of his faith, which would remain whatever the money was for.

activities.explanation: Correct: the hundred pesos was the sum he needed to sow his field again, so a different need would mean a different request.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Lencho began writing his letter at daybreak on Sunday.
Reason (R): Lencho knew how to write and believed God's eyes see everything.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but knowing how to write and believing in God's sight do not explain why he chose that particular morning to begin.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Lencho asked for a hundred pesos so that he could buy a new house for his family.
Reason (R): Lencho needed the money to sow his field again.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because the money was for sowing his field again, while the reason given is true.

activities.prompt: Explain why the letter was described as a letter to God and what this shows about Lencho's faith.
activities.answer: The letter was addressed 'To God' on the envelope, and Lencho placed a stamp and dropped it into the mailbox like any ordinary letter. This shows that his faith was simple and complete: he believed God's eyes see everything, so he trusted that God would read his words and answer them. He asked for a hundred pesos because he needed the money to sow his field again, and he never doubted that his request would reach the right reader.
points: He wrote 'To God' on the envelope
He stamped it and posted it in the mailbox
He believed God's eyes see everything
He asked for a hundred pesos to sow his field again
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A postman handed his boss a letter addressed to a place the postman had never come across in his whole career. The postmaster chuckled at first, but his smile soon faded. Wishing he had the writer's kind of faith, he resolved to reply so that the belief would not be shaken. Goodwill, ink and paper alone would not be enough, so he asked the employees for money, gave part of his own salary, and friends gave for charity. Still he could not gather the hundred pesos, sent only a little more than half, and signed the letter with the single word God.
activities.prompt: Why did the postmaster's laughter die away as he read the letter?
options: He realised the writer's belief was deep and sincere, and he began to respect it.
He was afraid the letter would get him into trouble with his seniors.
He thought the address on the envelope had been written wrongly on purpose.
He suddenly remembered he had left an urgent task unfinished.

why.He was afraid the letter would get him i: Fear of seniors is never suggested; his concern was with the letter's content, not his job.
why.He thought the address on the envelope h: The address was simply one the postman had never known; nothing points to deliberate error.
why.He suddenly remembered he had left an ur: Personal distraction is invented and does not fit the change from amusement to seriousness.

activities.explanation: Correct: his seriousness grew out of genuine admiration for the writer's faith, which he himself wished he had.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: A Letter to God

activities.prompt: Who was Lencho in the story?
options: A postman
A farmer
A postmaster
A shopkeeper
activities.explanation: Lencho was a farmer whose crops were ruined. Well done if you remembered him!

activities.prompt: In his letter, Lencho asked God for ______ pesos.
activities.hint: Think of the big sum he wrote in his letter.
activities.explanation: Lencho asked for a hundred pesos. That was the money he needed.

activities.prompt: Lencho compared the falling raindrops to new coins.
activities.explanation: Yes! Lencho said the raindrops were new coins, because rain meant good crops.

activities.prompt: Put these events from the story in the right order.
items: Hail rained for an hour and ruined the crop
All night Lencho thought of his one hope
On Sunday at daybreak he wrote a letter to God
He put a stamp on it and dropped it in the mailbox
The postman showed the letter to his boss
activities.explanation: Perfect order! The hail came first, then hope, then the letter, then the post office.

activities.prompt: Why did the postmaster decide to answer Lencho's letter?
options: So Lencho would write again
So he could laugh at the letter
So Lencho's faith would not be shaken
So the post office would earn money
activities.explanation: The postmaster did not want to shake the writer's faith. What a kind thought!

activities.prompt: The postman had often delivered letters to that address before.
activities.explanation: Not true! The postman had never known that address in his whole career.

activities.prompt: In his second letter, Lencho wrote that only ______ pesos had reached him.
activities.hint: It was a little more than half of what he had asked for.
activities.explanation: Lencho counted the money and wrote that only seventy pesos reached him.

activities.prompt: Lencho believed God could not make a mistake. So whom did he blame for the missing money?
options: The post office employees
His own sons
The people at the bank
The man at the market
activities.explanation: Lencho trusted God fully, so he blamed the post office employees and called them crooks.

activities.prompt: In the poem, from which tree did the dust of snow fall on the poet?
options: An oak tree
A hemlock tree
A mango tree
A pine tree
activities.explanation: A crow shook the dust of snow from a hemlock tree. It changed the poet's mood!

boss.sceneCaption: A stamp vending machine built into the counter of a post office, dispensing six denominations of stamps.

chapters.title: Nelson Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom
chapters.summary: In this chapter: before you read and the news item; the inauguration day and ceremony; mandela's speech at the inauguration; military display, anthems and sense of history.

lessons.title: Before You Read and the News Item

activities.prompt: How did a man who spent 30 years in prison become a president?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A New Dawn for South Africa
activities.body: For many years, South Africa had a system called apartheid. It separated people by the colour of their skin. Nelson Mandela and his party, the ANC, fought against it all their lives. Mandela even spent thirty years in prison. In 1994, democratic elections were held. Mandela became the first black President of a new nation.
keyPoints: Apartheid separated people by race.
Mandela and the ANC fought apartheid for a lifetime.
In 1994, Mandela became the first black President.
activities.explanation: This lesson opens with the story of a nation choosing freedom.

activities.prompt: A new boy joins your class after years at a school where children sat in separate rows by skin colour. On his first day, everyone votes together to pick a class captain. Why does his eyes fill with tears when the vote is counted?
steps: At his old school, children were separated by skin colour, so he never felt equal to others.
Being separated for years makes a person feel invisible and unheard.
In the vote, every child's choice counted the same, no matter their skin colour.
So his tears show joy, because a fair vote proves he finally belongs.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: The lesson you are about to read comes from a famous book. What is it?
options: A newspaper report about sports
Mandela's autobiography, Long Walk to Freedom
A book of short stories
A letter to a friend
activities.explanation: Well done! The extract is taken from Mandela's own life story, Long Walk to Freedom.

activities.prompt: Democratic elections were held in South Africa in ______.
activities.hint: Think of the year the news item talks about.
activities.explanation: Yes! 1994 was the year of South Africa's first democratic elections.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what the lesson says about it.
pairs: A system that separated people by race
activities.explanation: Great matching! You have remembered the key details of the lesson.

activities.prompt: In the first democratic elections, Mandela's ANC party won ______ of the 400 seats.
activities.hint: It is more than half of 400.
activities.explanation: Right! The ANC won 252 seats, a clear majority in the elections.

activities.prompt: Put these events from the lesson in the order they happened.
items: Mandela and the ANC fought apartheid
Mandela spent thirty years in prison
Democratic elections were held in 1994
Mandela became the first black President
The inauguration was held in Pretoria
activities.explanation: Perfect order! The long fight led to prison, then elections, then President, then the big inauguration day.

activities.prompt: Mandela's party fought a system that separated people by race for his whole life. He also lost thirty years locked in prison. He kept fighting anyway. What does this show about him?
options: He was too stubborn to admit his fight was hopeless.
He cared so much about equality that he never gave up.
He enjoyed prison life more than life outside it.
He fought only because his party ordered him to fight.

why.He was too stubborn to admit his fight w: This mistakes strong belief for foolish stubbornness.
why.He enjoyed prison life more than life ou: This wrongly imagines prison was pleasant for him.
why.He fought only because his party ordered: This wrongly makes him a follower, not a leader with his own beliefs.

activities.explanation: Right: a lifetime of fighting, even through thirty lost years, shows deep commitment to equality.

activities.prompt: A country changed its rules so every adult could vote for the first time. A party won most of the four hundred seats. The party's leader then became the head of the nation. Why did he become the head?
options: Because he had spent the longest time in prison.
Because the old rulers chose him as their favourite.
Because his party won the most seats in the fair vote.
Because he was the oldest leader in the whole country.

why.Because he had spent the longest time in: Prison time shows his sacrifice, but it is not how leaders are chosen.
why.Because the old rulers chose him as thei: This wrongly thinks the old unfair rulers still held power.
why.Because he was the oldest leader in the: Age has nothing to do with winning an election.

activities.explanation: Right: in a fair election, the party with most seats forms the government.

activities.prompt: A news report says a new leader took charge after more than three hundred years of rule by one group only. People of every race sang and danced together at the ceremony. How did the ordinary people most likely feel?
options: Nervous, because they feared the new leader would fail.
Angry, because the ceremony lasted too long for them.
Sleepy, because the ceremony happened early in the morning.
Joyful, because a long unfair time had finally ended.

why.Nervous, because they feared the new lea: The singing and dancing show happiness, not fear.
why.Angry, because the ceremony lasted too l: Anger does not match people singing and dancing with joy.
why.Sleepy, because the ceremony happened ea: The report never says the time of day, and dancing shows excitement.

activities.explanation: Right: singing and dancing of all races shows joy that centuries of unfair rule ended.

activities.prompt: Before 1994, one group of people ruled for over three centuries and kept others out of power. Then a fair vote was held and a Black leader won. Why was his win called historic?
options: Because it was the first time a Black person led that nation.
Because it was the first time the ceremony was held outdoors.
Because it was the first time the news reported a vote.
Because it was the first time the leader wore a suit.

why.Because it was the first time the ceremo: The place of the ceremony does not make an event historic.
why.Because it was the first time the news r: News reports happened before too; the change of power is what matters.
why.Because it was the first time the leader: Clothes have nothing to do with why the day made history.

activities.explanation: Right: after centuries of White rule, the first Black President was a first in history.

lessons.sceneAlt: Photographs showing the inauguration of Nelson Mandela as President of the Republic of South Africa.
lessons.sceneCaption: Photographs of the inauguration of Nelson Mandela as President of the Republic of South Africa on 10 May 1994.

lessons.title: The Inauguration Day and Ceremony

activities.prompt: What made a special day in South Africa feel so magical and hopeful?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Bright New Day for South Africa
activities.body: Tenth May dawned bright and clear. Dignitaries and world leaders came to pay their respects before the inauguration. It was the largest gathering ever of international leaders on South African soil. The ceremonies took place in the sandstone amphitheatre of the Union Buildings in Pretoria. There, South Africa's first democratic, non-racial government was installed.
keyPoints: Tenth May dawned bright and clear.
World leaders came before the inauguration.
The ceremony was at the Union Buildings in Pretoria.
It was the largest gathering of international leaders on South African soil.
activities.explanation: This lesson shows how a special day began a new government for all the people.

activities.prompt: The ceremony happened at the Union Buildings. For years, only white people held power there. Now people of all colours came there. Why was this place a special choice for the big day?
steps: The Union Buildings were the seat of white supremacy, so they stood for unfair rule.
The inauguration made South Africa's first democratic, non-racial government, so the old unfair rule was ending.
A rainbow gathering of different colours and nations met there, so the place now showed everyone together.
So the place was chosen because its meaning changed: from power for a few to power for all.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: From One Rule to All the People
activities.body: For decades, the Union Buildings had been the seat of white supremacy. Now the same place held a rainbow gathering of different colours and nations. This was for the installation of South Africa's first democratic, non-racial government. The old seat of unfair rule became the home of a fair new beginning.
keyPoints: The Union Buildings were once the seat of white supremacy.
Now they held a rainbow gathering of colours and nations.
A democratic, non-racial government was installed there.
activities.explanation: The same walls that once held unfair power now welcomed everyone.

activities.prompt: Where did the inauguration ceremonies take place?
options: At a market in Johannesburg
At the Union Buildings in Pretoria
On a beach near Cape Town
At a school in Soweto
activities.explanation: The ceremonies took place in the sandstone amphitheatre formed by the Union Buildings in Pretoria.

activities.prompt: Mandela was accompanied on this special day by his daughter ______.
activities.hint: Her name begins with the letter Z.
activities.explanation: Mandela's daughter Zenani was by his side on inauguration day.

activities.prompt: Who was sworn in first as second deputy president?
options: Thabo Mbeki
Zenani
Mr de Klerk
A world leader
activities.explanation: Mr de Klerk was sworn in first, as second deputy president.

activities.prompt: Match each person to what the lesson says about them.
pairs: Sworn in as second deputy president
Sworn in as first deputy president
activities.explanation: Each person had a special part to play on inauguration day.

activities.prompt: Put these moments of the ceremony in the order they happened.
items: Mr de Klerk was sworn in as second deputy president
Thabo Mbeki was sworn in as first deputy president
Mandela pledged to obey and uphold the Constitution
activities.explanation: First de Klerk took his oath, then Mbeki, and then Mandela made his pledge.

activities.prompt: What did Mandela pledge to do on inauguration day?
options: To obey and uphold the Constitution
To travel to visit world leaders
To build a new amphitheatre
To invite more dignitaries
activities.explanation: Mandela pledged to obey and uphold the Constitution and to devote himself to the well-being of the Republic and its people.

activities.prompt: Many important visitors kept coming to Mandela. They came before the inauguration day. He felt happy about it. What does 'besieged' mean here?
options: He was surrounded by many visitors
He was attacked by soldiers
He was locked inside his home
He was left alone by everyone

why.He was attacked by soldiers: Wrong: this takes the army meaning of the word, not the friendly one.
why.He was locked inside his home: Wrong: being kept inside is a prison idea, not a crowd of guests.
why.He was left alone by everyone: Wrong: this is the opposite; many people came, not none.

activities.explanation: Right: 'besieged' means crowded around, and 'pleasantly' shows he liked it.

activities.prompt: The ceremony was at the Union Buildings. For years, only white people held power there. Now all colours and nations gathered there. How did the place feel different that day?
options: It looked smaller than before
The old unfair rule had ended there
It became a school for children
It was closed to black people

why.It looked smaller than before: Wrong: the size of the buildings is not the point of the change.
why.It became a school for children: Wrong: nothing says it changed into a school.
why.It was closed to black people: Wrong: this was the old past, not the new day.

activities.explanation: Right: a seat of white supremacy now held a rainbow gathering, so unfair rule ended.

activities.prompt: De Klerk was sworn in as second deputy president. Mbeki was sworn in as first deputy president. Mandela was sworn in after them. What can we guess about Mandela's new job?
options: It was the smallest job
He had no real job
It was the same as de Klerk's
It was the highest job

why.It was the smallest job: Wrong: the deputies come first, so Mandela's job is not the smallest.
why.He had no real job: Wrong: he took a pledge, so he clearly had a big job.
why.It was the same as de Klerk's: Wrong: de Klerk was second deputy, so Mandela's job was higher.

activities.explanation: Right: the two deputies were sworn in first, so the top job came last, Mandela's.

activities.prompt: Mandela promised to obey the Constitution. He promised to work for the people's well-being. He said this at the inauguration. What does this promise show about him?
options: He wants to serve everyone fairly
He wants to rule alone
He is afraid of going to jail
He cares only about himself

why.He wants to rule alone: Wrong: ruling alone breaks the Constitution, which he promised to obey.
why.He is afraid of going to jail: Wrong: fear is not in the promise; it is about duty, not fear.
why.He cares only about himself: Wrong: the promise is about the people's well-being, not his own.

activities.explanation: Right: obeying the Constitution and working for the people show fair service to all.

activities.prompt: People of many colours and nations came together. The writer called the crowd a 'rainbow gathering'. The day was bright and clear. What does 'rainbow' mean here?
options: A sky after the rain
Only colourful clothes
Many different people together
A painting on a wall

why.A sky after the rain: Wrong: this is the weather meaning, not the meaning about people.
why.Only colourful clothes: Wrong: clothes are not mentioned; the people themselves were different.
why.A painting on a wall: Wrong: a painting is a picture, not a living crowd.

activities.explanation: Right: a rainbow has many colours, so it means many kinds of people together.

lessons.sceneAlt: Photographs showing Nelson Mandela arriving at his presidential inauguration ceremony in Pretoria on 10 May 1994.
lessons.sceneCaption: Nelson Mandela arrives at his inaugural ceremony in Pretoria on 10 May 1994, attended by world leaders.
