lessons.title: Mandela's Speech at the Inauguration

activities.prompt: What did a man once jailed for 27 years say on his first day as president?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Speech Full of Hope
activities.body: On the day he became leader, Mandela gave a speech to the whole world. He said a long human disaster was finally over. His people had won political emancipation, which means freedom to take part in public life. He called it a common victory for justice, peace and human dignity. He promised to fight poverty and unfair treatment. He ended with the words, 'Let freedom reign.'
keyPoints: Mandela said an extraordinary human disaster had lasted too long.
He said they had at last achieved their political emancipation.
He called the day a common victory for justice, peace and human dignity.
He ended with 'Let freedom reign. God bless Africa!'
activities.explanation: This speech turned a hard past into a bright promise for the future.

activities.prompt: A boy was punished for months for something he never did. One day the school says sorry and gives him a prize on stage. Why does he cry even though he is happy?
steps: He cried because the long unfair time made the happy day feel very big.
The prize feels sweet because he remembers the pain that came before it.
Freedom feels precious only to someone who once lived without it.
So joy after long suffering can bring tears, not just smiles.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did Mandela call the day of the inauguration?
options: A common victory for justice, peace and human dignity
A private gift for his own people only
A sad end to a long and lonely fight
A small step that did not matter much
activities.explanation: Well done! Mandela said the day belonged to everyone who wanted fairness and peace.

activities.prompt: Mandela ended his speech with the words, 'Let freedom ______.'
activities.hint: It means to rule like a king.
activities.explanation: Correct! 'Reign' means to rule, so freedom would rule over the land.

activities.prompt: What did Mandela and his people pledge to liberate all people from?
options: The continuing bondage of poverty and discrimination
The duty to speak more than one language
The need to travel to other countries
The habit of forgetting old friendships
activities.explanation: Great thinking! A pledge is a solemn promise, and this one was about ending suffering and unfair treatment.

activities.prompt: Match each phrase from the speech to what it means.
pairs: given glory and hope by all present
hosting the nations of the world on their own soil
would never again see one person oppressing another
activities.explanation: Lovely work! Each phrase carries a special idea from Mandela's speech.

activities.prompt: Put these ideas from the speech in order, from past to future.
items: An extraordinary human disaster lasted too long.
They had at last achieved their political emancipation.
They pledged to liberate all people from bondage.
Let freedom reign. God bless Africa!
activities.explanation: Perfect order! The speech moves from the sad past, to freedom won, to promises ahead, and ends with a blessing.

activities.prompt: According to Mandela, what kind of society must be born?
options: One that all humanity will be proud of
One that keeps its doors closed to guests
One that remembers only its own past pain
One that lets the sun set on its achievements
activities.explanation: Brilliant! Mandela dreamed of a society that would make every person on Earth feel proud.

activities.prompt: A team lost every match for ten years. Then they win the final. The captain says, 'This disaster lasted too long.' How does the captain feel about the win?
options: It feels bigger because the losing went on so long
It feels small because one match does not matter
It feels sad because the old matches are gone
It feels strange because the team did not practise

why.It feels small because one match does no: This thinks the captain does not care about the win at all.
why.It feels sad because the old matches are: This mixes sadness about the past with joy about the win.
why.It feels strange because the team did no: This adds a new reason that the speech never talks about.

activities.explanation: Right. Long suffering makes the happy moment feel much greater.

activities.prompt: A girl was not allowed inside the library for years. Now she cuts the ribbon to open it. She says, 'Not so long ago, I was an outsider here.' Why does she say this?
options: To show how far she has come from being shut out
To complain that the library is still closed to her
To warn the guests that the library is dangerous
To prove she reads more books than anyone else

why.To complain that the library is still cl: This thinks she is still shut out, but she is opening it now.
why.To warn the guests that the library is d: This thinks she is giving a warning, but she is celebrating.
why.To prove she reads more books than anyon: This thinks she is boasting, but she is remembering her past.

activities.explanation: Right. She contrasts her old rejection with her new welcome.

activities.prompt: A village gets clean water for the first time. The leader says, 'This is a common victory for everyone.' What does 'common' mean here?
options: Shared by all the people of the village
Ordinary and not worth celebrating
Cheap and easy to get
Very rare and special

why.Ordinary and not worth celebrating: This thinks common means plain, but here it means shared.
why.Cheap and easy to get: This thinks common means low cost, which is not the meaning here.
why.Very rare and special: This thinks common means rare, which is the opposite meaning.

activities.explanation: Right. A common victory belongs to everyone together.

activities.prompt: A country wins freedom but many people are still poor and hungry. Its new leader says, 'Our work has only begun.' What does the leader mean?
options: Freedom must also end poverty and unfair treatment
The fight for freedom must start again from zero
The people should stop hoping for a better life
The leader wants to give power to another country

why.The fight for freedom must start again f: This thinks political freedom was lost, but it was achieved.
why.The people should stop hoping for a bett: This thinks the leader has given up, but he is promising more work.
why.The leader wants to give power to anothe: This thinks the leader is giving away power, which he never says.

activities.explanation: Right. Political freedom is only the first step; deeper chains remain.

activities.prompt: A student says, 'The sun shall never set on our school's achievement.' What feeling is behind these words?
options: The achievement will shine forever without ending
The school will close when the sun goes down
The achievement is too small to be seen
The sun is angry with the school

why.The school will close when the sun goes: This takes the words about the sun too literally.
why.The achievement is too small to be seen: This thinks the achievement is small, but the words praise it.
why.The sun is angry with the school: This thinks the sun is a real angry thing, not a picture.

activities.explanation: Right. The sun never setting means the glory will never end.

activities.prompt: A country invites leaders from all over the world to its freedom day. The host says, 'You have given glory to our newborn liberty by coming.' Why does he thank them?
options: Their presence makes the new freedom look honoured
They paid money to buy the country's freedom
They came to take the country's land away
They came to teach the people a new language

why.They paid money to buy the country's fre: This thinks freedom was bought, but the guests only came.
why.They came to take the country's land awa: This thinks the guests are enemies, but they are honoured guests.
why.They came to teach the people a new lang: This thinks the visit is a lesson, but it is a celebration.

activities.explanation: Right. The guests' presence adds honour to the new liberty.

lessons.sceneAlt: A view of the Union Buildings in Pretoria, South Africa, the landmark where Mandela's inauguration was held.
lessons.sceneCaption: The Union Buildings in Pretoria, South Africa, the landmark venue of Nelson Mandela's inauguration.

lessons.title: Military Display, Anthems and Sense of History

activities.prompt: Why would soldiers who once jailed a leader now salute him?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Sky Full of Jets
activities.body: On the big day, South African jets, helicopters and troop carriers flew over the Union Buildings in perfect formation. It was a show of pinpoint precision and military force. But it was more than that. It showed that the army was loyal to democracy. The top generals and police leaders saluted Mandela and promised their loyalty. Mandela remembered that not long before, they would have arrested him.
keyPoints: Jets, helicopters and troop carriers flew in perfect formation.
The display showed the military's loyalty to democracy.
Generals who once might have arrested Mandela now saluted him.
activities.explanation: The sky roared with planes, but the real message was loyalty to the new democracy.

activities.prompt: Your school's old rival team visits your sports day. Their captain shakes your hand and promises fair play. You remember that last year this same captain cheated against you. Why does this handshake feel so special?
steps: The captain was your enemy before, so his promise could be fake.
But he came in front of everyone, so breaking the promise would shame him.
A promise from an old enemy in public shows real change, not just words.
So the handshake feels special because the enemy chose peace when he could still be mean.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Two Anthems, One Day
activities.body: The day was symbolised by two national anthems. Whites sang 'Nkosi Sikelel –iAfrika' and blacks sang 'Die Stem'. Each group sang the song they had once despised. And here is the surprising part: neither group knew the lyrics of that anthem. The songs swapped places, and both peoples learned new words for one country.
keyPoints: Two national anthems were played that day.
Whites sang 'Nkosi Sikelel –iAfrika'; blacks sang 'Die Stem'.
Neither group knew the lyrics of the anthem they once despised.
activities.explanation: Singing each other's anthem was a powerful symbol of sharing one country.

activities.prompt: What flew over the Union Buildings in perfect formation?
options: South African jets, helicopters and troop carriers
Ships sailing up a wide river
Balloons filled with bright colours
Trains crossing a long bridge
activities.explanation: Well done! The lesson says jets, helicopters and troop carriers roared over the Union Buildings.

activities.prompt: A chevron of ______ jets left a smoke trail in the colours of the new South African flag.
activities.hint: It is a kind of animal, and also the name of the jets.
activities.explanation: Great! The Impala jets painted the new flag's colours across the sky.

activities.prompt: The flying display was also a demonstration of the military's loyalty to democracy.
activities.explanation: Yes! The show of force carried a peaceful message: the army stood by democracy.

activities.prompt: Why was the generals' salute to Mandela so striking?
options: Because the generals were all much younger than him
Because not many years before they would have arrested him
Because the generals had never met a president before
Because the salute was part of a flying competition
activities.explanation: Exactly! The very men who once would have arrested him now pledged loyalty to him.

activities.prompt: Match each one to what the lesson says about it.
pairs: overwhelmed with a sense of history
activities.explanation: Perfect matching! You have connected the songs, the salute and the feeling of the day.

activities.prompt: Put these events of history in the order they happened.
items: In the first decade of the twentieth century, white-skinned peoples erected racial domination
Not many years before the ceremony, the generals would have arrested Mandela
The highest generals saluted Mandela and pledged loyalty
The old system was overturned and replaced by one recognising the rights and freedoms of all peoples
activities.explanation: Brilliant ordering! You traced the journey from racial domination to rights and freedoms for all.

activities.prompt: Planes and helicopters flew over a big celebration. They flew in perfect lines. This showed the army's loyalty to the new government. Years before, the army leaders would have arrested the new leader. Why did the army leaders salute him now?
options: They were afraid the planes would fall on them
They now promised to serve the new democracy
They wanted to show their planes were the fastest
They were saying sorry for flying badly before

why.They were afraid the planes would fall o: This mixes up the flying show with a feeling of fear, which is not the point.
why.They wanted to show their planes were th: This thinks the show was about skill in flying, not about loyalty.
why.They were saying sorry for flying badly: This thinks the salute was an apology for flying, not a promise of loyalty.

activities.explanation: Right. The salute and pledge showed the army now serves the democracy and its leader.

activities.prompt: A new leader watches the army generals salute him. He knows that years before, these same generals would have arrested him. What was he most likely feeling?
options: Bored, because he had seen salutes many times
Scared, because the generals still looked angry
Amazed, because old enemies now stood by him
Angry, because the generals had arrested his friends

why.Bored, because he had seen salutes many: This misses the special history between the leader and the generals.
why.Scared, because the generals still looke: Nothing says the generals looked angry; the fear idea is made up.
why.Angry, because the generals had arrested: The text shows wonder, not revenge or anger, in his thoughts.

activities.explanation: Right. Men who once would arrest him now pledged loyalty, so wonder fits.

activities.prompt: Jets flew in a chevron shape. They left smoke in the colours of the new flag. The smoke painted the sky. What did the smoke trail most likely mean to the watchers?
options: The pilots needed the smoke to find their way home
The new nation's flag was flying across the whole sky
The jets were practising for a race the next day
The smoke was a warning that a storm was coming

why.The pilots needed the smoke to find thei: This thinks of smoke as a tool for pilots, not a symbol for people below.
why.The jets were practising for a race the: This turns a celebration into a sports event, which the text never says.
why.The smoke was a warning that a storm was: This reads the smoke as a real warning, missing its symbolic purpose.

activities.explanation: Right. Flag-coloured smoke made the new nation's symbol fill the sky for all to see.

activities.prompt: At the celebration, two groups sang two anthems. Each group sang the song of the other group. Neither group knew the words of that song. What does this show about the two groups before that day?
options: They had lived apart and never learned each other's song
They were both too shy to sing in front of others
They had forgotten the words because they were old
They had no voices left after cheering all morning

why.They were both too shy to sing in front: Shyness is not the reason; they simply never learned the words.
why.They had forgotten the words because the: The songs were not old and forgotten; they were each group's own anthem.
why.They had no voices left after cheering a: This is a silly physical reason, not the real reason of separation.

activities.explanation: Right. Not knowing the other's anthem shows the groups lived separate lives for years.

activities.prompt: Whites sang the black people's anthem. Blacks sang the white people's anthem. Each group sang a song they once despised. What did this swapping most likely symbolise?
options: The two groups were now trying to share one country
The two groups had lost their old song books
The singers wanted to win a prize for singing
The songs were too long to sing twice each

why.The two groups had lost their old song b: This gives a practical excuse and misses the deep meaning of the swap.
why.The singers wanted to win a prize for si: This turns a symbolic moment into a competition, which it was not.
why.The songs were too long to sing twice ea: This is about song length, not about what the swap meant.

activities.explanation: Right. Singing each other's once-hated anthem showed groups reaching toward each other.

activities.prompt: Long ago, white-skinned peoples made a system of racial domination. Later, that system was overturned forever. A new system gave rights and freedoms to all peoples. The leader felt a deep sense of history. Why did he feel that way?
options: He was tired after watching the planes fly over
He saw the old unfair world change into a fair one
He wanted to write a book about the anthems
He was worried the old system might come back soon

why.He was tired after watching the planes f: Tiredness is a small physical feeling, not a sense of history.
why.He wanted to write a book about the anth: Writing a book is not what the text says he felt or wanted.
why.He was worried the old system might come: The system was overturned forever, so worry about its return is wrong.

activities.explanation: Right. He had lived through the fall of racial rule and the rise of rights for all.

lessons.title: Sacrifice, Apartheid's Wound, Courage and Humanity

activities.prompt: What makes an ordinary person brave enough to change a whole country?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Freedom Cost Something
activities.body: Freedom did not come free. Thousands of people gave up everything for it. Mandela felt he was simply the sum of all the African patriots who came before him. Apartheid had left a deep and lasting wound in his country. Yet he saw courage as triumph over fear, and he saw goodness as a flame that can never be put out.
keyPoints: Freedom came through the sacrifices of thousands of people.
Apartheid created a deep and lasting wound in the country.
Courage is not the absence of fear but triumph over it.
Man's goodness is a flame that can be hidden but never extinguished.
activities.explanation: Freedom was won by many brave people, and goodness always survives.

activities.prompt: Your class wins a big trophy. The captain says, 'I am not the winner. I am just all of you added together.' Why does the captain say this instead of taking all the credit?
steps: The captain knows the trophy came from everyone's hard work, not one person.
Saying 'I am all of you' shares the honour with the whole team.
Mandela did the same when he called himself the sum of all the patriots before him.
So the greatest leaders stay humble and give credit to the many people who sacrificed.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Mandela learned that courage is really about...
options: Never feeling fear at all
Triumphing over your fear
Running away from danger
Being the strongest person
activities.explanation: Courage is not the absence of fear. It is the triumph over it. Well done!

activities.prompt: Mandela compared man's goodness to a ______ that can be hidden but never extinguished.
activities.hint: It gives light, like a candle.
activities.explanation: A flame can be hidden for a while, but it never goes out. That is how goodness works.

activities.prompt: Mandela said that people are born hating others because of skin colour.
activities.explanation: No one is born hating another person. Hate is learned, so love can be taught too.

activities.prompt: Match each idea or person with what the lesson says about them.
pairs: A great leader of the struggle
activities.explanation: Each pair comes straight from the lesson. Great matching!

activities.prompt: Why did Mandela believe love can be taught?
options: Love comes free to every baby
Hate itself is learned by people
Hate is stronger than love
Only kind people can love
activities.explanation: If people can learn to hate, they can also be taught to love. Love comes more naturally to the human heart.

activities.prompt: Mandela stood proudly on the day of freedom. Why did he feel humble?
options: He felt he was the sum of earlier patriots
He thought he had won freedom alone
He wanted to thank only his family
He feared the crowd would not cheer
activities.explanation: He knew freedom came through the sacrifices of thousands. He saw himself as the sum of those patriots.

activities.prompt: Mandela became the leader of his country. He said he was the sum of all the patriots before him. Those patriots suffered and died for freedom. What does this show about Mandela?
options: He thinks he won freedom all by himself.
He feels humble and shares the honour.
He feels the old patriots were not important.
He wants people to forget the old patriots.

This is the opposite of his words; he points away from himself.
why.He feels the old patriots were not impor: He calls them patriots, so he honours them, not dismisses them.
why.He wants people to forget the old patrio: He remembers them by name in his heart, so he does not want them forgotten.

activities.explanation: Right: calling himself their 'sum' means he sees their sacrifice inside him.

activities.prompt: A girl is scared of walking home in the dark. She still walks home alone every evening. Her friend never feels any fear at all. Who does Mandela call brave?
options: The friend, because fear never comes to him.
The girl, because she wins over her fear.
Neither, because both of them are weak.
Both, because both of them walk at night.

why.The friend, because fear never comes to: No fear means nothing was conquered, so it is not Mandela's courage.
Mandela says the brave one conquers fear, so one of them is brave.
why.Both, because both of them walk at night: Walking at night is not the point; conquering fear is the point.

activities.explanation: Right: courage is triumph over fear, and she feels fear but still goes.

activities.prompt: A boy is taught to hate people of another colour. Mandela says no one is born hating. People learn to hate, so they can be taught to love. What does Mandela believe about the boy?
options: The boy can never change his hate.
The boy was born with hate inside him.
The boy can learn to love instead.
The boy's hate comes from his skin colour.

If hate is learned, it can be unlearned, so it is not fixed forever.
Mandela says the opposite: no one is born hating another person.
why.The boy's hate comes from his skin colou: Hate is learned from people around him, not caused by skin colour.

activities.explanation: Right: what is learned can be retaught, so love can replace hate.

activities.prompt: Apartheid hurt Mandela's country very deeply. Mandela said healing would take many years, maybe generations. Why did he say it would take so long?
options: The wound was deep, so healing is slow.
People did not really want freedom at all.
The leaders were too old to help anyone.
The country had no doctors for real wounds.

why.People did not really want freedom at al: The people fought hard for freedom, so they wanted it very much.
Leaders like Tambo and Sisulu came from that very oppression to help.
why.The country had no doctors for real woun: The wound is in hearts and minds, not a cut on the body.

activities.explanation: Right: a deep and lasting wound, like a deep cut, needs a long time to heal.

activities.prompt: In prison, a guard was sometimes kind to Mandela. Mandela saw a glimmer of humanity in him. Mandela says goodness is a flame that can be hidden but never put out. What does this mean?
options: Goodness dies when people act unkindly.
Even hard people keep some goodness inside.
Only guards inside prisons have goodness.
A flame needs a real fire to stay alive.

Mandela says the flame is never put out, so goodness never fully dies.
why.Only guards inside prisons have goodness: Mandela saw it in one guard, but he means goodness in all people.
The flame is a picture of goodness, not a real fire.

activities.explanation: Right: the kind guard shows goodness hiding inside even a harsh system.

lessons.title: Twin Obligations and the Hunger for Freedom

activities.prompt: Can you love your family and your country at the same time?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Duties, One Heart
activities.body: Every person has twin obligations: one to the family, and one to the people, the community and the country. In South Africa, a man of Mandela's birth and colour could hardly honour both. If he served his people, he was torn from his family. Mandela was born free, but he learned that his boyhood freedom was an illusion. When he saw his brothers and sisters were not free, he joined the African National Congress.
keyPoints: We owe duties to family and to our people.
In South Africa, a man of colour could not fulfil both duties.
Mandela was born free, but his boyhood freedom was an illusion.
Seeing his people unfree, he joined the African National Congress.
activities.explanation: Two duties pull at every heart; Mandela chose to serve both as best he could.

activities.prompt: A boy wants to help his family at home and also help people in his town. But a strict rule says he can only do one. He feels stuck. Why does he feel stuck, and what does this teach us?
steps: He feels stuck because both duties matter to him, not just one.
The rule is unfair because it forces him to drop a duty he did not choose to drop.
When a rule blocks a good duty, a person may feel torn or even punished for being good.
So a fair life should let a person honour both duties, and a rule that stops this is the real problem.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: According to the lesson, what twin obligations does every man have?
options: To family and to people, community, country
To school and to friends
To work and to rest
To himself and to his teacher
activities.explanation: The lesson says we owe duties to our family and also to our people and country.

activities.prompt: As a student, which freedoms did young Mandela want?
options: Staying out at night and reading what he pleased
Owning land and leading a party
Travelling abroad and earning money
Speaking on stage and writing books
activities.explanation: As a student he wanted small, passing freedoms, like night outings and reading freely.

activities.prompt: Mandela later learned that his boyhood freedom was an ______.
activities.hint: It only seemed real, like water shining on a hot road.
activities.explanation: His boyhood freedom was an illusion, because his people were not truly free.

activities.prompt: Match each kind of freedom with its example from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Passing joys were transitory freedoms; earning keep and family life were honourable freedoms.

activities.prompt: Why does the lesson say the oppressor must also be liberated?
options: Both oppressed and oppressor are robbed of their humanity
The oppressor is too tired to rule
The oppressor wants to join the Congress
The oppressor has no family of his own
activities.explanation: Oppressed and oppressor alike lose their humanity, so both need to be set free.

activities.prompt: Put Mandela's journey in the order the lesson tells it.
items: He was born free, with no hunger for freedom
He learned his boyhood freedom was an illusion
As a student, he wanted transitory freedoms
He yearned for basic and honourable freedoms
He saw his people were not free and joined the African National Congress
activities.explanation: The lesson moves from birth, to boyhood, to student days, to honourable hopes, to joining the Congress.

activities.prompt: Ravi loves his family. He also wants to help his whole town. A new rule says he may help only one side. Facts first: he cares about both. How does Ravi most likely feel?
options: Torn, because both duties matter to him
Happy, because one choice is now easier
Angry at his family for needing him
Bored, because the choice feels small

why.Happy, because one choice is now easier: Wrong. This thinks the rule is a gift, not a loss.
why.Angry at his family for needing him: Wrong. This blames the family instead of the unfair rule.
why.Bored, because the choice feels small: Wrong. This misses how serious the choice is for him.

activities.explanation: Right. He holds two real duties, so a forced choice hurts him.

activities.prompt: A boy plays freely in the fields. He thinks he is fully free. Then he learns his family must obey harsh rules he never saw. Facts first: his freedom felt real to him. What does he now realise?
options: His freedom was only true for him, not for his people
His family should stop complaining about rules
The fields were never a real place to play
Playing in fields is a bad thing to do

why.His family should stop complaining about: Wrong. This sides with the rules instead of seeing the unfairness.
why.The fields were never a real place to pl: Wrong. This doubts the place, not the false idea of freedom.
why.Playing in fields is a bad thing to do: Wrong. This blames the boy's play, not the hidden rules.

activities.explanation: Right. He learns his freedom was an illusion once he sees others' chains.

activities.prompt: As a teen, Meena only wanted to stay out late and read what she liked. Years later, she wants a fair job and a family of her own. Facts first: her wishes changed with age. What does this change show?
options: She now wants deeper freedoms, not small ones
She has stopped caring about being free at all
She only wants things money can buy now
She regrets ever wanting freedom as a teen

why.She has stopped caring about being free: Wrong. This thinks change means freedom stopped mattering.
why.She only wants things money can buy now: Wrong. This shrinks her wish to money alone.
why.She regrets ever wanting freedom as a te: Wrong. This reads change as regret, not growth.

activities.explanation: Right. Small, passing wishes grew into basic and honourable freedoms.

activities.prompt: One worker in a long line is chained. The speaker says, 'Then I am not free either.' Facts first: the speaker's own hands are open. Why does he say this?
options: Freedom is shared, so one chain binds them all
He wants the guards to chain him up too
He thinks the chained worker is his own brother
He is afraid the guards will notice him next

why.He wants the guards to chain him up too: Wrong. This thinks he wants punishment, not shared freedom.
why.He thinks the chained worker is his own: Wrong. This makes it about family ties, not shared freedom.
why.He is afraid the guards will notice him: Wrong. This makes it about fear, not a shared idea.

activities.explanation: Right. He sees freedom as indivisible; one chain is a chain on all.

activities.prompt: A bully hurts weaker children every day. The teacher says, 'That bully also needs to be set free.' Facts first: the bully seems strong, not trapped. What does the teacher mean?
options: Hurting others robs the bully of humanity too
The bully should be given more power to rule
The weak children should learn to fight back
The bully is too strong for anyone to stop

why.The bully should be given more power to: Wrong. This thinks freedom means more power to hurt.
why.The weak children should learn to fight: Wrong. This shifts the fix onto the victims.
why.The bully is too strong for anyone to st: Wrong. This says the bully cannot change, which is not the point.

activities.explanation: Right. The oppressor is also robbed of humanity and needs liberation.

activities.prompt: A man speaks up for his people. That night, he is taken far from his home and family. Facts first: he only did his duty to his people. What was the punishment meant to do?
options: Stop him from doing his duty to his people
Reward him for being brave and honest
Teach his family to travel to new places
Give him time to rest away from work

why.Reward him for being brave and honest: Wrong. This mistakes a punishment for a prize.
why.Teach his family to travel to new places: Wrong. This sees travel as the goal, not the harm.
why.Give him time to rest away from work: Wrong. This calls the punishment a rest, missing its purpose.

activities.explanation: Right. Ripping him from home was meant to break his duty to his people.

activities.context: A student is preparing a class presentation on the lesson from Long Walk to Freedom. She reads that apartheid separated people by race, and that Mandela and his African National Congress spent a lifetime fighting it, with Mandela spending thirty years in prison. She learns that democratic elections were held in South Africa in 1994, that the ANC won 252 of the 400 seats, and that Mandela became the first black President of a new nation. A BBC news item of 10 May 1994 reported this after more than three centuries of White rule. The inauguration took place in the Union Buildings amphitheatre in Pretoria, where more than 100,000 South African men, women and children of all races sang and danced with joy.
activities.prompt: If the 1994 elections had not been democratic, which outcome would most likely have been different?
options: Mandela could not have become the first black President through the people's vote
Mandela would have spent thirty more years in prison
Apartheid would have ended much earlier than it did
The inauguration would have been held outside Pretoria

why.Mandela would have spent thirty more yea: Wrong: his thirty years in prison happened before the elections and did not depend on them.
why.Apartheid would have ended much earlier: Wrong: apartheid ended because of the fight against it and the elections, not the other way round.
why.The inauguration would have been held ou: Wrong: the venue of the ceremony is not decided by whether the election is democratic.

activities.explanation: Correct: a democratic election is what allowed voters to choose Mandela as the first black President.

activities.context: A student is preparing a class presentation on the lesson from Long Walk to Freedom. She reads that apartheid separated people by race, and that Mandela and his African National Congress spent a lifetime fighting it, with Mandela spending thirty years in prison. She learns that democratic elections were held in South Africa in 1994, that the ANC won 252 of the 400 seats, and that Mandela became the first black President of a new nation. A BBC news item of 10 May 1994 reported this after more than three centuries of White rule. The inauguration took place in the Union Buildings amphitheatre in Pretoria, where more than 100,000 South African men, women and children of all races sang and danced with joy.
activities.prompt: Why did more than 100,000 South Africans of all races sing and dance at the inauguration?
options: Because the ceremony was held in the Union Buildings amphitheatre in Pretoria
Because a BBC news item was being broadcast that day
Because the end of White rule and the election of Mandela gave them a shared reason to celebrate
Because the ANC had won exactly 252 of the 400 seats

why.Because the ceremony was held in the Uni: Wrong: the venue only tells us where they gathered, not why they were joyful.
why.Because a BBC news item was being broadc: Wrong: the news item reported the event; it was not the cause of the celebration.
why.Because the ANC had won exactly 252 of t: Wrong: the exact number of seats won is a detail of the result, not the reason for public joy.

activities.explanation: Correct: the historic change after centuries of White rule united people of all races in joy.

activities.context: A student is preparing a class presentation on the lesson from Long Walk to Freedom. She reads that apartheid separated people by race, and that Mandela and his African National Congress spent a lifetime fighting it, with Mandela spending thirty years in prison. She learns that democratic elections were held in South Africa in 1994, that the ANC won 252 of the 400 seats, and that Mandela became the first black President of a new nation. A BBC news item of 10 May 1994 reported this after more than three centuries of White rule. The inauguration took place in the Union Buildings amphitheatre in Pretoria, where more than 100,000 South African men, women and children of all races sang and danced with joy.
activities.prompt: A classmate says Mandela's lifetime of struggle ended in failure because he was imprisoned for thirty years. What should the student point out?
options: That prison proves the ANC never really opposed apartheid
That the 1994 democratic elections and his becoming the first black President show the struggle succeeded
That he should have avoided prison by giving up the fight earlier
That the autobiography Long Walk to Freedom was written to describe his failures

why.That prison proves the ANC never really: Wrong: the ANC spent a lifetime fighting apartheid; imprisonment shows the cost of that fight, not its absence.
why.That he should have avoided prison by gi: Wrong: giving up the fight would have helped apartheid continue, not the cause.
why.That the autobiography Long Walk to Free: Wrong: the autobiography is the source of the lesson's extract, not a record of failure.

activities.explanation: Correct: the elections of 1994 and Mandela becoming the first black President are the results his struggle achieved.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The inauguration ceremony took place in the Union Buildings amphitheatre in Pretoria.
Reason (R): More than 100,000 South African men, women and children of all races gathered there and sang and danced with joy.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the joyful gathering happened at the venue; it is not the reason the ceremony was held there.

activities.prompt: Explain why the inauguration of 10 May 1994 is called a historic occasion in the lesson.
activities.answer: The inauguration is historic because it marked the end of more than three centuries of White rule in South Africa. After Mandela and the African National Congress spent a lifetime fighting apartheid, and Mandela endured thirty years in prison, democratic elections were finally held in 1994. The ANC won 252 of the 400 seats, and Mandela became the first black President of a new nation. The ceremony in the Union Buildings amphitheatre in Pretoria, where more than 100,000 South Africans of all races sang and danced with joy, showed a divided country becoming one.
points: Links the inauguration to the end of over three centuries of White rule
Mentions the lifetime fight against apartheid and Mandela's thirty years in prison
Refers to the 1994 democratic elections and the ANC's 252 of 400 seats
Notes the first black President and the joy of 100,000 people of all races
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: On the bright, clear morning of tenth May, Zenani stood beside her father in the sandstone amphitheatre formed by the Union Buildings in Pretoria. Dignitaries and world leaders had been arriving for days to pay their respects before the inauguration — the largest gathering ever of international leaders on South African soil. Below the seat of white supremacy of past decades, a rainbow gathering of different colours and nations waited for the installation of South Africa's first democratic, non-racial government. Mr de Klerk was sworn in first as second deputy president, then Thabo Mbeki as first deputy president, before Mandela rose to pledge obedience to the Constitution and devotion to the well-being of the Republic and its people.
activities.prompt: A visitor asks Zenani why such an important ceremony was held at the Union Buildings rather than at a brand-new venue. What is the best explanation she could give?
options: Because the building was chosen to give the old site a completely new meaning
Because it was the only hall in the country large enough for the crowd
Because the foreign leaders had demanded a familiar, historic location
Because the new government had no money to build anywhere else

why.Because it was the only hall in the coun: Wrong: the passage never mentions size or capacity as the reason for the choice.
why.Because the foreign leaders had demanded: Wrong: the leaders came to pay respects; nothing suggests they chose the venue.
why.Because the new government had no money: Wrong: cost is never mentioned, and the ceremony's symbolism, not budget, explains the site.

activities.explanation: Correct: a place once linked to white supremacy now hosting a non-racial installation shows the old order being transformed.

activities.context: On the bright, clear morning of tenth May, Zenani stood beside her father in the sandstone amphitheatre formed by the Union Buildings in Pretoria. Dignitaries and world leaders had been arriving for days to pay their respects before the inauguration — the largest gathering ever of international leaders on South African soil. Below the seat of white supremacy of past decades, a rainbow gathering of different colours and nations waited for the installation of South Africa's first democratic, non-racial government. Mr de Klerk was sworn in first as second deputy president, then Thabo Mbeki as first deputy president, before Mandela rose to pledge obedience to the Constitution and devotion to the well-being of the Republic and its people.
activities.prompt: A classmate notices that Mr de Klerk took his oath before Thabo Mbeki. If the master of ceremonies had mistakenly called Mbeki first, what would actually have gone wrong?
options: The order of the offices being filled would have been broken
Mandela would have had to take his oath twice
The foreign leaders would have refused to watch the ceremony
The Constitution would have had to be rewritten on the spot

why.Mandela would have had to take his oath: Wrong: Mandela's own oath was separate and would not be affected by the deputies' order.
why.The foreign leaders would have refused t: Wrong: nothing suggests the guests would walk out over a procedural slip.
why.The Constitution would have had to be re: Wrong: a mix-up in sequence would not change the written Constitution.

activities.explanation: Correct: de Klerk was second deputy president and Mbeki first, so the sequence followed the ranks of the offices.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The inauguration attracted leaders from many countries to South Africa.
Reason (R): It marked the installation of South Africa's first democratic, non-racial government.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the historic nature of the installation explains why world leaders came in such numbers.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Mandela's pledge showed that he accepted the Constitution as binding on himself.
Reason (R): Mandela was sworn in as the first deputy president of the new government.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The pledge is correctly described, but it was Thabo Mbeki who was sworn in as first deputy president, so the reason is false.

activities.prompt: Explain why holding the inauguration at the Union Buildings in Pretoria carried a special meaning beyond just being a convenient venue.
activities.answer: The Union Buildings in Pretoria had, for decades, been the seat of white supremacy, so it stood for the old unjust order. Holding the installation of South Africa's first democratic, non-racial government there turned a symbol of exclusion into a symbol of inclusion. The amphitheatre that once represented rule by one race now held a rainbow gathering of different colours and nations, so the very ground on which the oaths were taken announced that the past had been replaced by a shared future.
points: Identifies the Union Buildings as the former seat of white supremacy
Links the venue to the first democratic, non-racial government
Explains the contrast between the old meaning and the rainbow gathering
Concludes that the location itself symbolised the change
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A newly free nation holds its first democratic ceremony. Its leader, who was treated as an outlaw not so long ago, now stands before distinguished international guests and thanks them for coming. He says an extraordinary human disaster has lasted too long but has at last ended, and that all present confer glory and hope to newborn liberty. He calls the day a common victory for justice, peace and human dignity, pledges to liberate all people from continuing bondage of poverty, deprivation, suffering and discrimination, and promises the land will never again see the oppression of one by another.
activities.prompt: Visitors from many countries filled the ceremony. Why did hosting them matter so much to the new nation?
options: It showed how far the nation had come, from being treated as outlaws to being trusted to welcome the nations of the world on its own soil.
It showed the nation had bought the guests' friendship by paying them to attend the ceremony.
It showed the guests had come mainly to check whether the new government was ruling fairly.
It showed the nation still needed outsiders' permission before it could govern itself.

why.It showed the nation had bought the gues: Wrong: nothing in the lesson suggests the guests were paid; the privilege was earned, not purchased.
why.It showed the guests had come mainly to: Wrong: the guests came to honour the occasion, not to judge or monitor the new government.
why.It showed the nation still needed outsid: Wrong: the nation was now independent and free; hosting guests was a sign of dignity, not dependence.

activities.explanation: Correct: the contrast between being outlaws not long ago and being hosts on their own soil is exactly the point Mandela drew.

activities.context: A newly free nation holds its first democratic ceremony. Its leader, who was treated as an outlaw not so long ago, now stands before distinguished international guests and thanks them for coming. He says an extraordinary human disaster has lasted too long but has at last ended, and that all present confer glory and hope to newborn liberty. He calls the day a common victory for justice, peace and human dignity, pledges to liberate all people from continuing bondage of poverty, deprivation, suffering and discrimination, and promises the land will never again see the oppression of one by another.
activities.prompt: The new leaders pledged to liberate all people from the continuing bondage of poverty, deprivation, suffering and discrimination. What is most likely to happen if they treat this pledge as already completed?
options: The victory they celebrated will remain incomplete, because the pledge deals with wrongs that continue even after political freedom is won.
The pledge will complete itself automatically, since political emancipation covers every kind of freedom.
The international guests will take over the task, since they were honoured at the ceremony.
The pledge will only lose meaning if another country publicly points out the failure.

why.The pledge will complete itself automati: Wrong: Mandela clearly separated what was achieved from what was still pledged; political freedom does not end poverty or discrimination by itself.
why.The international guests will take over: Wrong: the guests were there to be thanked and honoured; the responsibility for the pledge belongs to the nation's own leaders and people.
why.The pledge will only lose meaning if ano: Wrong: the pledge matters because of the people still in bondage, not because of what outsiders may or may not say.

activities.explanation: Correct: Mandela said political emancipation was achieved 'at last', but his pledge was for the future, against bondage that is 'continuing' — so ignoring it leaves the work undone.

activities.context: A newly free nation holds its first democratic ceremony. Its leader, who was treated as an outlaw not so long ago, now stands before distinguished international guests and thanks them for coming. He says an extraordinary human disaster has lasted too long but has at last ended, and that all present confer glory and hope to newborn liberty. He calls the day a common victory for justice, peace and human dignity, pledges to liberate all people from continuing bondage of poverty, deprivation, suffering and discrimination, and promises the land will never again see the oppression of one by another.
activities.prompt: At the close of his address, the leader wants the audience to carry the spirit of the day with them. Which ending best matches what he actually said?
options: A picture of an achievement so glorious that it will never fade, closing with a blessing on the land.
A warning that the long disaster could return unless the foreign guests keep helping.
A list of punishments for those responsible for the years of suffering.
A request that the audience applaud the leader personally for his own triumph.

why.A warning that the long disaster could r: Wrong: his ending was hopeful and triumphant, not a warning that depended on the guests.
why.A list of punishments for those responsi: Wrong: he looked forward to a society all humanity can be proud of, not backwards to punishing anyone.
why.A request that the audience applaud the: Wrong: he called it a common victory, belonging to all, not a personal triumph for himself.

activities.explanation: Correct: Mandela said the sun shall never set on so glorious a human achievement and ended with 'Let freedom reign. God bless Africa!' — lasting glory and a blessing.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Mandela called the day a common victory for justice, peace and human dignity.
Reason (R): He believed the achievement belonged to everyone present, not to one person alone.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the idea of a shared, common achievement is exactly why he called it a common victory.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Mandela said the sun shall never set on so glorious a human achievement.
Reason (R): He said this because the inauguration ceremony would finish before the sun went down that day.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false — the line is figurative, meaning the achievement's glory will last forever, not a comment on the time of day.

activities.prompt: Explain why Mandela thanked the international guests and described hosting them as a rare privilege.
activities.answer: Mandela thanked the distinguished international guests for coming because their presence honoured the newborn liberty. Not so long ago, he said, they had been outlaws — rejected and treated as criminals. Now the same nation was given the rare privilege of hosting the nations of the world on its own soil. This dramatic change from outcast to honoured host conferred glory and hope on the new freedom, and showed the world stood with the country as it built a society all humanity would be proud of.
points: He thanked the distinguished international guests for coming.
They were outlaws not so long ago, so the change in their status is striking.
Hosting the nations of the world on their own soil was a rare privilege.
The guests' presence conferred glory and hope to newborn liberty.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: On inauguration day, a chevron of Impala jets trailed smoke in the colours of the new South African flag while helicopters and troop carriers roared over the Union Buildings in perfect formation. The highest generals of the defence force and police saluted Mandela and pledged their loyalty. Two anthems were played: whites sang 'Nkosi Sikelel –iAfrika' and blacks sang 'Die Stem', each group fumbling over lyrics they had once despised. Mandela, overwhelmed with a sense of history, remembered that not many years earlier these same men would have arrested him.
activities.prompt: Why did the flypast matter more as a message than as entertainment?
options: It showed that the armed forces now accepted and served the new democratic order
It gave the crowds an exciting spectacle to remember the day by
It proved that the pilots had trained hard for many months
It warned other countries about the strength of the air force

why.It gave the crowds an exciting spectacle: Spectacle was only the surface; the deeper point was political, not entertainment
why.It proved that the pilots had trained ha: Training explains the skill shown, not the meaning of the display
why.It warned other countries about the stre: Nothing in the situation points to a warning aimed at foreign powers

activities.explanation: Correct: pinpoint flying by the very forces that once oppressed was really a pledge of loyalty to democracy

activities.context: On inauguration day, a chevron of Impala jets trailed smoke in the colours of the new South African flag while helicopters and troop carriers roared over the Union Buildings in perfect formation. The highest generals of the defence force and police saluted Mandela and pledged their loyalty. Two anthems were played: whites sang 'Nkosi Sikelel –iAfrika' and blacks sang 'Die Stem', each group fumbling over lyrics they had once despised. Mandela, overwhelmed with a sense of history, remembered that not many years earlier these same men would have arrested him.
activities.prompt: If one group had refused to sing the other's anthem, what would most directly have been spoiled?
options: The sound quality of the music at the ceremony
The symbol of two peoples honouring each other's heritage at one moment
The generals' pledge of loyalty to Mandela
The timing of the jets' smoke trail in the flag colours

why.The sound quality of the music at the ce: Sound quality is trivial and unrelated to why both anthems were played
why.The generals' pledge of loyalty to Mande: The pledge came from the generals separately and did not depend on the singing
why.The timing of the jets' smoke trail in t: The smoke trail was a separate symbol and would not be affected by singing

activities.explanation: Correct: each group singing the anthem it once despised was the shared-nation symbol of the day

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Nelson Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom

activities.prompt: What was apartheid?
options: A school for leaders
A system that separated people by race
A festival of songs
A plan for free elections
activities.explanation: Apartheid separated people by race. Mandela and his ANC fought against it all their lives.

activities.prompt: Mandela had to spend thirty years in prison.
activities.explanation: That is right. Mandela gave thirty years of his life for freedom, and still kept hope alive.

activities.prompt: Democratic elections were held in South Africa in ______.
activities.hint: Think of the year in the BBC news item.
activities.explanation: Well done. In 1994, South Africans of all races voted together for the first time.

activities.prompt: Where did the inauguration ceremony take place?
options: The Union Buildings amphitheatre in Pretoria
A jail in Robben Island
A school hall in Johannesburg
A stadium in Cape Town
activities.explanation: The ceremonies were held in the lovely sandstone amphitheatre of the Union Buildings in Pretoria.

activities.prompt: Match each person or party with the right description.
pairs: Sworn in as second deputy president
Sworn in as first deputy president
activities.explanation: Great matching. You know the key people of this historic day.

activities.prompt: At the ceremony, white people sang 'Die Stem' and black people sang 'Nkosi Sikelel –iAfrika'.
activities.explanation: It was the other way round. Whites sang 'Nkosi Sikelel –iAfrika' and blacks sang 'Die Stem'. Each group sang the anthem they once did not like.

activities.prompt: Mandela's ANC won ______ of the 400 seats in the first democratic elections.
activities.hint: It is more than half of the seats.
activities.explanation: Correct. Winning 252 of 400 seats made the ANC the clear choice of the people.

activities.prompt: What did Mandela learn about courage from his comrades?
options: Courage means never feeling afraid
Courage is triumph over fear, not absence of fear
Courage comes from being strong alone
Courage is only for soldiers
activities.explanation: The brave man is not one who feels no fear, but one who conquers that fear.

activities.prompt: Put Mandela's journey in the order the chapter tells it.
items: He was born free, with no hunger to be free
He learned his boyhood freedom was an illusion
As a student, he wanted transitory freedoms
He yearned for basic and honourable freedoms
He joined the ANC when he saw his people were not free
activities.explanation: Perfect order. Mandela's idea of freedom grew step by step until he fought for everyone.

activities.prompt: According to Mandela, who must be set free along with the oppressed?
options: Only the leaders of the world
The guards at the prison
The family of the oppressed
The oppressor too
activities.explanation: Mandela believed the oppressor must be liberated too, because both are robbed of their humanity.

chapters.title: Two Stories about Flying
chapters.summary: In this chapter: his first flight — alone on the ledge; his first flight — the first dive; the black aeroplane — into the storm; the black aeroplane — the strange pilot.

lessons.title: His First Flight — Alone on the Ledge

activities.prompt: Why couldn't the young seagull take his very first flight?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Alone on the Ledge
activities.body: A young seagull sat alone on his ledge. His two brothers and his sister had flown away the day before. He had been too afraid to fly with them. When he ran to the brink and flapped his wings, fear filled him. The sea seemed miles down. He felt sure his wings would never hold him up.
keyPoints: The young seagull was alone because his family had already flown away.
He was afraid his wings would not support him.
The sea below looked miles down, which made him more scared.
activities.explanation: Fear kept the young seagull on his ledge while his family flew free.

activities.prompt: A puppy is alone on a high step. Its brothers jumped down yesterday. It wants to jump but its legs shake. Why does it stay on the step?
steps: The puppy wants to go down, so fear is not about wanting.
It saw its brothers jump safely, so fear is not about danger.
Its legs shake because it does not trust its own legs yet.
So it stays because it cannot believe in itself, not because it cannot jump.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Who Flew Away?
activities.prompt: Who had already flown away the day before?
options: His two brothers and his sister
His father and his mother
His two cousins and his uncle
activities.explanation: His brothers and sister flew away the day before. He stayed behind because he was afraid.

activities.title: Miles Below
activities.prompt: The sea stretched down beneath the ledge and seemed ______ down.
activities.hint: A long, long way — think of the word used for distance.
activities.explanation: The sea seemed miles down. That great drop made his heart shrink with fear.

activities.title: Picture Pairs
activities.prompt: Match each thing with what it means in the story.
pairs: the narrow shelf where he sat
the very edge he ran to
what he feared would fail him
activities.explanation: Each word paints a part of the picture: the ledge, the edge, his wings and the deep sea.

activities.title: What Happened at the Brink?
activities.prompt: What happened when he ran to the brink and tried to flap his wings?
options: He became afraid and stopped
He flew over the sea at once
He called his brothers loudly
activities.explanation: Fear gripped him at the very edge. He could not make himself fly.

activities.title: His Day in Order
activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: His brothers and sister flew away the day before
He ran to the brink and became afraid
He felt sure his wings would never support him
He went back to the little hole where he slept
activities.explanation: First the family flew, then he tried at the brink, then doubt filled him, and at last he crept back to his hole.

activities.title: Why Could He Not Move?
activities.prompt: His siblings flew and dove for fish, and his parents scolded him. Yet he could not move. Why?
options: Fear told him his wings would fail
His parents asked him to stay
His wings were tired from diving
activities.explanation: For the life of him he could not move, because he believed his wings would never support him. Fear, not his family, held him back.

activities.prompt: Riya can swim. She watched her friends swim yesterday. Today she sits by the pool. She says, 'My arms are too weak.' What is really stopping her?
options: Her arms are truly too weak today
She does not believe her arms will hold her
She does not know how to swim at all
Her friends told her not to swim today

why.Her arms are truly too weak today: This takes her words as true facts, but the story shows fear, not weak arms.
why.She does not know how to swim at all: This forgets she already knows how to swim well.
why.Her friends told her not to swim today: This adds a fact that is not in the story at all.

activities.explanation: Right. She can swim, so the real problem is doubt in herself, like the seagull.

activities.prompt: The young seagull had shorter wings than his brothers and sister. Even they flew away. Why does the story tell us this?
options: To show his wings were not the real problem
To show his brothers were lucky that day
To show small birds fly better than big birds
To show his family did not love him much

why.To show his brothers were lucky that day: This thinks the story is about luck, not about courage.
why.To show small birds fly better than big: This makes up a rule about birds that the story never says.
why.To show his family did not love him much: This confuses scolding with not loving, which the story does not show.

activities.explanation: Right. Weaker flyers could do it, so his fear, not his wings, held him back.

activities.prompt: The parents called shrilly and scolded him. They said he could starve on his ledge. What did they really want?
options: They wanted him to feel sad and alone
They wanted him to leave and learn to fly
They wanted to keep all the food for themselves
They wanted him to sleep more in his hole

why.They wanted him to feel sad and alone: This thinks the parents were cruel, but scolding was their push.
why.They wanted to keep all the food for the: This reads the threat as selfishness about food, which is wrong.
why.They wanted him to sleep more in his hol: This mixes his sleeping hole with what the parents wanted.

activities.explanation: Right. The harsh words were a push to make him fly.

activities.prompt: A boy must dive from the high board. He walks to the edge, looks down, and walks back. What does walking back show about him?
options: He is too sick to jump today
The pool is too shallow for diving
Fear beat him at the last moment
He forgot how to dive in the water

why.He is too sick to jump today: This makes up a sickness that the situation never shows.
why.The pool is too shallow for diving: This blames the pool, but the boy is the one who turned back.
why.He forgot how to dive in the water: This confuses fear with forgetting a skill he already has.

activities.explanation: Right. He reached the edge like the seagull, then fear won.

activities.prompt: The seagull watched his parents teach his brothers and sister to skim the waves and dive for fish. What does this watching do to him?
options: It makes him forget his family completely
It makes him feel left out and more afraid
It makes him hungry for fish every day
It makes him want to sleep in his hole

why.It makes him forget his family completel: This says he forgets, but watching keeps his family in his mind.
why.It makes him hungry for fish every day: This focuses on food, but the point is being left behind.
why.It makes him want to sleep in his hole: Sleep is where he hides, not what watching makes him want.

activities.explanation: Right. Everyone flies but him, so he feels left out and more scared.

lessons.sceneAlt: A single seagull flying above the blue sea.
lessons.sceneCaption: A seagull flying over the sea in Garopaba.

sceneCredit.creator: Heylenny

lessons.title: His First Flight — The First Dive

activities.prompt: What could make a hungry young bird finally take his very first dive?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Morning of the Big Step
activities.body: The young bird sat on his ledge as the sun rose and blazed on it. He had not eaten since the previous nightfall, so he felt the heat badly. His family took no notice of him. Only his mother looked at him. She tore at a piece of fish, then picked one up and flew across to him. When she halted just out of reach, hunger pushed him to dive at the fish — and he fell outwards and downwards into his very first flight.
keyPoints: He had not eaten since the previous nightfall, so he felt weak and hot.
His family ignored him, but his mother watched him and flew to him with fish.
She stopped just out of reach, so hunger made him dive at the fish.
activities.explanation: Hunger and his mother's clever trick pushed him to make his first dive.

activities.prompt: You have not eaten since last night. You feel weak and hot. Your mother holds food just out of reach. What will you do, and why?
steps: Hunger makes the body feel weak and hot, so his heat comes from no food, not just the sun.
His mother shows food but does not give it, so she is testing him, not teasing him cruelly.
When food is almost within reach, hunger becomes stronger than fear, so he jumps at it.
So the dive happens because hunger pushes him past his fear, which is exactly what his mother wanted.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A Blazing Morning
activities.prompt: As the sun rose, where was its light blazing?
options: On his south-facing ledge
On the sea below him
On his mother's beak
On the fish she carried
activities.explanation: The lesson says the rising sun blazed on his south-facing ledge. Well spotted!

activities.title: Who Was Watching?
activities.prompt: His brothers and sisters dozed and his father preened. Who was the only one looking at him?
options: His father
His mother
His siblings
Nobody at all
activities.explanation: The rest of the family took no notice. Only his mother was watching him.

activities.title: Mother's Little Game
activities.prompt: His mother picked up a piece of ______ and flew across to him.
activities.hint: It was the tasty food he was begging for.
activities.explanation: She carried a piece of fish across to him, but she did not hand it over at once.

activities.title: Who Did What?
activities.prompt: Match each bird or feeling to what happened in the lesson.
pairs: Tore at a piece of fish
activities.explanation: Each bird had its own part to play that morning. You matched them all!

activities.title: The Moment of the Dive
activities.prompt: Maddened by hunger, he dived at the fish. What seized him as he fell outwards and downwards?
options: A monstrous terror
A sudden storm
A piece of fish
His mother's scream
activities.explanation: A monstrous terror seized him and his heart stood still. But he dived all the same — that took courage!

activities.title: Put the Morning in Order
activities.prompt: Put these moments from the story in the right order, from first to last.
items: He stood on one leg and pretended to sleep
His mother tore at a piece of fish
She flew across to him with the fish
She halted with the fish almost within reach
He dived at the fish and fell outwards and downwards
activities.explanation: First he pretended to sleep, then mother teased him with fish, and at last hunger made him dive. What a brave step!

activities.prompt: Ravi has not eaten since last night. The sun shines hot on him. He feels weak and dizzy. Why does he feel this way?
options: The sun alone made him dizzy and weak.
Hunger from no food since last night made him weak.
He is sleepy because he slept very late.
He is scared of the hot sun outside.

Right: hunger since last night is the real cause of his weakness.
Wrong: sleep is not mentioned as the cause of his weakness.
Wrong: fear of the sun is not the reason given here.

activities.explanation: Wrong: this blames only the sun and forgets the missing food.

activities.prompt: A boy wants his sister to try the swimming pool. She is scared. He holds a chocolate just out of her reach near the water. Why does he do this?
options: He wants her to jump toward it and forget her fear.
He wants to eat the chocolate himself later.
He wants to make her angry and shout at him.
He wants to show her that he owns the chocolate.

why.He wants to eat the chocolate himself la: Wrong: eating it himself is not his purpose in holding it out.
why.He wants to make her angry and shout at: Wrong: making her angry is not the goal of the trick.
why.He wants to show her that he owns the ch: Wrong: showing ownership has nothing to do with helping her.

activities.explanation: Right: like the mother bird, he uses food to push her past fear.

activities.prompt: The mother tears a piece of fish and scrapes her beak on the rock. She does this in front of her hungry son. What is she trying to do?
options: She is cleaning her beak after eating.
She is making the food look tasty to him.
She is showing him she is very hungry too.
She is telling him the fish is not good.

Right: she acts before his eyes to wake up his hunger for food.
why.She is showing him she is very hungry to: Wrong: her own hunger is not the point of the show.
Wrong: she never says the fish is bad; she offers it soon.

activities.explanation: Wrong: cleaning is not her aim; she does it where he can see.

activities.prompt: The mother screams back at her begging son. She holds food but does not drop it. What does her scream really mean?
options: She is angry and will never feed him now.
She is pushing him to act for himself.
She has lost her voice from screaming.
She wants the other birds to hear her.

why.She is angry and will never feed him now: Right: her harsh reply is a push toward flying, not a refusal of food.
Wrong: her voice is fine; the scream is on purpose.
Wrong: calling others is not why she screams at him.

activities.explanation: Wrong: she does feed him soon, so she has not refused forever.

activities.prompt: The bird dives at the fish. Then a monstrous terror seizes him and his heart stands still. What has just happened to him?
options: He has left the ledge and is falling through air.
He has caught the fish in his beak at last.
He has fallen asleep on his one hidden leg.
He has flown back to his safe warm ledge.

why.He has caught the fish in his beak at la: Wrong: he missed the fish; the terror shows he has not caught it.
why.He has fallen asleep on his one hidden l: Wrong: sleep is impossible when terror seizes him mid-air.
why.He has flown back to his safe warm ledge: Wrong: he fell outwards and downwards, not back to safety.

activities.explanation: Right: the dive took him off the ledge, so now he is falling.

lessons.sceneAlt: A fulmar parent and its chick stand together on rocky cliffs by the sea in Orkney, Scotland.
lessons.sceneCaption: A fulmar and its chick rest together on the rocks at Marwick Head in Orkney, Scotland.
