lessons.title: The Black Aeroplane — Into the Storm

activities.prompt: What would you do if a storm suddenly swallowed your plane?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Night Flight Begins
activities.body: A pilot flies his old Dakota plane over France, going back to England. The night is calm. The moon rises in the east, stars shine, and no cloud is in the sky. He dreams of his holiday and his family. At one thirty in the morning, he calls Paris Control. They tell him to turn twelve degrees west. Then huge storm clouds appear ahead.
keyPoints: He was flying an old Dakota from France to England.
The night started calm, with no clouds.
Paris Control told him to turn twelve degrees west.
Huge storm clouds appeared when Paris was about 150 kilometres behind him.
activities.explanation: A happy, easy flight is about to meet a big storm.

activities.prompt: The pilot is flying at night and feels happy. But soon he will need to talk to Paris Control. Why does he look at his watch before calling?
steps: It is dark, so he cannot see the ground well, so he must trust his instruments and the radio.
He looks at his watch because he wants to know how far he has flown and how much time has passed.
He knows Paris Control will ask where he is, so he needs the time to work out his position.
So the watch is not for fun; it helps him stay safe and know when to call for directions.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Where Was He Flying?
activities.prompt: The pilot was flying his old Dakota aeroplane over France. Where was he going?
options: Back to England
Back to France
On to Paris
activities.explanation: He was flying over France on his way back to England. Well done!

activities.title: Checking the Watch
activities.prompt: The pilot looked at his watch. It was one ______ in the morning.
activities.hint: Think of the time halfway past one.
activities.explanation: It was one thirty in the morning when he checked his watch.

activities.title: Turning the Plane
activities.prompt: Paris Control gave the pilot an instruction. What did he do after hearing it?
options: He checked his map and compass, then turned west.
He landed at once and waited for morning.
He flew higher to look for the city lights.
activities.explanation: After Paris Control spoke, he checked the map and compass, switched fuel tanks and turned west. Good thinking!

activities.title: Match the Flight Details
activities.prompt: Match each thing on the left with what goes with it on the right.
activities.explanation: Each detail comes from the pilot's night flight. You matched them all!

activities.title: Put the Flight Steps in Order
activities.prompt: Put these steps of the flight in the order they happened.
items: He saw the lights of a big city in front of him.
He switched on the radio and called as Dakota DS 088.
Paris Control told him to turn twelve degrees west.
He checked the map and compass and switched to his last fuel tank.
He turned the plane towards the west.
activities.explanation: First the city lights, then the radio call, then the instruction, then the checks, and last the turn.

activities.title: Why Did He Feel Happy?
activities.prompt: The pilot thought it was an easy flight. Why did he feel this way?
options: He hoped to be in time for breakfast with his family.
He knew the storm clouds would pass quickly.
Paris Control had promised him extra fuel.
activities.explanation: He was dreaming of his holiday and looking forward to being with his family, in time for breakfast.

activities.prompt: The sky is clear. Stars are shining. The pilot smiles as he flies alone. He looks down at the quiet land below. How does he feel about flying alone?
options: He feels afraid to be alone up there.
He enjoys the calm and quiet of the night.
He is angry that nobody flies with him.
He feels bored and wants to land quickly.

This mistakes being alone at night for danger, but he is smiling, not scared.
This reads the smile as anger, but nothing shows he is upset with anyone.
why.He feels bored and wants to land quickly: This confuses feeling calm with feeling bored; he is happy, not in a hurry.

activities.explanation: Right: his happiness and the peaceful night show he enjoys flying alone.

activities.prompt: The pilot sees the lights of a big city ahead. He turns on his radio at once. He gives the name of his plane. Why does he do this quickly?
options: He wants to check that his radio still works for fun.
He wants to ask the control tower for directions.
He wants to tell his family he is coming home.
He wants to hear music while he flies at night.

why.He wants to check that his radio still w: This misses the purpose; the radio is a tool for talking to control, not a toy.
why.He wants to tell his family he is coming: This confuses the radio with a phone call home; control is not his family.
why.He wants to hear music while he flies at: This treats the radio as entertainment; pilots use it to talk, not to listen to songs.

activities.explanation: Right: he identifies himself so Paris Control can guide him on his route.

activities.prompt: Paris Control tells the pilot to turn twelve degrees west. He looks at his map and compass. Then he turns the plane. Why does he check them first?
options: He wants to make sure he turns the right way.
He wants to count how many clouds he can see.
He wants to show the compass to Paris Control.
He wants to check if his family is awake.

why.He wants to count how many clouds he can: This mixes up checking direction with looking outside; the tools guide the turn.
why.He wants to show the compass to Paris Co: This misunderstands the tools; control cannot see his compass from far away.
why.He wants to check if his family is awake: This confuses the map with a phone; the map shows places, not people.

activities.explanation: Right: the map and compass show him where west is, so the turn is correct.

activities.prompt: The pilot switches to his second and last fuel tank. He thinks the flight is easy. He thinks he will be in time for breakfast. What does the word 'last' tell us?
options: He has plenty of fuel and can fly all day.
He has no more fuel left after this tank.
He will land soon to buy more fuel.
He forgot to fill the fuel tanks before flying.

why.He has plenty of fuel and can fly all da: This ignores the word 'last'; plenty of fuel would not be called the last tank.
This adds a plan the story does not mention; he expects to fly on to England.
why.He forgot to fill the fuel tanks before: This blames the pilot for a mistake; the story shows he planned his tanks.

activities.explanation: Right: 'last' means nothing remains after this tank, so fuel is running low.

activities.prompt: Paris is about 150 kilometres behind the pilot. Suddenly he sees huge storm clouds ahead. He was thinking about breakfast. How does his feeling change now?
options: He feels even happier about his easy flight.
He stops thinking about breakfast and worries.
He feels proud that he flew so far already.
He feels sleepy and wants to rest the plane.

why.He feels even happier about his easy fli: This keeps his old happy mood, but storm clouds are a danger, not good news.
why.He feels proud that he flew so far alrea: This looks back at his success, but the storm makes him look ahead with worry.
why.He feels sleepy and wants to rest the pl: This adds a tired feeling that the story does not show at this moment.

activities.explanation: Right: danger ahead pushes the happy breakfast thought out of his mind.

lessons.title: The Black Aeroplane — The Strange Pilot

activities.prompt: Who was the mysterious pilot that guided him safely through the storm?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Strange Helper in the Clouds
activities.body: The pilot is lost in black clouds. Then he sees another aeroplane near him. It has no lights on its wings, yet it flies beside him. Its pilot waves and turns north, so it is easy to follow. Our pilot follows like an obedient child. His fuel will last only five or ten minutes. Soon he sees two lines of lights — a runway and an airport. He is safe.
keyPoints: A strange aeroplane with no lights appears in the black clouds.
Its pilot waves and turns north so the lost pilot can follow.
The fuel is almost finished, but the strange plane leads him to a runway and an airport.
activities.explanation: A mysterious pilot guides the lost flyer out of the clouds to safety.

activities.prompt: You are walking home in thick fog. You cannot see the road. A stranger on a bicycle rings his bell and waves, 'Follow me.' Should you follow him? Why?
steps: You are lost, so you need help, and any friendly person feels like a chance.
The stranger waves you to follow, so he seems to know the way, and that gives you hope.
But he is a stranger, so you cannot be sure he is kind, and that makes you a little afraid.
Still, with no other choice, you follow him carefully, because following is better than staying lost in the fog.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Spotting the Strange Plane
activities.prompt: What was odd about the other aeroplane's wings?
options: They had no lights on them
They were painted bright red
They had two lamps each
They were covered in ice
activities.explanation: The other aeroplane had no lights on its wings, yet it flew right next to him.

activities.title: Like an Obedient Child
activities.prompt: He followed the strange aeroplane like an ______ child.
activities.hint: It means doing what you are told, like a well-behaved child.
activities.explanation: He trusted the strange pilot and followed quietly, just like an obedient child.

activities.title: Why Turn North?
activities.prompt: Why did the strange pilot turn north in front of the Dakota?
options: So it would be easier to follow
So he could fly home quickly
So the clouds would go away
So he could land at once
activities.explanation: Turning north in front of the Dakota made it easy for the lost pilot to follow.

activities.title: Match What Happened
activities.prompt: Match each thing with what it means in the story.
pairs: How long the fuel would last
activities.explanation: Each clue fits its meaning in the story. You are thinking like a detective!

activities.title: Put the Story in Order
activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happen.
items: He sees another aeroplane in the black clouds
The strange pilot waves and turns north
He follows like an obedient child
The fuel in the last tank is nearly finished
He sees two lines of lights and lands safely
activities.explanation: First the strange plane appears, then the wave, the following, the low fuel, and finally the safe landing.

activities.title: Feelings and the Ending
activities.prompt: How did he feel when he came out of the clouds and saw the runway?
options: Safe and glad
Angry and upset
Lost and lonely
Sleepy and tired
activities.explanation: It was a runway and an airport, and he was safe at last. What a happy ending!

activities.prompt: You are lost in a big market. You feel alone and scared. Then a kind shopkeeper smiles at you. In the story, the pilot saw the other pilot's face and felt glad. Why did seeing the face make him glad?
options: He felt less alone, because someone was there to help.
He felt glad because he knew the pilot's name already.
He felt glad because he wanted to race the other plane.
He felt glad because the face looked funny to him.

why.He felt glad because he knew the pilot's: Wrong: this thinks he already knew the pilot, but the pilot was a stranger.
why.He felt glad because he wanted to race t: Wrong: this thinks he was playing, but he was lost and needed help.
why.He felt glad because the face looked fun: Wrong: this thinks he was laughing at the face, but he felt thankful, not amused.

activities.explanation: Right: he was lost and afraid, so a friendly face meant help and comfort.

activities.prompt: A small child holds mother's hand and follows her in a crowd. He does not ask where she is going. The pilot followed the strange aeroplane like an obedient child. What does this show about him?
options: He trusted the strange pilot and followed without asking questions.
He was angry with the strange pilot and did not want help.
He was flying his plane faster than the strange plane.
He had forgotten how to fly his own plane alone.

why.He was angry with the strange pilot and: Wrong: this thinks he refused help, but the words 'obedient child' mean he followed.
why.He was flying his plane faster than the: Wrong: this thinks about speed, but the line is about trust, not speed.
why.He had forgotten how to fly his own plan: Wrong: this thinks he lost his skill, but he followed by choice, not by weakness.

activities.explanation: Right: an obedient child follows without questions, so the pilot trusted the stranger completely.

activities.prompt: Your phone battery shows two minutes left. You are far from home. In the story, only five or ten minutes of fuel were left. Then the strange pilot started going down. Why did the writer feel frightened again?
options: His plane could stop flying soon, because the fuel was almost finished.
He was scared of the dark clouds around him only.
He was scared because he did not like the strange pilot.
He was scared because he wanted to fly higher but could not.

why.He was scared of the dark clouds around: Wrong: this blames the clouds, but the new fear came from the empty fuel tank.
why.He was scared because he did not like th: Wrong: this blames the stranger, but the writer was glad to follow him.
why.He was scared because he wanted to fly h: Wrong: this thinks he wanted to go up, but the danger was having no fuel.

activities.explanation: Right: with almost no fuel, the plane could fall, so going down was his last chance.

activities.prompt: At night, a car with no lights is hard to see on the road. The strange aeroplane had no lights on its wings. Still it flew quietly next to him. What does this tell us about the aeroplane?
options: It was strange and mysterious, not like a normal plane.
Its lights were too bright for anyone to look at.
It was flying only in the bright light of day.
It was flying much slower than the Dakota plane.

why.Its lights were too bright for anyone to: Wrong: this thinks the lights were too bright, but the plane had no lights at all.
why.It was flying only in the bright light o: Wrong: this thinks it was daytime, but he was flying inside dark storm clouds.
why.It was flying much slower than the Dakot: Wrong: this thinks about speed, but the detail about lights shows it was mysterious.

activities.explanation: Right: a plane with no lights, yet flying safely beside him, feels strange and mysterious.

lessons.sceneCaption: A storm cloud seen from an aeroplane, like the dark clouds the pilot flew into.

lessons.title: How to Tell Wild Animals

activities.prompt: How can you tell which wild animal is sneaking up on you?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Funny Guide to Wild Beasts
activities.body: This poem jokes about how to know wild animals. It gives dangerous ways to tell them apart. A large tawny beast that roars at you is the Asian Lion. A beast with black stripes on a yellow ground is the Bengal Tiger. A spotted beast that leaps on you is the Leopard. A creature that hugs you hard in your yard is a Bear. Hyenas come with merry smiles, but weeping ones are Crocodiles.
keyPoints: The poem suggests dangerous ways to identify wild animals.
Each animal is known by one funny clue, like stripes or spots.
A novice might be puzzled to tell beasts of prey apart.
activities.explanation: The poem teaches animal names through jokes about meeting them.

activities.prompt: Ravi reads that a spotted beast will leap on you. He wonders: why does the poem say roaring with pain will do no good?
steps: The spotted beast is the Leopard, and it leaps on you at once, so the attack has already started.
Roaring with pain is your cry, but the Leopard does not care about your cry.
The poem says he will only leap and leap again, so your cry changes nothing.
So roaring with pain is useless because the Leopard keeps attacking anyway.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: You go by chance to the jungles in the east. A large tawny beast advances and roars at you. Which animal is it?
options: Bengal Tiger
Asian Lion
Leopard
activities.explanation: The lesson says a large tawny beast in the eastern jungles may roar at you. If it roars as you are dying, you know it is the Asian Lion.

activities.prompt: If a beast's hide is covered with ______, and it leaps on you, you will know it is the Leopard.
activities.hint: Think of a pattern you might see on its skin.
activities.explanation: A spotted hide is the clue for the Leopard in the poem.

activities.prompt: A creature in your yard hugs you very hard. What is it, and what happens if you have doubts?
options: A Bear; it gives you one more caress
A Leopard; it leaps and leaps again
A Hyena; it comes with a merry smile
activities.explanation: A hard hug in your yard means it is a Bear. If you have doubts, it will give you just one more caress.

activities.prompt: Match each animal to its funny clue from the poem.
activities.explanation: Each animal in the poem has its own clue, from a roar to a hug to tears.

activities.prompt: Put these moments in order, as the poem tells them for the Leopard.
items: You see a beast whose hide is covered with spots
It leaps on you
You roar with pain
It leaps and leaps again
activities.explanation: First you spot the hide, then it leaps, then you roar, and it leaps again.

activities.prompt: Why does roaring with pain do no good when the Leopard leaps on you?
options: Because he will only leap and leap again
Because he will give you one more caress
Because he will greet you with black stripes
activities.explanation: The poem says roaring with pain does no good. The Leopard will only keep leaping.

activities.prompt: A noble wild beast with black stripes on a yellow ground greets you. The poet says you should notice if it eats you. Why does the poet say this?
options: Because eating shows the beast is still hungry.
Because you will know it is the tiger only too late.
Because tigers like to share their food with people.
Because the stripes may wash off when it eats.

why.Because eating shows the beast is still: She thinks the line is about hunger; it is really about knowing the beast too late.
why.Because tigers like to share their food: She takes the funny line as a kind act; the poem is joking about danger.
why.Because the stripes may wash off when it: She invents a reason about stripes; the line is about the danger, not stripes.

activities.explanation: Right: the joke is that you learn the rule only while being eaten.

activities.prompt: A creature in Sana's yard hugs her very hard. Her little brother says, "It loves you!" What does the poem make us understand about this hug?
options: The hug is a friendly game from a pet.
The hug is a danger sign; it is a Bear.
The hug means the creature wants some food.
The hug means the creature is afraid of her.

She takes the hug as play; the poem warns a hard hug is a Bear.
why.The hug means the creature wants some fo: She thinks hugging means hunger; the poem gives no such meaning.
why.The hug means the creature is afraid of: She thinks hugging comes from fear; the poem links it to the Bear.

activities.explanation: Right: a very hard hug in your yard means you can be sure it is a Bear.

activities.prompt: If you have doubts, the Bear will give you just one more caress. What does this tell us about the Bear's caress?
options: The caress is safe and gentle to feel.
The caress proves the Bear is your friend.
The caress is also dangerous for you.
The caress means the Bear will run away.

She thinks a caress is always gentle; here it comes from a dangerous Bear.
why.The caress proves the Bear is your frien: She thinks the caress shows friendship; it is really another risky hug.
She thinks the caress ends the meeting; the poem says nothing about leaving.

activities.explanation: Right: one more caress from a Bear is one more dangerous squeeze.

lessons.title: The Ball Poem

activities.prompt: Why can't money fix every loss we feel?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What the poem is about
activities.body: A boy loses his ball. It bounces down the street and falls into the water. He stands rigid and trembling with grief. The poet does not offer him money for a new ball. Money cannot buy back what is lost. The boy is learning his first lesson about loss in a world of possessions.
keyPoints: A boy loses his ball and is very upset.
The ball bounces down the street and into the water.
The poet will not intrude or offer money.
The boy learns his first lesson about loss.
activities.explanation: The poem uses one lost ball to teach a big lesson about loss.

activities.prompt: Ravi loses his favourite toy car in a pond. His friend says, 'I will buy you a new one.' Why does Ravi still feel sad?
steps: The old car was his own thing, so losing it hurts him inside.
A new car costs money, but money cannot bring back the old one.
This is his first time losing something, so he must learn to accept loss.
So Ravi is sad because a new car cannot replace what he lost.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Where did the ball go after bouncing down the street?
options: Into a shop
Over into the water
Into a friend's bag
Under a bus
activities.explanation: The poet saw the ball bounce merrily down the street and then over into the water.

activities.prompt: The boy stares down into the ______, where his ball went.
activities.hint: It is the place by the water where ships rest.
activities.explanation: Great thinking. The boy stares into the harbour, watching where his ball disappeared.

activities.prompt: Why does the poet say a dime for another ball is worthless?
options: Money is external and cannot buy back the lost ball
The boy does not like money at all
Balls cost more than a dime in the market
The poet has no money to give
activities.explanation: A dime, another ball, is worthless. No one buys a ball back, because money is external.

activities.prompt: Match each phrase from the poem with what it tells us.
activities.explanation: Each phrase paints one part of the picture: the boy's grief, the lost ball, and why money cannot help.

activities.prompt: Put these events from the poem in the right order.
items: The ball bounces merrily down the street
The ball goes over into the water
The boy stands rigid and trembling
The boy stares down into the harbour
The boy learns the epistemology of loss
activities.explanation: Superb. The ball is lost first, then the grief strikes, then the boy watches and slowly learns.

activities.prompt: What big lesson is the boy learning behind his desperate eyes?
options: How to swim in the harbour
How to earn money for new balls
His first responsibility in a world of possessions
How to bounce a ball down the street
activities.explanation: Wonderful. The boy senses his first responsibility in a world of possessions, where things are lost and cannot be bought back.

activities.prompt: Meena's kite flew away into a tree. She stands still and stares at it. What is she feeling?
options: She is planning how to climb the tree.
She is feeling a deep shock at losing it.
She is bored and wants to go home.
She is angry with the wind.

This thinks she wants to act, but standing still shows grief, not a plan.
This misses her feelings; staring at the kite shows she cares about it.
This blames something outside, but her stillness shows grief, not anger.

activities.explanation: Right: standing still and staring show a big, shaking sadness inside.

activities.prompt: Arjun's marble rolls into a drain. His mother says, 'I will get you ten more.' Why does this not help him?
options: Because he does not like his mother's gifts.
Because he wants ten marbles, not one.
Because money cannot bring back that marble.
Because he is too shy to take a gift.

why.Because he does not like his mother's gi: This thinks he rejects her kindness, but the problem is the loss itself.
This thinks he wants more marbles, but he wants his own old one.
This adds shyness, which is not the real reason he stays sad.

activities.explanation: Right: money is outside him; it cannot buy back his own lost thing.

activities.prompt: The poet watches a boy lose his ball. He stands back and does not speak. Why does he do this?
options: He is busy watching the water in the harbour.
He wants the boy to learn the loss himself.
He does not know how to buy a new ball.
He thinks the boy will not see him there.

why.He is busy watching the water in the har: This confuses the poet's looking with a reason to stay silent.
This thinks the poet's problem is money, but it is about the boy's learning.
why.He thinks the boy will not see him there: This thinks the poet is hiding, but he stays back on purpose.

activities.explanation: Right: the poet will not intrude, because the boy must learn loss himself.

activities.prompt: A girl loses her first pet fish. Her brother says, 'Fish die all the time.' What does this tell her about life?
options: That her brother does not love fish at all.
That she should keep her fish tank cleaner.
That losing things is a part of life.
That she must never keep a pet again.

why.That her brother does not love fish at a: This thinks the brother is unkind, but he is stating a fact about life.
why.That she should keep her fish tank clean: This looks for a fix, but the lesson is about loss, not cleaning.
This jumps to fear; the lesson is accepting loss, not giving up pets.

activities.explanation: Right: like balls, things we love get lost always, and we must learn this.

lessons.title: Test practice
lessons.sceneAlt: A single seagull flying above the blue sea.
lessons.sceneCaption: A seagull flying over the sea in Garopaba.

sceneCredit.text: Seagull flying over the sea by Heylenny, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Heylenny

activities.context: A young seagull stood alone on his ledge. The day before, his two brothers and his sister had flown away, though their wings were shorter than his. He had run to the brink to join them, but when he looked down at the sea, which seemed miles below, fear gripped him and he flapped back to the little hole where he slept. His parents called shrilly and scolded him, threatening to let him starve on his ledge, yet he could not move. He watched them teach the others to skim the waves and dive for fish.
activities.prompt: If the young seagull's wings had been shorter than his siblings' wings, what would most likely have happened when he reached the brink?
options: He would still have hesitated, because his fear came from doubt in himself, not from his wings.
He would have flown away at once, since short wings always fly better.
He would have fallen straight into the sea, because short wings cannot flap at all.
He would have stayed on the ledge happily, as his parents would stop scolding him.

why.He would have flown away at once, since: Wrong: nothing suggests short wings make flying easier; this reverses the passage's point.
why.He would have fallen straight into the s: Wrong: the passage never says short wings stop a bird from flapping or cause falling.
why.He would have stayed on the ledge happil: Wrong: his parents scolded him for not flying, so staying would not please them.

activities.explanation: Correct: the passage shows his real problem was lack of courage, since even shorter-winged siblings flew.

activities.context: A young seagull stood alone on his ledge. The day before, his two brothers and his sister had flown away, though their wings were shorter than his. He had run to the brink to join them, but when he looked down at the sea, which seemed miles below, fear gripped him and he flapped back to the little hole where he slept. His parents called shrilly and scolded him, threatening to let him starve on his ledge, yet he could not move. He watched them teach the others to skim the waves and dive for fish.
activities.prompt: Why did his parents threaten to let him starve on his ledge?
options: To push him past his fear by making staying on the ledge more painful than trying to fly.
Because they were angry that he had eaten all the fish the family had caught.
Because they wanted him to sleep longer in the little hole under the ledge.
Because they had decided to abandon him and fly to a new home forever.

why.Because they were angry that he had eate: Wrong: the passage gives no mention of him eating fish or stealing food.
why.Because they wanted him to sleep longer: Wrong: they wanted him off the ledge, not resting in the hole.
why.Because they had decided to abandon him: Wrong: they kept calling and teaching the others nearby, not leaving him.

activities.explanation: Correct: hunger would force him to act, turning his fear of flying into a greater need.

activities.context: A young seagull stood alone on his ledge. The day before, his two brothers and his sister had flown away, though their wings were shorter than his. He had run to the brink to join them, but when he looked down at the sea, which seemed miles below, fear gripped him and he flapped back to the little hole where he slept. His parents called shrilly and scolded him, threatening to let him starve on his ledge, yet he could not move. He watched them teach the others to skim the waves and dive for fish.
activities.prompt: If his parents had stopped calling to him and simply flown off with the siblings, what would most likely have happened to the young seagull?
options: He would probably have remained alone and hungry, since only his family's pressure and example were pulling him towards flight.
He would immediately have dived for fish, because hunger teaches birds to hunt by instinct.
He would have flown away the same day, since birds always copy their brothers and sisters.
He would have grown brave on his own, because loneliness removes all fear.

why.He would immediately have dived for fish: Wrong: he could not even move from the ledge, so hunting at sea was impossible for him.
why.He would have flown away the same day, s: Wrong: he had already failed to copy his siblings the day before.
why.He would have grown brave on his own, be: Wrong: the passage shows his fear deepened with waiting, not that solitude made him brave.

activities.explanation: Correct: without their calls, scolding and example, nothing would push him past his paralysis.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The young seagull went back to the little hole under the ledge where he slept at night.
Reason (R): When he ran to the brink and tried to flap his wings, he became afraid.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: His fear at the brink directly caused him to retreat to the hole under the ledge, so the reason explains the assertion.

activities.prompt: Explain why the young seagull could not fly even though his wings were not the problem.
activities.answer: The young seagull's real problem was fear, not weakness. When he ran to the brink and tried to flap his wings, he became afraid, because the sea stretched down beneath and seemed miles down. He felt certain his wings would never support him. Yet his brothers and sister, whose wings were even shorter, had flown away the day before. This proves his wings were capable; it was his lack of courage that kept him rooted to the ledge, unable to move even when his parents scolded him and threatened to let him starve.
points: States that fear, not weak wings, held him back
Quotes the detail of the sea seeming miles down
Uses the siblings' shorter wings as proof his wings were fine
Mentions his certainty that his wings would not support him
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: The sun was rising and blazing on the south-facing ledge where the young bird stood alone. He had not eaten since the previous nightfall, and the heat made his hunger sharper. He stepped to the brink, stood on one leg, hid the other under his wing, and pretended to sleep, though only his mother was watching him. She tore at a piece of fish and scrapped her beak on the rock. The sight maddened him; he begged loudly, but she screamed back derisively, picked up a piece of fish, and flew across to him.
activities.prompt: The mother halts just opposite him with the fish almost within reach, but does not come closer. What is she most likely trying to make happen?
options: She wants his hunger to push him off the ledge towards her
She is too tired to fly the last little distance
She wants the father to take the fish from her
She is waiting for the siblings to wake up and share it

why.She is too tired to fly the last little: She flew across easily, so tiredness does not fit the situation.
why.She wants the father to take the fish fr: The father is busy preening and takes no notice of the young bird.
why.She is waiting for the siblings to wake: The siblings are dozing and the mother's attention is fixed on this one bird.

activities.explanation: Correct: by keeping the fish just out of reach, she uses his hunger to force him into moving off the ledge.

activities.context: The sun was rising and blazing on the south-facing ledge where the young bird stood alone. He had not eaten since the previous nightfall, and the heat made his hunger sharper. He stepped to the brink, stood on one leg, hid the other under his wing, and pretended to sleep, though only his mother was watching him. She tore at a piece of fish and scrapped her beak on the rock. The sight maddened him; he begged loudly, but she screamed back derisively, picked up a piece of fish, and flew across to him.
activities.prompt: Suppose the mother had dropped the fish straight into his beak while he stood on the ledge. What would most probably have been the result?
options: He would have eaten and stayed where he was, still afraid to move off
He would have dived into the air immediately after swallowing
He would have chased her out over the sea for more fish
He would have woken his siblings and fought them for food

why.He would have dived into the air immedia: Nothing in the situation suggests eating would suddenly give him the courage to fly.
why.He would have chased her out over the se: He is too weak and frightened to chase anyone; he is begging, not attacking.
why.He would have woken his siblings and fou: The siblings are asleep and there is no sign of quarrelling among them.

activities.explanation: Correct: feeding him on the ledge removes the hunger that is the only force strong enough to make him leave.

activities.context: The sun was rising and blazing on the south-facing ledge where the young bird stood alone. He had not eaten since the previous nightfall, and the heat made his hunger sharper. He stepped to the brink, stood on one leg, hid the other under his wing, and pretended to sleep, though only his mother was watching him. She tore at a piece of fish and scrapped her beak on the rock. The sight maddened him; he begged loudly, but she screamed back derisively, picked up a piece of fish, and flew across to him.
activities.prompt: After he dives at the fish and falls outwards and downwards, a monstrous terror seizes him and his heart stands still. What does this moment most clearly show about what was really holding him back on the ledge?
options: His fear of the fall itself, which only left him once he was actually in the air
His anger with his mother for teasing him with the fish
His weakness from hunger, which made standing impossible
His dislike of the blazing heat on the ledge

why.His anger with his mother for teasing hi: He begs for food eagerly; anger at his mother is not what grips him in the air.
why.His weakness from hunger, which made sta: Hunger made him act, not freeze; the freezing comes from terror at falling.
why.His dislike of the blazing heat on the l: The heat made him hungrier, but it is not what seizes him mid-fall.

activities.explanation: Correct: the terror striking only when he is falling shows fear of the drop, not of hunger or heat, was the real barrier.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The young bird dived at the piece of fish and fell outwards and downwards off the ledge.
Reason (R): Maddened by hunger after a night without food, he could not resist the fish held almost within his reach.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and his desperate hunger directly explains why he dived at the fish.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The young bird's father flew across to him carrying a piece of fish.
Reason (R): While the siblings dozed and the father preened, only the mother was looking at the young bird.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because it was the mother who flew across with the fish, though the reason stated is true.

activities.prompt: Explain why the mother's behaviour, though it looked cruel, was actually the best way to help the young bird.
activities.answer: The mother's behaviour looked cruel because she screamed derisively at her begging child and teased him with fish she never delivered. Yet it was the best help she could give, because hunger was the only force strong enough to overcome his fear. By tearing at fish, scrapping her beak and halting just out of reach, she tempted him until maddened hunger drove him to dive. Had she simply fed him on the ledge, he would have remained there, and he would never have taken his first flight.
points: Her actions seemed cruel: derisive screaming and withholding the fish
Hunger was the only force strong enough to beat his fear
She deliberately tempted him by halting just out of reach
Feeding him directly would have kept him on the ledge forever
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: It was one thirty in the morning. The pilot of an old Dakota was flying over France back to England. The moon was coming up behind him and stars were shining; there was no cloud in the sky. Happy to be alone above the sleeping countryside, he was dreaming of his holiday and his family. He saw the lights of a big city, called Paris Control as Dakota DS 088, was told to turn twelve degrees west, checked his map and compass, switched to his second and last fuel tank, and turned. Paris was about 150 kilometres behind him when huge storm clouds appeared.
activities.prompt: Why did switching to the second fuel tank matter so much once he had turned twelve degrees west?
options: On the new heading he was flying on his final supply of fuel, so any delay left him with nothing in reserve.
The act of turning burned up the whole first tank in one go.
Paris Control had told him that the first tank was nearly empty.
Aeroplanes always need both tanks running together when flying west.

why.The act of turning burned up the whole f: A turn of direction does not empty a fuel tank; this confuses the turn with fuel use.
why.Paris Control had told him that the firs: Paris Control only gave him a heading; nothing was said about fuel.
why.Aeroplanes always need both tanks runnin: This is a made-up general rule; the real reason is simply that the second tank was his last one.

activities.explanation: Correct: the second tank was his last, so after the turn there was no spare fuel if anything went wrong.

activities.context: It was one thirty in the morning. The pilot of an old Dakota was flying over France back to England. The moon was coming up behind him and stars were shining; there was no cloud in the sky. Happy to be alone above the sleeping countryside, he was dreaming of his holiday and his family. He saw the lights of a big city, called Paris Control as Dakota DS 088, was told to turn twelve degrees west, checked his map and compass, switched to his second and last fuel tank, and turned. Paris was about 150 kilometres behind him when huge storm clouds appeared.
activities.prompt: If the pilot had NOT radioed Paris Control when he saw the lights of the big city, what would most likely have happened next?
options: He would have kept flying on his original heading and would never have turned twelve degrees west.
He would have landed at the big city below to take on more fuel.
The huge storm clouds would not have formed in his path.
He would have reached England sooner and had an even better breakfast.

why.He would have landed at the big city bel: Nothing in the situation suggests he wanted or needed to land; he was heading home.
why.The huge storm clouds would not have for: The storm clouds were already there; his radio call could not change the weather.
why.He would have reached England sooner and: Without the instruction he would be off the planned route, not ahead of schedule.

activities.explanation: Correct: the instruction to turn twelve degrees west came only because he contacted Paris Control.

activities.context: It was one thirty in the morning. The pilot of an old Dakota was flying over France back to England. The moon was coming up behind him and stars were shining; there was no cloud in the sky. Happy to be alone above the sleeping countryside, he was dreaming of his holiday and his family. He saw the lights of a big city, called Paris Control as Dakota DS 088, was told to turn twelve degrees west, checked his map and compass, switched to his second and last fuel tank, and turned. Paris was about 150 kilometres behind him when huge storm clouds appeared.
activities.prompt: Paris is about 150 kilometres behind him and huge storm clouds have appeared. What is the pilot's real situation at that moment?
options: He is committed to a new heading on his last fuel tank, so the flight is no longer the easy trip he imagined.
He can simply turn back to Paris and land safely before the storm reaches him.
The storm is no problem because the sky was completely clear when he checked his watch.
He should switch back to the first fuel tank to power his way out of the storm.

why.He can simply turn back to Paris and lan: Turning back is not offered as an option, and his fuel situation makes a long return risky.
why.The storm is no problem because the sky: The clear sky was at the start of the flight; it says nothing about the storm ahead now.
why.He should switch back to the first fuel: The first tank has already been used; he is on his second and last one.

activities.explanation: Correct: the new route plus the last tank means the storm now threatens both his path and his fuel.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The pilot knew he was flying on his final supply of fuel for the rest of the journey.
Reason (R): He had already switched to his second and last fuel tank.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and being on the second and last tank is exactly why the remaining fuel was his final supply.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The pilot expected to be in time for breakfast.
Reason (R): Paris Control promised him that he would land early.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The pilot did expect breakfast, but Paris Control only gave him a heading and made no promise about landing early.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between the pilot's situation before he turned twelve degrees west and his situation after the turn?
activities.answer: Before the turn, the pilot was on his own original course over France. He had seen the lights of a big city, identified himself to Paris Control as Dakota DS 088, and was still deciding when to call them. After Paris Control told him to turn twelve degrees west, he checked his map and compass, switched to his second and last fuel tank, and followed their instruction. The difference is that he was now flying a route chosen by Control rather than his own plan, and he had used up his first tank, leaving only his final reserve. Soon afterwards, with Paris 150 kilometres behind, the storm clouds appeared.
points: Before: on his own course, had seen city lights, was thinking of calling Paris Control.
After: obeyed Paris Control's instruction to turn twelve degrees west.
After: checked map and compass and switched to the second and last fuel tank.
Notes the result: committed to the new route with only final fuel, then met the storm.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Flying his old Dakota through storm clouds, the narrator suddenly saw another aeroplane in the black clouds near him. It had no lights on its wings, yet it flew steadily beside him. Its pilot turned his face towards him, and the narrator felt glad. The pilot lifted one hand and waved, telling him to follow, and then turned north in front of the Dakota so it would be easier to follow. The narrator, who believed this stranger knew he was lost, followed like an obedient child, though his last tank held fuel for only five or ten minutes.
activities.prompt: If the strange aeroplane had stayed in the clouds for another twenty minutes instead of starting to go down, the narrator would most likely have —
options: climbed above the clouds and found his own way safely
run out of fuel before reaching any runway
seen the two lines of lights without any help
turned back through the storm to his original route

why.climbed above the clouds and found his o: Wrong: he was lost inside the clouds; climbing would not have shown him the way.
why.seen the two lines of lights without any: Wrong: he could not see anything in the black clouds; the lights appeared only after coming out.
why.turned back through the storm to his ori: Wrong: turning back into the storm would have made his danger worse, not better.

activities.explanation: Right: the last tank held only five or ten minutes of fuel, so extra time in the clouds would finish it.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Two Stories about Flying

activities.prompt: Why could the young seagull not fly away with his brothers and sister?
options: He was afraid his wings would not support him.
He did not like the taste of fish.
He wanted to sleep in his little hole all day.
His parents told him to stay behind.
activities.explanation: He felt sure his wings would never hold him, so fear kept him on the ledge. Well done for spotting his real worry!

activities.prompt: The mother seagull flew across and dropped the fish straight into her chick's beak.
activities.explanation: She halted just out of reach with the fish. Her hunger-maddened chick had to dive at it, and that is how he fell outwards and learnt to fly.

activities.prompt: Over the radio, the pilot said he was Dakota DS ______.
activities.hint: Three digits, like a room number.
activities.explanation: He switched on the radio and gave his plane's full name. Great memory!

activities.prompt: Match each clue from the poem to the animal it points to.
pairs: Roars at you as you die
Covered with spots and leaps on you
Hugs you very hard in your yard
activities.explanation: The poem gives funny, dangerous ways to tell wild animals apart. You matched every clue perfectly!

activities.prompt: Put the events of the seagull's first flight in the right order.
items: He was too afraid to fly with his family.
His parents scolded him and threatened to let him starve.
His mother flew across to him with a piece of fish.
She halted with the fish just out of his reach.
He dived at the fish and fell outwards and downwards.
activities.explanation: Fear came first, then hunger, then the dive that changed everything. You know this story well!

activities.prompt: Why did the pilot follow the strange black aeroplane like an obedient child?
options: He thought the pilot knew he was lost and was helping.
He wanted to race the other plane through the clouds.
He hoped the other plane had spare fuel for him.
He was following the lights of a big city below.
activities.explanation: The strange pilot waved him to follow, and he believed help had come. Lovely careful reading!

activities.prompt: Paris Control told the pilot to turn twelve degrees east.
activities.explanation: Paris Control said twelve degrees west, and he turned west after checking his map and compass. Watch those directions!

activities.prompt: Behind his desperate eyes, the boy is learning the epistemology of ______.
activities.hint: It is the sad thing that happened to his ball.
activities.explanation: Losing the ball teaches him what loss truly means. A big idea, and you found it!

activities.prompt: In The Ball Poem, why is a dime for a new ball worthless?
options: Money is external and cannot buy back what is lost.
The boy does not know where shops are.
The ball was too old to be replaced.
The poet refuses to give the boy any money.
activities.explanation: No one buys a ball back, because money is external. The boy learns his first lesson about possessions.

activities.prompt: Put the events of the pilot's night flight in the right order.
items: His watch showed one thirty in the morning.
Paris Control told him to turn twelve degrees west.
Huge storm clouds appeared about 150 kilometres past Paris.
A strange aeroplane waved for him to follow.
He came out of the clouds and saw the runway lights.
activities.explanation: From a peaceful start to storm, rescue and a safe landing. You ordered the whole journey like a true navigator!

chapters.title: The Diary of a Young Girl
chapters.summary: In this chapter: before you read: anne frank and her diary; anne begins her diary; anne's brief sketch of her life; saturday, 20 june 1942: class and first essay.

lessons.title: Before You Read: Anne Frank and Her Diary

activities.prompt: Who was the girl behind the world's most famous diary?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet Anne Frank
activities.body: Anne Frank was a German-born Jewish girl. Her family moved to Amsterdam when the Nazis gained power in Germany. As persecutions grew worse, they hid in hidden rooms in her father's office building. Anne wrote a diary while hiding with her family and four friends. After two years, the group was betrayed. Only her father Otto survived and later published her diary.
keyPoints: Anne Frank was a German-born Jewish girl who lived in Amsterdam.
She wrote her diary while hiding with her family and four friends.
Her father Otto was the only survivor and published her diary.
activities.explanation: This little girl's diary became one of the most famous books in the world.

activities.prompt: A family moves to a new country when a scary group takes power. Later they hide inside secret rooms. Why would they do both things?
steps: The family is Jewish, and the new rulers hurt Jewish people, so home no longer feels safe.
Moving to another city helps at first, because the scary group rules only their old country.
But the scary group later takes over the new city too, so even there they can be caught.
So hiding in secret rooms is the next step, because walls can hide them better than a new address can.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What was Anne Frank's full name?
options: Anne Marie Frank
Anneliese Marie Frank
Anneliese Otto Frank
Marie Anneliese Frank
activities.explanation: Her full name was Anneliese Marie Frank. Anne was her short name.

activities.prompt: Anne's family moved to ______ after the Nazis gained power in Germany.
activities.hint: It is a city in the Netherlands where her father's office building was.
activities.explanation: The family moved to Amsterdam to be safe. That is where they later went into hiding.

activities.prompt: Why did Anne's family go into hiding in July 1942?
options: Because their school closed down
Because persecutions increased
Because their house was too small
Because Otto changed his job
activities.explanation: As persecutions increased, the family went into hiding. It was a dangerous time for Jewish families.

activities.prompt: Match each person or group to what the lesson says about them.
pairs: wrote a diary while in hiding
the only survivor who returned to Amsterdam
hid with the family in the hidden rooms
activities.explanation: Each person played a part in Anne's story. You matched them all correctly!

activities.prompt: Put these events from Anne's story in the correct order.
items: The Nazis gained power in Germany
Anne's family moved to Amsterdam
The family went into hiding in July 1942
After two years, the group was betrayed
Otto returned to Amsterdam as the only survivor
activities.explanation: The story moves step by step: power, move, hiding, betrayal, return. You followed it perfectly.

activities.prompt: What did Otto Frank do after he returned to Amsterdam?
options: He burned Anne's diary
He moved back to Germany
He had her diary published in English
He wrote a new diary himself
activities.explanation: Otto had Anne's diary published in English as The Diary of a Young Girl. The whole world could then read her words.

activities.prompt: Riya's family leaves their town when a mean group takes power there. They go to a town far away. Why did the family move?
options: They wanted a bigger house in a new town.
They felt safer far from the mean group.
Riya's school in the old town closed.
They wanted to live near their old friends.

why.They wanted a bigger house in a new town: This thinks about comfort, but the story says fear made them move.
This thinks about school, but fear is the real reason given.
why.They wanted to live near their old frien: This thinks about friends, but the family left because of danger.

activities.explanation: Right. A mean group in power makes people feel unsafe, so they run.

activities.prompt: Some people hide in secret rooms behind a wall in an office. Soldiers are searching houses outside. Why did they pick secret rooms?
options: Office rooms are big and very comfortable to live in.
They wanted to keep working in the office daily.
Hidden rooms are hard for the soldiers to find.
They could not pay rent for a normal house.

why.Office rooms are big and very comfortabl: This thinks about comfort, but hiding is about safety, not comfort.
why.They wanted to keep working in the offic: This thinks about work, but the goal is to stay unseen.
why.They could not pay rent for a normal hou: This thinks about money, but danger, not rent, made them hide.

activities.explanation: Right. 'Hidden' means hard to find, which keeps them safe.

activities.prompt: A girl writes a diary while hiding. Years later, her father prints the diary as a book for everyone to read. How did the father probably feel about the diary?
options: He felt it was too sad to show anyone.
He felt it was precious and should be shared.
He felt it was a private thing to lock away.
He felt it was boring and not worth reading.

Sadness may be true, but printing it shows he valued it.
why.He felt it was a private thing to lock a: Keeping it private is the opposite of printing it for all.
why.He felt it was boring and not worth read: Nobody prints a book they think is boring.

activities.explanation: Right. Printing a book means you think it is worth sharing.

activities.prompt: The word 'persecution' means being hurt or hunted for who you are. A family hides when 'persecutions increased'. What does 'increased' tell you happened?
options: The persecutions became worse over time.
The persecutions stopped after some time.
The persecutions moved to a new country.
The persecutions were written in a book.

why.The persecutions stopped after some time: If it stopped, they would not need to hide at all.
Moving to a new place is not what 'increased' means.
Writing in a book has nothing to do with 'increased'.

activities.explanation: Right. 'Increased' means the danger grew bigger, so they hid.

activities.prompt: A hiding family is caught after two years. The story says they were 'betrayed'. What must have happened?
options: The family got lost and walked out by mistake.
The secret rooms slowly broke and fell down.
Someone told the enemy where the family was.
The family decided to stop hiding and leave.

why.The family got lost and walked out by mi: Getting lost is an accident, but 'betrayed' means a person did it.
why.The secret rooms slowly broke and fell d: Broken rooms are about the building, not about a person's act.
why.The family decided to stop hiding and le: Choosing to leave is their own act, not a betrayal.

activities.explanation: Right. To betray is to give away a secret to the enemy.

lessons.title: Anne Begins Her Diary

activities.prompt: Why would a girl call a notebook her best friend?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why Anne Starts a Diary
activities.body: Anne says writing in a diary is a strange experience. She has never written anything before. She starts one because she has no real friend, though about thirty people can be called friends. She feels like writing and needs to get things off her chest. She remembers a saying: 'Paper has more patience than people.'
keyPoints: Anne had never written anything before.
She started the diary because she did not have a friend.
She remembers: 'Paper has more patience than people.'
She needs to get things off her chest.
activities.explanation: Anne writes to share her feelings with paper, her patient new friend.

activities.prompt: Meera has many classmates who smile at her. But she feels lonely at home in the evening. She starts writing her feelings in a notebook. Why does she do this?
steps: Meera has classmates, but classmates are not the same as a close friend, so she has no one to really talk to.
Because she cannot share her feelings with a person, the feelings stay inside her chest and feel heavy.
A notebook never interrupts, never laughs, and never gets tired of listening, so it is safer than people.
So she writes to get her feelings out, and the notebook becomes her quiet friend.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Why did Anne start writing a diary?
options: She wanted to win a prize
She did not have a friend
Her teacher told her to
She loved writing stories
activities.explanation: Anne started the diary because she did not have a friend. Well done!

activities.prompt: How many people can Anne call friends?
options: About thirty people
About ten people
Only one person
Nobody at all
activities.explanation: There are about thirty people she can call friends, but none is a real friend.

activities.prompt: Anne remembered the saying: 'Paper has more ______ than people.'
activities.hint: It means waiting calmly without complaining.
activities.explanation: Paper never interrupts or gets tired of listening. That is why it has more patience.

activities.prompt: Match each phrase from Anne's diary page with its meaning.
activities.explanation: These phrases show how Anne felt that day. Great matching!

activities.prompt: Put the events from Anne's day in the right order.
items: She felt bored, wondering whether to stay in or go out
She stayed where she was, brooding
She thought of the saying about paper and people
She felt like writing and began her diary
activities.explanation: First she felt bored, then she sat brooding, then the saying came to her, and at last she wrote.

activities.prompt: Anne thinks nobody will care about her musings later. Why does she write anyway?
options: She wants to become famous
Her sister asked her to write
She needs to get things off her chest
She wants to teach others
activities.explanation: She feels like writing and needs to get things off her chest. That is a brave and honest reason!

activities.prompt: Sara has a loving mother and a kind brother. She has many friendly classmates. Still, at night she feels alone. What does this show?
options: Kind people around you may still not feel like true friends.
She does not really love her mother or her brother.
Her classmates are unkind and treat her badly.
She only feels happy when she is at school.

why.She does not really love her mother or h: Wrong. Feeling lonely does not mean she lacks love for her family.
why.Her classmates are unkind and treat her: Wrong. The classmates are friendly; the problem is closeness, not unkindness.
why.She only feels happy when she is at scho: Wrong. Nothing in the situation says school makes her happy.

activities.explanation: Right. Like Anne, you can have loving family and many friends yet lack one true friend.

activities.prompt: Nina sits with her chin in her hands. She feels low and bored. She does not know whether to go out or stay in. What will she most likely do next?
options: Stay where she is and think deeply about her feelings.
Jump up happily and call all her friends outside.
Go to sleep at once and forget everything.
Start cleaning her room to feel busy again.

why.Jump up happily and call all her friends: Wrong. Her low, bored mood does not match jumping up happily.
why.Go to sleep at once and forget everythin: Wrong. Brooding means thinking, not sleeping.
why.Start cleaning her room to feel busy aga: Wrong. Nothing shows she wants to do chores.

activities.explanation: Right. Feeling low and bored with nowhere to go leads to sitting and brooding, like Anne.

activities.prompt: A boy says, 'Paper has more patience than people.' He just had a fight with his friends. What does his line mean?
options: A page listens to your feelings without ever getting tired of you.
Paper is stronger than people in a real fight.
People should always write letters instead of talking.
Paper lasts longer than people live in this world.

why.Paper is stronger than people in a real: Wrong. He means patience, not physical strength.
why.People should always write letters inste: Wrong. He is not saying people should stop talking to each other.
why.Paper lasts longer than people live in t: Wrong. This takes the word 'longer' too literally.

activities.explanation: Right. Patience here means a page never interrupts or judges you while you pour out feelings.

activities.prompt: Anu writes in her diary every day. She says, 'Later, maybe nobody, not even me, will read this.' But she keeps writing. Why does she keep writing?
options: Writing helps her empty the heavy feelings inside her.
She wants to become famous for her writing one day.
She hopes her teacher will collect and mark it.
She is practising to win a writing prize.

why.She wants to become famous for her writi: Wrong. She expects no readers at all, so fame is not her goal.
why.She hopes her teacher will collect and m: Wrong. A private diary is not written for a teacher's marks.
why.She is practising to win a writing prize: Wrong. Winning a prize needs readers, which she does not expect.

activities.explanation: Right. Like Anne, she writes to get things off her chest, not for readers.

lessons.sceneCaption: The cover of the diary of Anne Frank.

lessons.title: Anne's Brief Sketch of Her Life

activities.prompt: Why did Anne decide to tell Kitty her whole life story first?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why Anne Tells Her Life Story
activities.body: Anne wants to write her stories to Kitty, her diary. But she feels no one would understand them without knowing her first. So she gives a brief sketch of her life. She tells us about her parents, her sister Margot, and how her family moved from Germany to Holland.
keyPoints: Anne writes a sketch of her life so people will understand her stories to Kitty.
Her family lived in Frankfurt before moving to Holland.
Her sister Margot is older than her.
activities.explanation: Anne shares her past so her diary friend Kitty can really know her.

activities.prompt: Anne writes her life story for Kitty, a diary. Why does she stop and explain her whole past first?
steps: Kitty is a diary, so Kitty cannot ask Anne questions about her family.
If Anne jumps into her stories, Kitty will not know who the people are.
So Anne first gives a short sketch of her life so the stories make sense.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Why does Anne write a brief sketch of her life?
options: Her teacher asked her to write it
No one would understand her stories to Kitty
She wanted to win a writing prize
Her sister Margot asked her for it
activities.explanation: Anne says nobody would understand her stories to Kitty without knowing her life first. Well done!

activities.prompt: Anne lived in Frankfurt until she was ______ years old.
activities.hint: Think of a small child's age, not a school year.
activities.explanation: Anne lived in Frankfurt until she was four, then her family's life changed.

activities.prompt: Where was Anne's sister Margot born?
options: In Holland
In Aachen
In Frankfurt in Germany
In England
activities.explanation: Margot was born in Frankfurt in Germany in 1926. Great thinking!

activities.prompt: Match each person or place to what the lesson says about them.
pairs: Anne's mother, who went to Holland in September
Anne's sister, born in Frankfurt in 1926
Headmistress and Anne's teacher in the sixth form
Town where the girls stayed with their grandmother
activities.explanation: You have matched the people and places from Anne's life story beautifully.

activities.prompt: Put these events from Anne's move to Holland in the correct order.
items: Anne's father emigrated to Holland in 1933
Anne's mother went with him to Holland in September
Margot and Anne were sent to Aachen to stay with Grandma
Margot went to Holland in December
Anne followed in February
activities.explanation: First the father went, then the mother, then the girls waited in Aachen and followed one by one.

activities.prompt: Anne says she was plunked down on the table as a birthday present for Margot. What does this tell you about the age gap between the sisters?
options: Anne was born a few years after Margot
Anne and Margot were twins
Margot was born after Anne
Anne was older than Margot
activities.explanation: Margot was born in 1926 and Anne in 1929, so Anne arrived later as a sweet birthday surprise.

activities.prompt: Anne tells Kitty about her school days. Kitty is a diary. Anne first explains who Mrs Kuperus is. Why does Anne do this?
options: Because Mrs Kuperus asked Anne to write about her.
Because a diary cannot ask her who that person is.
Because Anne wants to show she had many teachers.
Because Anne forgot the other teachers' names.

why.Because Mrs Kuperus asked Anne to write: Wrong: the facts never say the headmistress asked for this.
why.Because Anne wants to show she had many: Wrong: Anne is not showing off; she is helping Kitty understand.
why.Because Anne forgot the other teachers': Wrong: forgetting names is not the reason she explains things.

activities.explanation: Right: Kitty is a diary, so Anne must explain people because it cannot ask her.

activities.prompt: Anne's father married at thirty-six. Her mother was twenty-five then. Anne was born in 1929. What does this suggest about her parents?
options: They waited some years before starting their family.
They married after Anne was already born.
They did not want any children at all.
They were the same age when they married.

why.They married after Anne was already born: Wrong: they married years before Anne was born in 1929.
Wrong: nothing says they refused to have children.
why.They were the same age when they married: Wrong: thirty-six and twenty-five are different ages, not the same.

activities.explanation: Wrong: the ages show a gap, not that they rushed into a family.

activities.prompt: Anne lived in Frankfurt until she was four. Then her parents went to Holland. Anne went later, in two steps. What does this show about the move?
options: The whole family left Frankfurt together on one day.
The family was split up for some months.
Anne's parents never really left Germany.
Anne travelled alone by ship to Holland.

why.The whole family left Frankfurt together: Wrong: the parents left first and the girls came later, not together.
why.Anne's parents never really left Germany: Wrong: the parents did leave Germany and went to Holland.
Wrong: the facts never say Anne travelled by ship alone.

activities.explanation: Right: the parents went first, the girls stayed behind, so they were apart for months.

activities.prompt: Margot and Anne stayed with their grandmother in Aachen. Their parents were already in Holland. How did the two girls probably feel?
options: Happy, because they were on a long holiday with Grandma.
Sad or unsure, because their parents were far away.
Angry, because their parents broke their toys.
Excited, because they had moved to a new school.

why.Happy, because they were on a long holid: Wrong: it was not a holiday; their parents had already left for Holland.
why.Angry, because their parents broke their: Wrong: nothing in the facts says the girls were angry about toys.
why.Excited, because they had moved to a new: Wrong: the facts talk about the move, not about a new school yet.

activities.explanation: Right: young children living away from both parents would likely feel sad or unsure.

activities.prompt: Anne was 'plunked down on the table as a birthday present for Margot'. What does the word 'plunked' suggest about baby Anne?
options: She was placed down gently and very carefully.
She was set down in a quick, simple way.
She was thrown across the room by her parents.
She was hidden inside a wrapped gift box.

why.She was placed down gently and very care: Wrong: 'plunked' sounds quick and rough, not gentle and careful.
why.She was thrown across the room by her pa: Wrong: she was set on the table, not thrown across a room.
why.She was hidden inside a wrapped gift box: Wrong: she was like a present, not really inside a box.

activities.explanation: Right: 'plunked' means put down quickly and simply, like dropping something softly.

activities.prompt: Anne's grandmother died in January 1942. Anne had lived with her in Aachen as a small girl. Anne writes about her in her diary. Why does Grandma matter so much in Anne's story?
options: Because Grandma was rich and gave Anne many toys.
Because Grandma cared for the girls when their parents left.
Because Grandma moved to Holland with the whole family.
Because Grandma was Anne's teacher in the sixth form.

why.Because Grandma was rich and gave Anne m: Wrong: the facts never say Grandma was rich or gave toys.
why.Because Grandma moved to Holland with th: Wrong: the girls were sent to Grandma, not Grandma going with them.
why.Because Grandma was Anne's teacher in th: Wrong: the sixth form teacher was Mrs Kuperus, not Grandma.

activities.explanation: Right: Grandma looked after Margot and Anne in Aachen while their parents were away.

lessons.title: Saturday, 20 June 1942: Class and First Essay

activities.prompt: Why is Anne's whole class shaking in its boots?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Nervy Class and a Naughty Girl
activities.body: The whole class is quaking in its boots. Why? Soon the teachers will meet and decide who moves up and who is kept back. Half the class is making bets about it. Anne is not worried about her girlfriends or herself. But Mr Keesing, the maths teacher, was annoyed with her for ages. After warnings, he gave her extra homework: an essay on 'A Chatterbox'.
keyPoints: The class is nervous about the meeting where teachers decide who moves up.
Half the class is making bets on the results.
Mr Keesing gave Anne an essay on 'A Chatterbox' as extra homework.
activities.explanation: Everyone is jittery about results, and Anne has her own maths trouble too.

activities.prompt: Why does the whole class feel scared, even the students who study hard?
steps: The class is quaking in its boots, so something scary is coming soon.
The scary thing is the meeting where teachers decide who moves up and who is kept back.
Even good students feel scared because teachers can be unpredictable, like Anne says.
So the fear comes from not knowing the teachers' decision, not from the work itself.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Why the Wobbly Knees?
activities.prompt: Why is the entire class quaking in its boots?
options: A big sports match is coming soon
Teachers will decide who moves up
The school holidays are ending early
A new maths test was announced
activities.explanation: Well done! The teachers are meeting to decide who moves up and who is kept back.

activities.title: A Big Wager
activities.prompt: What did the two boys behind Anne stake on their bet?
options: Their entire holiday savings
Their entire lunch money
Their entire comic collection
Their entire homework notes
activities.explanation: Good thinking! C.N. and Jacques staked their entire holiday savings on their bet.

activities.title: Anne's Honest Guess
activities.prompt: Anne thinks that a ______ of the class should be kept back.
activities.hint: It is one part out of four.
activities.explanation: That's right! Anne thinks a quarter of the class should be kept back.

activities.title: One Wobbly Subject
activities.prompt: Anne is not worried about her girlfriends or herself. Which is the only subject she is not sure about?
options: History
Maths
English
Geography
activities.explanation: Correct! Maths is the only subject Anne is not sure about.

activities.title: Who and What
activities.prompt: Match each person or thing to what the lesson says about them.
pairs: the maths teacher who was annoyed
the two boys who made a bet
the two girls who laughed at the boys
activities.explanation: Brilliant! You have kept all the people and their stories straight.

activities.title: How It All Unfolded
activities.prompt: Put these events from the lesson in the order they happened.
items: Mr Keesing was annoyed with Anne for ages
He gave her warnings
He assigned an essay on 'A Chatterbox'
The class quaked in its boots
Half the class made bets
activities.explanation: Perfect order! First came the annoyance and warnings, then the essay, and now the nervy class waits.

activities.prompt: Some students are betting money on who will fail. Two boys bet all their holiday savings. What does this show about their feelings?
options: They are very sure about their guess.
They want the teacher to notice them.
They do not really care about school.
They are saving money for a trip.

This thinks the bet is a way to get attention from teachers.
This thinks betting means they dislike school, but betting shows interest.
This forgets the money is staked on a bet, not saved for later.

activities.explanation: Right: you only risk everything when you feel certain you will win.

activities.prompt: Anne laughs at the two boys with her friend. But she is not worried about her own results. Why can she laugh?
options: She thinks she will pass her subjects.
She finds the boys' bet very boring.
She wants the boys to give her money.
She does not like the boys at all.

This thinks laughing means boredom, but she laughs at their silly risk.
This thinks the laugh is about money, but she is not part of the bet.
This thinks laughing shows dislike, but the text does not say that.

activities.explanation: Right: she is calm about herself, so she can enjoy the boys' worry.

activities.prompt: Anne gets along well with all her teachers. But maths makes her unsure about passing. What can we work out from this?
options: Her maths teacher is the problem, not the subject.
She is bad at every subject in school.
She wants to change her school soon.
Her friends are also failing the maths class.

This forgets she is sure about all her other subjects.
Nothing in the lesson says she wants to leave the school.
why.Her friends are also failing the maths c: The lesson says nothing about her friends' marks in maths.

activities.explanation: Right: she likes her teachers, but one maths teacher was annoyed with her.

activities.prompt: The maths teacher warned Anne many times. Then he gave her an essay called 'A Chatterbox'. Why did he choose that title?
options: He wanted her to think about her talking habit.
He wanted her to write about a bird box.
He wanted the class to laugh at her essay.
He wanted her to stop doing her homework.

This reads the title as a real box, missing the talking meaning.
why.He wanted the class to laugh at her essa: The essay is a punishment for her, not a joke for the class.
why.He wanted her to stop doing her homework: The essay is extra homework, not a way to stop homework.

activities.explanation: Right: a chatterbox talks too much, so the essay points at her habit.

activities.prompt: Anne thinks a quarter of the class should be kept back. Half the class is making bets. What does Anne's thought show about her?
options: She has her own clear idea about results.
She is angry with half of her class.
She wants to join the boys' money bet.
She thinks every student will move up.

Her thought is about results, not about feeling angry at friends.
Nothing shows she wants to bet money like the boys do.
Her own thought says some should be kept back, not all pass.

activities.explanation: Right: she has thought about it and made her own judgement.
