lessons.title: Mr Keesing's Second and Third Essays

activities.prompt: Can a naughty student turn the tables on her teacher?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two More Essays!
activities.body: Mr Keesing had a good laugh at Anne's first essay. But when she talked again in the next lesson, he gave her a second essay: 'An Incorrigible Chatterbox'. She handed it in, and he had nothing to complain about for two whole lessons. Then he had enough! He gave her a third essay with a silly title: 'Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox'. The class roared. Her friend Sanne was good at poetry and offered to help her write it in verse. Anne jumped for joy. Mr Keesing was playing a joke on her, but she made sure the joke was on him!
keyPoints: Talking in class led to a second essay: 'An Incorrigible Chatterbox'.
After two quiet lessons, Mr Keesing set a third, silly essay title.
Sanne helped Anne write the third essay as a poem.
activities.explanation: Mr Keesing tried to joke with Anne, but Anne's poem turned the joke back on him.

activities.prompt: A boy keeps talking in class. The teacher gives him a funny writing task as a punishment. The boy writes something so clever and funny that the teacher laughs and stops being angry. Why did the funny task backfire on the teacher?
steps: The teacher wanted to shame the boy, so the punishment was meant to feel embarrassing, and that is why he chose a silly title.
But the boy did not feel ashamed; he saw the silly title as a game, so he joined in and made it even funnier.
The teacher laughed, because the writing was good, and laughing made his anger melt away.
So the punishment failed: the teacher tried to joke first, but the boy turned the joke back on him, and the teacher ended up pleased instead of angry.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Second Essay
activities.prompt: What was the title of the second essay Mr Keesing gave?
options: An Incorrigible Chatterbox
Quack, Quack, Quack
A Quiet Pupil
Mistress Chatterbox Sings
activities.explanation: The second essay was supposed to be on 'An Incorrigible Chatterbox'. Well done!

activities.title: Finish the Title
activities.prompt: The third essay was called 'Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress ______'.
activities.hint: It is the same word as in the second essay's title.
activities.explanation: Both essay titles called her a chatterbox. The duck sound made the class roar!

activities.title: Why a Third Essay?
activities.prompt: Why did Mr Keesing give a third essay?
options: During the third lesson he had finally had enough.
She forgot to write the second essay.
The class asked him for another essay.
She asked him for more homework.
activities.explanation: She had been quiet for two lessons, but during the third he had had enough.

activities.title: Who Did What?
activities.prompt: Match each person or thing with what happened.
activities.explanation: Sanne offered poetry help, the class roared, and Anne jumped for joy.

activities.title: Put the Story in Order
activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: She talked through the next lesson.
Mr Keesing assigned a second essay.
He had nothing to complain about for two lessons.
He set the essay 'Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox'.
The class roared.
activities.explanation: First she talked, then came the second essay, two quiet lessons, the third essay, and the roar!

activities.title: The Joke Was On Him
activities.prompt: Mr Keesing chose a ridiculous subject to play a joke on her. What did Anne do?
options: She made sure the joke was on him.
She said sorry and stopped talking.
She asked the class to help her complain.
She wrote the essay in silence.
activities.explanation: With Sanne's help, she wrote a clever poem in verse. The joke went back to Mr Keesing!

activities.prompt: After the first essay, the teacher has nothing to complain about for two lessons. Then she talks again. What does this show about her?
options: She could not change for long
She was scared of the teacher
She had finished all her talking
She did not like the teacher

why.She was scared of the teacher: Wrong: she kept talking freely, so fear was not the reason she stopped earlier.
why.She had finished all her talking: Wrong: she talked again in the third lesson, so the talking was not finished.
why.She did not like the teacher: Wrong: nothing shows dislike; the problem was her talking habit.

activities.explanation: Right: she stayed quiet for a while, but her old habit came back, so she could not change for long.

activities.prompt: The teacher gives a very silly essay title. The whole class roars with laughter. How does the girl probably feel at that moment?
options: She feels embarrassed in front of everyone
She feels proud of her old essays
She feels bored by the easy title
She feels angry at her classmates

why.She feels proud of her old essays: Wrong: her old essays are not being praised right now.
why.She feels bored by the easy title: Wrong: the title is a public joke on her, not a treat for her.
why.She feels angry at her classmates: Wrong: the class is laughing at the teacher's joke, not being mean to her.

activities.explanation: Right: everyone is laughing at her title, so embarrassment is the natural feeling.

activities.prompt: Sanne is good at poetry. She offers to help write the essay in verse. The girl jumps for joy. Why does she jump?
options: She sees a way to win the joke
She wants to skip the essay
She hopes the teacher will forget it
She thinks poems are never marked

why.She wants to skip the essay: Wrong: she still plans to write it, just in a smarter way.
why.She hopes the teacher will forget it: Wrong: she is excited to answer, not hoping the task disappears.
why.She thinks poems are never marked: Wrong: poems can be marked; her joy is about the clever plan.

activities.explanation: Right: a clever poem can beat the teacher's joke, so she sees a way to win.

activities.prompt: The teacher thinks a silly title will teach her a lesson. But she writes a poem and the joke lands on him. What does 'the joke was on him' mean here?
options: His trick made him look funny instead
He told the joke to the whole class
He laughed louder than everyone else
He gave her extra work as a joke

why.He told the joke to the whole class: Wrong: telling a joke aloud is not the same as a joke backfiring.
why.He laughed louder than everyone else: Wrong: laughing loudly is not what the phrase means here.
why.He gave her extra work as a joke: Wrong: the extra essay was his plan, not the meaning of the phrase.

activities.explanation: Right: his own trick turned against him, so he ended up the funny one.

activities.prompt: The teacher reads her poem about ducklings. He laughs at her arguments. What will he most likely do next?
options: He will stop punishing her for talking
He will give her a fourth essay soon
He will ask her to sit far away
He will tell her parents about it

why.He will give her a fourth essay soon: Wrong: he is pleased, not planning more essays right now.
why.He will ask her to sit far away: Wrong: moving her seat is a new punishment with no reason here.
why.He will tell her parents about it: Wrong: parents are not needed; he is happy with her answer.

activities.explanation: Right: his good laugh shows her words won him over, so the punishment game ends.

lessons.sceneCaption: A duck says quack quack, just like in Anne's funny essay title.

lessons.title: Amanda!

activities.prompt: Why does Amanda dream of escaping to a faraway sea?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Who is Amanda?
activities.body: Amanda is a girl who hears instructions all day. She is told not to bite her nails, not to hunch her shoulders, and to sit up straight. She must finish her homework and clean her shoes. So she escapes into her imagination. There she pictures a green sea and roams the street as an orphan, free and quiet.
keyPoints: Amanda keeps getting instructions about small things.
She escapes into her imagination to feel free.
She says silence is golden and freedom is sweet.
activities.explanation: The poem shows how constant nagging makes a child dream of freedom.

activities.prompt: Amanda keeps hearing instructions all day. Then she dreams of a quiet sea. Why does her mind go there?
steps: All day, people tell Amanda to stop biting her nails and sit straight, so she feels watched all the time.
Because she feels watched, she wants a place where nobody gives her orders.
A calm green sea has no voices and no rules, so it feels like the opposite of her day.
So the sea shows that Amanda is not being naughty; she is escaping the nagging to feel free.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What is Amanda told not to bite?
options: Her nails
Her pencil
Her lips
Sweets
activities.explanation: Well done! The poem opens with this instruction to Amanda.

activities.prompt: In her imagination there is a languid, ______ sea.
activities.hint: Think of a deep green jewel.
activities.explanation: Lovely! The sea in Amanda's dream is emerald, a rich green colour.

activities.prompt: Match each thing to what Amanda is told about it.
activities.explanation: Great matching! Each instruction is about a small, everyday thing.

activities.prompt: In her dream of freedom, what does Amanda say about silence?
options: It is golden
It is golden and loud
It is boring
It is frightening
activities.explanation: Yes! She says silence is golden and freedom is sweet.

activities.prompt: Put these instructions in the order they come in the poem.
items: Do not bite your nails
Do not hunch your shoulders
Sit up straight
Have you finished your homework?
Clean your shoes
activities.explanation: Well done! You followed the poem's order from nails to shoes.

activities.prompt: As an orphan, she patterns soft dust with her hushed, ______ feet.
activities.hint: She wears nothing on her feet.
activities.explanation: Super! Her bare feet press patterns into the soft dust as she roams.

activities.prompt: A mother says the same kind of orders to Amanda all day. Amanda closes her eyes and pictures a calm sea. What does the sea most likely mean to her?
options: A place where no one gives her orders
A place where she can swim very fast
A place where she will learn to sit straight
A place where she can find her lost shoes

why.A place where she can swim very fast: Wrong: this thinks the dream is about swimming, not about escaping orders.
why.A place where she will learn to sit stra: Wrong: this thinks the dream copies the orders, but the dream escapes them.
why.A place where she can find her lost shoe: Wrong: this mixes a small chore from her day into her big dream of freedom.

activities.explanation: Right: the sea is quiet and free, the opposite of a day full of orders.

activities.prompt: Amanda says, 'Silence is golden. Freedom is sweet.' She says this while imagining she is alone. What does this line show about her real life?
options: Her real life is full of noise and orders
Her real life is quiet and she is already free
She loves gold more than anything else
She wants to buy sweets with golden coins

why.Her real life is quiet and she is alread: Wrong: this takes the words as true about her life, but she only dreams of them.
why.She loves gold more than anything else: Wrong: this reads 'golden' as real gold, missing that it means precious.
why.She wants to buy sweets with golden coin: Wrong: this reads 'sweet' as candy, missing that it means lovely to feel.

activities.explanation: Right: she calls silence and freedom sweet because her real life lacks them.

activities.prompt: Amanda imagines she is an orphan walking alone on the street. Her feet make soft patterns in the dust. Why does she pick an orphan in her dream?
options: An orphan has no one to keep telling her what to do
An orphan gets new shoes and clean clothes free
An orphan never has to do any homework at all
An orphan can eat chocolate every single day

why.An orphan gets new shoes and clean cloth: Wrong: this thinks the dream is about gifts, not about freedom.
why.An orphan never has to do any homework a: Wrong: this picks one chore she hates, but the dream is about all orders.
why.An orphan can eat chocolate every single: Wrong: this mixes the chocolate rule into the dream's real wish for freedom.

activities.explanation: Right: with no parent, no one nags her, so she feels free.

activities.prompt: The speaker keeps saying 'Don't do this' and 'Don't do that' to Amanda. She is told not to bite her nails and not to eat chocolate. What does the speaker most likely feel?
options: Worried that Amanda is growing up the wrong way
Angry because Amanda never listens at all
Bored and wants Amanda to go away
Proud because Amanda does everything perfectly

why.Angry because Amanda never listens at al: Wrong: the orders sound strict, but worry, not hate, makes people nag.
why.Bored and wants Amanda to go away: Wrong: a bored person would not bother giving so many careful orders.
why.Proud because Amanda does everything per: Wrong: proud people praise; this speaker only points out faults.

activities.explanation: Right: so many small warnings show care mixed with worry about her habits.

activities.prompt: Someone is speaking to Amanda. She is told to look at that person. Amanda would rather dream of her green sea. What does this order imply about Amanda?
options: She often stops listening and drifts into her dreams
She cannot see well and needs to look harder
She is rude and never wants to talk to anyone
She is deaf and cannot hear people speaking

why.She cannot see well and needs to look ha: Wrong: this takes the order as about eyesight, not about attention.
why.She is rude and never wants to talk to a: Wrong: daydreaming is escaping, not being rude on purpose.
why.She is deaf and cannot hear people speak: Wrong: the order is about looking, so hearing is not the problem.

activities.explanation: Right: being told to look suggests her eyes wander to her dream world.

sceneCredit.creator: Dietmar Rabich

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Anne Frank wrote her diary while she was in hiding in Amsterdam.
Reason (R): Her family went into hiding in hidden rooms in her father Otto Frank's office building during the German occupation of the Netherlands.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the location and circumstances of the hiding explain where and how she wrote the diary.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between Anne Frank's fate and her father Otto Frank's fate after the group was betrayed?
activities.answer: After two years in hiding, the group was betrayed and transported to the concentration camp system. Anne, the German-born Jewish girl born on 12 June 1929, died there in February/March 1945, still a young teenager. Her father Otto, however, was the only survivor of the group. He returned to Amsterdam, and it was he who had her diary published in English as The Diary of a Young Girl, turning her written record into a book the world could read.
points: States the group was betrayed after two years and sent to the concentration camp system
Gives Anne's death in February/March 1945
Identifies Otto as the only survivor who returned to Amsterdam
Credits Otto with publishing the diary in English as The Diary of a Young Girl
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A student sits at her desk after school, chin in hands, feeling low. She has never kept a diary before, so writing one feels strange to her. She has loving parents and a sixteen-year-old sister, and there are about thirty people she can call friends, yet she feels she has no real friend. Bored and listless, she wonders whether to stay in or go out, then stays where she is, brooding, and remembers that paper has more patience than people.
activities.prompt: Why does the student decide to begin a diary even though she believes nobody will care about her musings later?
options: Because she wants to release feelings she has been holding inside
Because she hopes her family will read it and praise her
Because she wants to become a famous writer one day
Because her sister has asked her to keep a record

why.Because she hopes her family will read i: Wrong: she plans to keep the diary away from everyone unless she finds a real friend
why.Because she wants to become a famous wri: Wrong: she actually doubts anyone, including herself, will be interested later
why.Because her sister has asked her to keep: Wrong: nothing in the situation suggests her sister prompted the diary

activities.explanation: Correct: she feels like writing to unburden herself, not for an audience

activities.context: A student sits at her desk after school, chin in hands, feeling low. She has never kept a diary before, so writing one feels strange to her. She has loving parents and a sixteen-year-old sister, and there are about thirty people she can call friends, yet she feels she has no real friend. Bored and listless, she wonders whether to stay in or go out, then stays where she is, brooding, and remembers that paper has more patience than people.
activities.prompt: If the student suddenly found a real friend next week, what would most likely change about her diary?
options: She might allow that one person to read it
She would stop writing in it completely
She would hand it over to her sister to read
She would start writing only about her school lessons

why.She would stop writing in it completely: Wrong: she writes because she feels like writing and needs to unburden herself, which would not stop
why.She would hand it over to her sister to: Wrong: her sister is family, not the real friend she feels she lacks
why.She would start writing only about her s: Wrong: the diary is for her own thoughts, not a school record

activities.explanation: Correct: her only condition for sharing was finding a real friend

activities.context: A student sits at her desk after school, chin in hands, feeling low. She has never kept a diary before, so writing one feels strange to her. She has loving parents and a sixteen-year-old sister, and there are about thirty people she can call friends, yet she feels she has no real friend. Bored and listless, she wonders whether to stay in or go out, then stays where she is, brooding, and remembers that paper has more patience than people.
activities.prompt: The student chooses to stay where she is instead of going out. What does this choice most clearly show about her at that moment?
options: She would rather sit with her own thoughts than seek company
She is too physically tired to leave the house
She has been forbidden by her parents to go out
She is waiting for one of her thirty friends to visit

why.She is too physically tired to leave the: Wrong: her state is emotional, not physical exhaustion
why.She has been forbidden by her parents to: Wrong: her parents are loving, and nothing suggests a restriction
why.She is waiting for one of her thirty fri: Wrong: she feels friendless, so waiting for a visitor does not fit

activities.explanation: Correct: bored and listless, she stays put and broods, matching her low mood

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The student finds writing in a diary a strange experience.
Reason (R): She had never written anything before this.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Having never written before directly explains why diary-writing feels strange to her.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The student decided to keep her diary completely private.
Reason (R): She had a small circle of close friends she trusted with everything.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true because she plans to share it only with a real friend, but the reason is false since she feels she has no real friend despite thirty acquaintances.

activities.context: A new classmate who has never read Anne's diary asks her who Kitty is and admits that the entries sound like letters to someone sharing her whole world. Anne decides to write a short sketch of her life first. She recalls that her parents married when her father was thirty-six and her mother twenty-five, that Margot was born in Frankfurt in Germany in 1926 and she herself on 12 June 1929, that the family left Frankfurt when she was four, and that the grandmother in Aachen, with whom the girls once stayed, died in January 1942.
activities.prompt: If Anne hands the classmate her diary without first giving the sketch of her life, what is the most likely result?
options: The classmate will be puzzled, because the entries assume the reader already knows Anne's family and past.
The classmate will enjoy the entries more, since unexplained references make a diary exciting.
The classmate will correct the dates in the diary, because Anne has noted them wrongly.
The classmate will stop being Anne's friend, because the diary was meant to be private.

why.The classmate will enjoy the entries mor: Wrong: the problem is confusion, not extra enjoyment; Anne writes the sketch precisely to remove difficulty.
why.The classmate will correct the dates in: Wrong: nothing suggests the dates are wrong; the issue is missing background, not inaccuracy.
why.The classmate will stop being Anne's fri: Wrong: friendship is not at stake; the sketch is about making the diary understandable.

activities.explanation: Correct: the whole reason for the sketch is that no one would understand the stories to Kitty without background.

activities.context: A new classmate who has never read Anne's diary asks her who Kitty is and admits that the entries sound like letters to someone sharing her whole world. Anne decides to write a short sketch of her life first. She recalls that her parents married when her father was thirty-six and her mother twenty-five, that Margot was born in Frankfurt in Germany in 1926 and she herself on 12 June 1929, that the family left Frankfurt when she was four, and that the grandmother in Aachen, with whom the girls once stayed, died in January 1942.
activities.prompt: The classmate wants to list the family's move to Holland in the correct order. Which event should Anne place immediately after her father emigrated?
options: Margot travelling on to Holland in December.
The mother going over to Holland in September.
Anne following her family in February.
The two girls being sent to their grandmother in Aachen.

why.Margot travelling on to Holland in Decem: Wrong: Margot's December journey comes after the girls have already stayed with the grandmother.
Wrong: Anne's February journey is the last step of the whole move, not the one after the father left.
why.The two girls being sent to their grandm: Wrong: the girls went to Aachen only after the mother had already gone to Holland.

activities.explanation: Correct: the mother followed the father to Holland in September, before anything else in the move.

activities.context: A new classmate who has never read Anne's diary asks her who Kitty is and admits that the entries sound like letters to someone sharing her whole world. Anne decides to write a short sketch of her life first. She recalls that her parents married when her father was thirty-six and her mother twenty-five, that Margot was born in Frankfurt in Germany in 1926 and she herself on 12 June 1929, that the family left Frankfurt when she was four, and that the grandmother in Aachen, with whom the girls once stayed, died in January 1942.
activities.prompt: The classmate guesses that Anne has spent her whole childhood in Holland. What should Anne say to correct this?
options: That she was actually born in Holland and only visited Germany later.
That her earliest years were spent in the German city where she was born.
That she was born at her grandmother's home in Aachen.
That she left Germany as a baby, travelling with both her parents.

why.That she was actually born in Holland an: Wrong: Anne was born in Frankfurt, not in Holland, so this reverses the truth.
why.That she was born at her grandmother's h: Wrong: Aachen was only where the girls stayed with their grandmother during the move, not her birthplace.
why.That she left Germany as a baby, travell: Wrong: her father went first and her mother followed later; the baby Anne did not travel with both parents.

activities.explanation: Correct: she lived in Frankfurt until she was four, so her first years were in her birthplace.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Anne provides a brief sketch of her life at the start of her diary.
Reason (R): Her father emigrated to Holland in 1933, earlier than the rest of the family.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the father's early emigration is not the reason Anne wrote the sketch.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Margot and Anne travelled to Holland before their mother did.
Reason (R): Their mother went to Holland in September, before either of the girls made the journey.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because the mother went first; the reason correctly states her September journey.

activities.prompt: Explain why Anne begins by giving a sketch of her life even though the diary is addressed to Kitty.
activities.answer: Anne realises that the intimate stories she tells Kitty will mean nothing to anyone who does not already know her. Her diary mentions people, places and events as if every reader shares her world. She therefore provides a brief sketch of her life first: where and when she was born, how the family moved from Frankfurt to Holland, and other basic facts. This introduction supplies the background a stranger needs, so that even someone who has never met her can follow and understand her entries to Kitty.
points: The diary entries assume the reader already knows Anne's world.
No outsider would understand the stories to Kitty without background.
The sketch supplies basic facts: birth, family and the move to Holland.
Its purpose is to make the diary understandable to any future reader.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A class is quaking in its boots because the teachers are about to meet and decide who moves up and who is kept back. Half the class is making bets on the result. One girl is not worried about herself or her friends, though maths is the only subject she feels unsure about. Her maths teacher, an old fogey who has been annoyed with her for ages because she talks too much, has already given her warnings and then extra homework: an essay on 'A Chatterbox'.
activities.prompt: If the girl stops chatting during maths lessons from tomorrow, what is the most likely result?
options: The teacher will have no fresh reason to give her another punishing written assignment
The teacher will set her a second essay at once because he enjoys giving them
The teacher will decide at the meeting that she must be kept back
The teacher will join the half of the class that is making bets

why.The teacher will set her a second essay: Wrong: the essay was a punishment for a habit, not something given for enjoyment.
why.The teacher will decide at the meeting t: Wrong: being kept back is decided by the teachers' meeting about work, not by chatting alone.
why.The teacher will join the half of the cl: Wrong: betting is done by students in the class, not by the teacher.

activities.explanation: Correct: the essay came only after warnings failed, so ending the chatter removes the cause of the punishment.

activities.context: A class is quaking in its boots because the teachers are about to meet and decide who moves up and who is kept back. Half the class is making bets on the result. One girl is not worried about herself or her friends, though maths is the only subject she feels unsure about. Her maths teacher, an old fogey who has been annoyed with her for ages because she talks too much, has already given her warnings and then extra homework: an essay on 'A Chatterbox'.
activities.prompt: If the meeting ends with a quarter of the class being kept back, what should the girl reasonably conclude about herself?
options: She can feel safe about everything except maths, her one uncertain subject
She must now fear being kept back in every subject she studies
She should place a bet like the others to find out her result
She should stop getting along with her teachers so they notice her more

why.She must now fear being kept back in eve: Wrong: her worry was limited to one subject, not all of them.
why.She should place a bet like the others t: Wrong: betting cannot change or reveal the teachers' decision about her.
why.She should stop getting along with her t: Wrong: good relations with teachers already exist and would not be spoiled on purpose.

activities.explanation: Correct: she is unworried about herself generally, and maths is the only doubt she has.

activities.context: A class is quaking in its boots because the teachers are about to meet and decide who moves up and who is kept back. Half the class is making bets on the result. One girl is not worried about herself or her friends, though maths is the only subject she feels unsure about. Her maths teacher, an old fogey who has been annoyed with her for ages because she talks too much, has already given her warnings and then extra homework: an essay on 'A Chatterbox'.
activities.prompt: Why did the maths teacher set an essay instead of simply giving up on the girl?
options: His earlier warnings had failed, so extra homework was his next step to check her talking
He wanted her to fail maths so that she would be kept back for certain
He was copying the betting game that half the class was playing
He believed she was the best essay writer in the whole class

why.He wanted her to fail maths so that she: Wrong: giving written work is a way of correcting a pupil, not a wish to fail her.
why.He was copying the betting game that hal: Wrong: the betting was among pupils about results, unrelated to his punishment.
why.He believed she was the best essay write: Wrong: the essay was given as a punishment for talking, not as a reward for writing.

activities.explanation: Correct: the essay followed warnings, showing a step-by-step attempt to correct her.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The whole class is quaking in its boots.
Reason (R): Half the class is making bets on who will move up.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both are true, but the betting is a sign of the nervous mood, not the cause of it; the cause is the teachers' meeting.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Anne is not worried about her girlfriends and herself.
Reason (R): Anne is certain she will do well in maths.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because maths is the only subject she is unsure about.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: The Diary of a Young Girl

activities.prompt: Anne started writing a diary even though she had loving parents and about thirty friends. Why did she do this?
options: She wanted to become a famous writer one day
She did not feel she had a real friend to talk to
Her teacher asked her to write every day
She wanted to copy her sister Margot
activities.explanation: Anne had many people around her, yet she felt no one was a true friend. So she poured her heart into the diary instead.

activities.prompt: Anne thought of the saying 'Paper has more patience than people' while she felt depressed and sat with her chin in her hands.
activities.explanation: Well done! She was feeling low and brooding, and that is when this saying came to her mind.

activities.prompt: Anne's father emigrated to Holland in the year ______.
activities.hint: It was the year after Margot was born in Frankfurt.
activities.explanation: Her father moved to Holland in 1933, and her mother Edith followed him in September.

activities.prompt: Match each person from the chapter to who they were.
pairs: Her friend who was good at poetry
The headmistress in the sixth form
activities.explanation: Great memory! Each of these people plays a special part in Anne's story.

activities.prompt: Mr Keesing gave Anne extra homework again and again. Put her three essays in the order she wrote them.
items: 'A Chatterbox'
'An Incorrigible Chatterbox'
'Quack, Quack, Quack, Said Mistress Chatterbox'
activities.explanation: First came 'A Chatterbox', then 'An Incorrigible Chatterbox', and finally the duck poem that turned the joke on Mr Keesing!

activities.prompt: In the poem, Amanda is always being told what to do. What does she imagine herself as to escape it all?
options: A mermaid in a deep cave
A queen on a golden throne
An orphan roaming the street
A bird flying over the sea
activities.explanation: Amanda imagines being an orphan roaming the street, where no one can nag her. In her thoughts, silence is golden and freedom is sweet.

activities.prompt: Half the class staked their entire holiday savings on their bets about who would be kept back.
activities.explanation: Half the class was making bets, but it was the two boys, C.N. and Jacques, who staked their entire holiday savings.

activities.prompt: As persecutions increased, Anne's family went into hiding in July ______.
activities.hint: It was the same year her grandma died in January.
activities.explanation: The family hid in July 1942, in hidden rooms in her father Otto Frank's office building.

activities.prompt: Anne wrote a brief sketch of her life before her diary entries. Why did she feel she needed to do this?
options: Her teacher wanted a life story for homework
No one would understand her stories to Kitty otherwise
She wanted to practise writing before the big test
Her father asked her to record the family history
activities.explanation: Anne wrote to Kitty as if to a friend. She felt no one would understand those stories without knowing her life first.

activities.prompt: Put these events from Anne's life in the correct time order.
items: Anne was born on 12 June 1929
Her father emigrated to Holland in 1933
The family went into hiding in July 1942
Her father had her diary published in English
activities.explanation: From her birth in 1929, to Holland, to hiding, and finally her diary published by Otto — that is the journey of her story.

chapters.title: Glimpses of India: A Baker from Goa
chapters.summary: In this chapter: old portuguese days and the pader; the baker in childhood; bread, dress and prosperity; coorg: land and people.

lessons.title: Old Portuguese Days and the Pader

activities.prompt: Why do Goa's grandmas still smile when they remember the old bread-seller?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Pader of Goa
activities.body: In Goa, the elders often remember the old Portuguese days with love. They remember the Portuguese and their famous loaves of bread. The people who ate those loaves may have vanished, but the makers are still here. Mixers, moulders and loaf-bakers still live among the people. The baker is still known as pader in Goa.
keyPoints: Goa's elders remember the old Portuguese days fondly.
The bread-eaters may have vanished, but the bread-makers are still there.
The baker in Goa is still called the pader.
activities.explanation: The pader is a living link with Goa's old Portuguese days.

activities.prompt: Ravi's grandfather smiles when he talks about the old Portuguese days and their bread. The bread eaters of that time are gone. But the bakers are still there. Why does the grandfather smile?
steps: The grandfather remembers the old days with love, so the bread reminds him of happy times.
The people who ate that bread have vanished, so those days cannot come back.
But the bakers and their furnaces are still alive, so a little of those days still lives on.
So the grandfather smiles because the old days feel gone, yet the bakers keep them alive.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: How do Goa's elders remember the old Portuguese days?
options: With anger
Fondly
With fear
With sadness
activities.explanation: Well done! The elders remember those days fondly, with warm feelings.

activities.prompt: In Goa, the baker is still known as the ______.
activities.hint: It is a special Goan word for the bread-maker.
activities.explanation: Yes! Even today, the baker is called the pader in Goa.

activities.prompt: Match each word from the lesson with what it means.
activities.explanation: Lovely matching! These words help you talk about the pader and his bread.

activities.prompt: Put the bread-makers in the order they work, from first to last.
items: The mixer mixes the dough
The moulder shapes the dough
The loaf-baker bakes the loaves
activities.explanation: Perfect order! First mixing, then moulding, then baking the loaves.

activities.prompt: Meera's grandfather talks about the old Portuguese days. He smiles and talks about their famous loaves of bread. He looks happy, not sad. Why does he feel happy?
options: He ate those loaves and remembers them with love.
He wants to buy a new oven for his house.
He is happy because the Portuguese still live there.
He forgot what he wanted to say to Meera.

why.He wants to buy a new oven for his house: Wrong. This thinks the smile is about buying things, not about fond old memories.
why.He is happy because the Portuguese still: Wrong. This mixes up remembering the past with the Portuguese living there now.
why.He forgot what he wanted to say to Meera: Wrong. This thinks the smile means confusion, but it really means warm memory.

activities.explanation: Right. The elders remember the old days fondly, and the famous loaves are part of that sweet memory.

activities.prompt: The people who ate the old loaves of bread have vanished. But the makers of the loaves are still there. What does this tell us?
options: The baker's work has lived longer than the bread eaters.
The loaves of bread were too hard to eat.
The bread eaters moved away to bake bread themselves.
Nobody in Goa likes bread any more today.

why.The loaves of bread were too hard to eat: Wrong. This blames the bread, but the story says nothing bad about the loaves.
why.The bread eaters moved away to bake brea: Wrong. This mixes up the eaters leaving with the makers staying.
why.Nobody in Goa likes bread any more today: Wrong. This thinks bread is unpopular, but the bakers are still there making it.

activities.explanation: Right. The eaters are gone, but the makers still live among the people, so their work outlived them.

activities.prompt: An old baker in Goa dies. His son does not look for another job. He wakes up early and bakes loaves like his father did. Why does the son do this?
options: He wants to continue the family profession with pride.
He is waiting for his father to come back home.
He does not know how to read or write.
He hopes to sell the old furnace for money.

why.He is waiting for his father to come bac: Wrong. This misses that the father has died, so he cannot come back.
Wrong. This makes up a reason about school that is not in the story.
why.He hopes to sell the old furnace for mon: Wrong. This thinks the son wants to end the work, not continue it.

activities.explanation: Right. Even if the father is not alive, the son continues the family profession.

activities.prompt: In a Goan village, an old furnace still stands. The fire in it has not gone out. Bread is baked in it every morning. What does the burning fire show?
options: The old baking tradition is still alive and working.
The furnace is new and was built last week.
The villagers are getting ready to break the furnace.
The fire is burning by accident with no purpose.

why.The furnace is new and was built last we: Wrong. This forgets the furnace is old and time-tested, not new.
why.The villagers are getting ready to break: Wrong. This reads the fire as a sign of ending, not of continuing.
why.The fire is burning by accident with no: Wrong. This thinks the fire is useless, but it bakes bread with purpose.

activities.explanation: Right. The time-tested furnace and its living fire show the old baking still goes on.

activities.prompt: When the author was a child in Goa, the baker came at least twice a day. The children ran to him happily. The author called him a friend, companion and guide. Why did the author feel this way?
options: The baker visited so often that he felt like family.
The baker gave the children money every visit.
The baker took the children to school each day.
The baker was afraid of the children and ran away.

why.The baker gave the children money every: Wrong. This adds a gift of money that the facts never mention.
why.The baker took the children to school ea: Wrong. This confuses the word guide with a school teacher.
why.The baker was afraid of the children and: Wrong. This flips the feeling; the children loved his visits, not feared them.

activities.explanation: Right. Coming at least twice a day made the baker a familiar friend and guide.

activities.prompt: A man walks through a Goan village with a basket of loaves. The elders do not call him a shopkeeper. They call him the pader. From this, what does the word pader mean?
options: The traditional bread baker of the village
The doctor who treats sick village children
The teacher who runs the village school
The postman who brings letters every day

why.The doctor who treats sick village child: Wrong. A doctor treats people, but this man carries bread, not medicine.
why.The teacher who runs the village school: Wrong. A teacher teaches, but this man's basket is full of loaves.
why.The postman who brings letters every day: Wrong. A postman brings letters, but this man's basket holds bread.

activities.explanation: Right. The man carries loaves, and the bakers of Goa are still known as pader.

lessons.title: The Baker in Childhood

activities.prompt: Why did children run to the baker if not for the bread?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Baker's Morning Visit
activities.body: Every morning, the baker came on his selling round. The jingling thud of his bamboo woke the children. They ran to meet and greet him. They did not run for the love of the loaf. They longed for bread-bangles and chose them carefully. A maid-servant like Paskine or Bastine bought the loaves.
keyPoints: The jingling thud of the baker's bamboo woke the children.
The children ran to greet him, not for the loaf.
The children longed for bread-bangles.
A maid-servant bought the loaves.
activities.explanation: The baker's visit was a happy start to the day for the children.

activities.prompt: The children ran to the baker every morning. But they did not run for the loaf. Why did they run then?
steps: The loud 'jhang, jhang' of the bamboo woke them, so the sound itself pulled them out of bed.
The loaves went to the maid-servant, so the children knew the bread was not for them.
The children wanted bread-bangles, and they chose them with care, so a small sweet thing mattered more to them than the loaf.
So they ran for the fun, the bangles, and the excitement, not for the bread itself.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Woke the Children?
activities.prompt: What sound woke the children in the morning?
options: The ringing of a temple bell
The jingling thud of the baker's bamboo
The crowing of a cock
The beating of a drum
activities.explanation: The jingling thud of the baker's bamboo woke the children as he set out on his round.

activities.title: Who Bought the Loaves?
activities.prompt: The loaves were bought by a maid-servant like Paskine or ______.
activities.hint: Her name starts with B, like Paskine starts with P.
activities.explanation: Well done! Paskine and Bastine were the maid-servants who bought the loaves.

activities.title: How Did the Baker Carry His Basket?
activities.prompt: How did the baker carry his basket and bamboo?
options: He pushed the basket on a cart and held the bamboo up
He hung the basket on his arm and tapped the bamboo softly
He held the basket on his head with one hand and banged the bamboo with the other
He carried the basket on his back and swung the bamboo
activities.explanation: He supported the basket on his head with one hand and banged the bamboo on the ground with the other.

activities.title: Sounds and Words of the Baker
activities.prompt: Match each thing with what it goes with.
activities.explanation: Each part of the baker's visit had its own sound or treat.

activities.title: The Baker's Visit, Step by Step
activities.prompt: Put the baker's morning visit in the right order.
items: The jingling bamboo woke the children
The children ran to meet and greet him
He greeted the lady of the house with Good morning
The children were pushed aside with a mild rebuke
The loaves were delivered to the servant
activities.explanation: First the bamboo woke everyone, then the children ran, then the greeting, then the push aside, then the delivery.

activities.title: What the Author Still Recalls
activities.prompt: What does the author still recall about those loaves?
options: The typical fragrance of the loaves
The price paid by the maid-servant
The shape of the bread-bangles
The colour of the basket
activities.explanation: The author still recalls the typical fragrance of those loaves. A sweet memory!

activities.prompt: The baker says 'Good morning' to the lady. Then he gently pushes the children aside. He is not angry with them. Why does he push them?
options: He must first give the loaves to the servant.
He hates children and wants them to cry.
He wants the children to run away forever.
He is hiding something bad in his basket.

Wrong. This mistakes a gentle push for hate.
why.He wants the children to run away foreve: Wrong. This thinks a small push means a big anger.
why.He is hiding something bad in his basket: Wrong. This adds a bad secret that is not in the story.

activities.explanation: Right. His job comes first; the push is mild, not mean.

activities.prompt: The basket sits high on the baker's head. The children are small. They climb a bench or the parapet. Why do they climb?
options: They want to peep into the high basket.
They want to jump over the house wall.
They want to hide from the maid-servant.
They want to sit and eat their lunch.

Wrong. This links the parapet to escaping, not looking.
Wrong. This mixes the servant's job with the children's wish.
Wrong. This thinks the bench is for resting, not peeping.

activities.explanation: Right. Climbing lifts their eyes up to the basket.

activities.prompt: Many years pass. The writer forgets many things. But he still remembers the smell of those loaves. What does this show?
options: The smell was special and stayed in his heart.
The smell was bad, so he never forgot it.
He never really smelled the loaves at all.
He smells the same loaves in his kitchen now.

why.The smell was bad, so he never forgot it: Wrong. This thinks we remember only bad things.
why.He never really smelled the loaves at al: Wrong. This says the memory is fake, but he recalls it clearly.
why.He smells the same loaves in his kitchen: Wrong. This mixes an old memory with a thing happening now.

activities.explanation: Right. Only a loved memory stays fresh for so many years.

activities.prompt: Paskine, the maid-servant, pays for the loaves. The children get bread-bangles instead. Who eats the big loaves at home?
options: The people of the house, through the servant.
The children, because they ran to the baker.
The baker, because he baked the loaves.
Nobody, because the loaves were only for show.

why.The children, because they ran to the ba: Wrong. This thinks running to the baker means getting the loaf.
Wrong. This confuses the maker of bread with the eater.
why.Nobody, because the loaves were only for: Wrong. This thinks bought bread is wasted, which is silly.

activities.explanation: Right. The servant buys for the house, so the family eats them.

lessons.sceneCaption: The traditional Goan pao, the bread sold by bakers in Goa, seen at Mapusa market.

lessons.title: Bread, Dress and Prosperity

activities.prompt: Why did a baker's family never go hungry in the old days?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Bread is the heart of every happy day
activities.body: In the old days, bread touched every big moment. A marriage gift meant nothing without the sweet bread called bol. A party lost its charm without bread. The lady of the house made sandwiches for her daughter's engagement. Cakes and bolinhas were a must at Christmas. The baker wore a special dress called the kabai, and his family never starved.
keyPoints: Marriage gifts are meaningless without bol.
A party or feast loses charm without bread.
The baker wore a peculiar dress called the kabai.
Baking was a profitable profession.
activities.explanation: Bread was not just food. It was part of every celebration.

activities.prompt: A village is planning a big feast. The cook asks: can we skip the bread and cook only rice and curry? The elders say no. Why do the elders say no?
steps: The feast is for the whole village, so everyone must enjoy it, because a feast is about shared joy.
The elders remember that a party loses its charm without bread, because bread is the heart of every celebration.
They also remember that the baker's furnace in the village is essential, because without it no fresh bread can be made.
So the elders say no, because without bread the feast would lose its charm, and the village furnace must keep working.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The baker's month
activities.body: Bakers wore a shirt and trousers shorter than full-length ones. Even today, anyone wearing a half pant just below the knees is said to be dressed like a pader. The baker collected his bills at the end of the month. The monthly accounts were written in pencil on some wall.
keyPoints: A half pant just below the knees means dressed like a pader.
Bills were collected at the end of the month.
Accounts were recorded on a wall in pencil.
activities.explanation: The baker's dress and habits are still remembered today.

activities.prompt: A marriage gift is meaningless without which sweet bread?
options: Bol
Bolinha
Sandwich
Cake
activities.explanation: Well done! The sweet bread called bol makes a marriage gift complete.

activities.prompt: A party or feast loses its charm without bread.
activities.explanation: Yes! Bread was needed to make a feast feel special.

activities.prompt: The baker of those days wore a peculiar dress called the ______.
activities.hint: It starts with the letter k.
activities.explanation: Great! The kabai was the baker's special dress.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what it belongs to.
activities.explanation: Lovely work! Each one has its own special place in the lesson.

activities.prompt: Someone wears a half pant just below the knees. People say he is dressed like a ______.
options: Pader
Baker's furnace
Bolinha
Kabai
activities.explanation: Correct! That dress is said to look like a pader, the baker.

activities.prompt: The baker collected his bills every week.
activities.explanation: Not quite. He collected his bills at the end of the month, not every week.

activities.prompt: Put the baker's month in the right order.
items: The baker sells bread all through the month
The end of the month arrives
The baker collects his bills
The monthly accounts are written in pencil on a wall
activities.explanation: Perfect order! First the bread is sold, then the bills come, then the wall gets the accounts.

activities.prompt: Ravi's uncle wears pants that stop just below his knees. People in the bazaar smile and say he is dressed like a pader. Why do people say this?
options: Because old bakers wore short pants just like these
Because the uncle is learning to bake bread now
Because short pants are the newest fashion in town
Because the uncle works in a bakery every day

why.Because the uncle is learning to bake br: This thinks the words describe his job today, but the saying comes from old dress, not new work.
why.Because short pants are the newest fashi: This thinks it is about fashion, but the saying is about the baker's old dress.
why.Because the uncle works in a bakery ever: This thinks the words describe his workplace, but the saying is only about how the pants look.

activities.explanation: Right. Bakers wore a peculiar dress, and short pants below the knees remind people of the pader's old dress.

activities.prompt: In an old village, the baker's children never looked hungry. They always ate good food at home. What does this tell us about baking?
options: It was a job that gave the family enough money
It was a job that the whole village helped with
It was a job that needed very little hard work
It was a job that only rich families could start

why.It was a job that the whole village help: This thinks others did the work, but the lesson says the baker's own family never starved.
why.It was a job that needed very little har: This thinks the work was easy, but the lesson talks about profit, not easy work.
why.It was a job that only rich families cou: This thinks only the rich could bake, but the lesson says it was a profitable job for bakers.

activities.explanation: Right. Baking was profitable in the old days, so the baker's family never starved.

lessons.title: Coorg: Land and People

activities.prompt: Why might Coorg's people trace their roots to Alexander's army?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Piece of Heaven in the Hills
activities.body: Coorg, also called Kodagu, is the smallest district of Karnataka. It lies midway between Mysore and the coastal town of Mangalore. It is a land of rolling hills with martial men, beautiful women and wild creatures. Evergreen rainforests, spices and coffee plantations cover its lovely face. The writer calls it a piece of heaven that drifted from the kingdom of god.
keyPoints: Coorg, or Kodagu, is the smallest district of Karnataka.
It lies midway between Mysore and Mangalore.
It has rainforests, spices and coffee plantations.
activities.explanation: Coorg is a small, beautiful hill district with forests and farms.

activities.prompt: Anita wants to visit Coorg. Her uncle says, 'Do not go in July. Wait till September.' She wonders why the same place is bad in one month and lovely in another.
steps: In the monsoons, Coorg gets very heavy rain, so many visitors stay away.
The season of joy starts in September and goes on till March.
So the rain decides when a trip will feel good or bad.
Anita understands she should travel after the monsoon, from September onwards.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The People of Coorg
activities.body: The people of Coorg are fiercely independent. They may be of Greek or Arabic descent. One story says a part of Alexander's army moved south along the coast and settled here. These people married among the locals. Their culture is still seen in martial traditions, marriage and religious rites.
keyPoints: Coorg people may be of Greek or Arabic descent.
Alexander's army is said to have settled here and married locals.
Their culture lives on in traditions, marriage and religious rites.
activities.explanation: The people of Coorg carry a proud story from faraway lands.

activities.title: Where is Coorg?
activities.prompt: Coorg is the smallest district of which state?
options: Kerala
Karnataka
Goa
Tamil Nadu
activities.explanation: Well done! Coorg, or Kodagu, is the smallest district of Karnataka.

activities.title: How Much Forest?
activities.prompt: Evergreen rainforests cover ______ per cent of the district of Coorg.
activities.hint: Think of the number of days in a month.
activities.explanation: Right! Thirty per cent of Coorg is evergreen rainforest.

activities.title: Midway Between Two Towns
activities.prompt: Coorg lies midway between Mysore and the coastal town of Mangalore.
activities.explanation: Yes! That is exactly where Coorg sits on the map.

activities.title: Match the Coorg Words
activities.prompt: Match each word on the left with what it means in the lesson.
pairs: Forests that cover thirty per cent
activities.explanation: Great matching! You know the places and plants of Coorg well.

activities.title: Choosing the Right Month
activities.prompt: Ravi wants to visit Coorg in a happy season. Which month should he pick, and why?
options: July, because the monsoon pours then
September, because the season of joy starts then
June, because the rains keep crowds away
May, because the season of joy ends then
activities.explanation: Well thought! The season of joy starts in September and lasts till March.

activities.title: The Story in Order
activities.prompt: Put the old story of the Coorg people in the right order.
items: A part of Alexander's army moved south along the coast.
The soldiers settled in Coorg.
They married among the locals.
Their culture is seen in martial traditions, marriage and religious rites.
activities.explanation: Lovely work! You retold the old story in the right order.

activities.prompt: Coorg lies midway between Mysore and Mangalore. A tourist drives from Mangalore to Mysore. He stops at the halfway point. Where has he reached?
options: He has reached Coorg.
He has reached Mysore.
He has reached Mangalore.
He has reached the sea coast.

He mixed up the halfway point with the end of the trip.
He mixed up the halfway point with the starting place.
He thought 'midway' meant near the coast, not between the towns.

activities.explanation: Right. Halfway between the two towns is exactly where Coorg lies.

activities.prompt: During the monsoons, Coorg pours with heavy rain. The rain keeps many visitors away. Meena plans a trip in July. Her friend says, 'Come in September instead.' Why does the friend say this?
options: September starts the season of joy there.
July has far too many visitors there.
September has the heaviest rain there.
July is too cold for any travel there.

She got it backwards; heavy rain keeps visitors away, not brings them.
She mixed up the rainy months with the happy season.
The passage says rain keeps visitors away, not cold weather.

activities.explanation: Right. The season of joy begins in September, so it is a good time.

activities.prompt: Coorg has evergreen rainforests. Thirty per cent of the district is covered by them. Evergreen trees do not drop all their leaves. A visitor walks there in the dry months. He still sees green hills everywhere. Why?
options: The forests stay green all year.
It rains there every single day.
Visitors paint the hills green.
Snow covers the hills all year.

Heavy rain comes in the monsoons, not every day of the year.
Painting hills is a silly idea no one would really do.
Coorg has rainforests, not snowy hills.

activities.explanation: Right. Evergreen forests keep their leaves, so they stay green.

activities.prompt: The people of Coorg have martial traditions. Their culture shows in marriage and religious rites. A guest attends a Coorg wedding. He sees customs of soldiers in it. What does this show?
options: Old culture is still alive there.
The wedding is an army practice.
Every guest must become a soldier.
Marriages there happen only in war.

A wedding with soldier customs is not real army training.
Guests only watch the customs; nobody is forced to join.
The customs are part of normal weddings, not of war.

activities.explanation: Right. Martial customs in weddings show the old culture lives on.

lessons.title: Coorg: Hospitality, Army, Nature and Adventure

activities.prompt: What makes a tiny hill town so brave, so welcoming, and so wild?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The People and Pride of Coorg
activities.body: Coorg is a land of warm hearts and brave stories. Coorgi homes welcome guests with a tradition of hospitality. Families love to tell tales of valour about their sons and fathers. Many Coorgis serve in the Indian Army. The Coorg Regiment is one of the most decorated in the Indian Army. General Cariappa, the first Chief of the Indian Army, was a Coorgi. Kodavus are the only people in India allowed to carry firearms without a licence.
keyPoints: Coorgi homes have a tradition of hospitality.
The Coorg Regiment is one of the most decorated in the Indian Army.
General Cariappa, the first Chief of the Indian Army, was a Coorgi.
Kodavus are the only people in India allowed to carry firearms without a licence.
activities.explanation: Coorg is proud of its warm welcome and its brave soldiers.

activities.prompt: Ravi visits a Coorgi home for the first time. He is shy and quiet. The family gives him food and then talks proudly about their father's army days. Why do they act this way?
steps: The family offers food at once, because hospitality is a strong tradition in Coorgi homes.
They talk about their father with pride, because tales of valour about sons and fathers are loved there.
Their pride makes sense, because the Coorg Regiment is one of the most decorated in the Indian Army.
So Ravi sees that the family's warmth and pride come from the same Coorgi way of life.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Rivers, Creatures and Adventure
activities.body: The river Kaveri gets its water from the hills and forests of Coorg. Its waters teem with life. Mahaseer, a large freshwater fish, abound in these waters. Kingfishers dive for their catch, while squirrels and langurs drop partly eaten fruit. Elephants enjoy being bathed and scrubbed in the river by their mahouts. Even laidback people become converts to high-energy adventure here. The climb to Brahmagiri hills gives a panoramic view of the misty landscape of Coorg.
keyPoints: The Kaveri gets its water from the hills and forests of Coorg.
Mahaseer, a large freshwater fish, abound in these waters.
Even laidback people become converts to high-energy adventure.
The climb to Brahmagiri hills gives a panoramic view of the misty landscape.
activities.explanation: Coorg's river and hills are full of life and adventure.

activities.prompt: What tradition do Coorgi homes have?
options: A tradition of silence
A tradition of hospitality
A tradition of fasting
A tradition of travel
activities.explanation: Coorgi homes are famous for welcoming guests warmly. That is what hospitality means.

activities.prompt: Who are the only people in India allowed to carry firearms without a licence?
options: Kodavus
Fishermen
Mahouts
Langurs
activities.explanation: Kodavus have this special right. No other people in India have it.

activities.prompt: General Cariappa, the first Chief of the Indian Army, was a Coorgi.
activities.explanation: Yes, General Cariappa was a Coorgi. Coorg is proud of him.

activities.prompt: The river ______ gets its water from the hills and forests of Coorg.
activities.hint: Think of the river that flows from Coorg.
activities.explanation: The hills and forests of Coorg give the Kaveri its water. Well done!

activities.prompt: Match each creature or person to what it does in Coorg.
pairs: Are bathed and scrubbed by mahouts
activities.explanation: Each one has its own way of enjoying the river. You matched them all!

activities.prompt: Why would a visitor climb to the Brahmagiri hills?
options: To bathe elephants in the river
To see a panoramic view of the misty landscape
To buy a firearm licence
To swim with the mahaseer
activities.explanation: The climb to Brahmagiri hills gives a panoramic view of the misty landscape of Coorg. What a reward!

activities.prompt: Meera's family in Coorg invites a tired stranger for dinner. They do not ask him any questions first. What does this show about Coorgi homes?
options: They help any guest because welcoming people is their habit
They want the stranger to pay them for the dinner
They feel lonely and want someone to talk to
They are afraid the stranger may get angry

why.They want the stranger to pay them for t: This thinks hospitality is a business deal, not a tradition.
why.They feel lonely and want someone to tal: This confuses a warm tradition with a feeling of loneliness.
why.They are afraid the stranger may get ang: This thinks fear drives them, but the reason is their welcoming tradition.

activities.explanation: Right: hospitality is a tradition in Coorgi homes, so they welcome guests freely.

activities.prompt: An old Coorgi man keeps telling stories about his son's brave acts in the army. His neighbour says, 'Why boast so much?' What does the old man's storytelling really show?
options: He is proud of his son and loves sharing tales of valour
He wants money and gifts from his neighbours
He is sad because his son never visits him
He is trying to scare the young children nearby

why.He wants money and gifts from his neighb: This mistakes family pride for a wish to gain something.
why.He is sad because his son never visits h: This reads the stories as sadness, but they come from pride.
why.He is trying to scare the young children: This thinks the stories are threats, not proud family tales.

activities.explanation: Right: Coorgis are willing to tell many tales of valour about their sons and fathers.

activities.prompt: A boy reads that a Coorgi man became the first Chief of the Indian Army. He feels a sudden pride in his own village. Why does he feel this way?
options: A man from his own land reached the top army post
He wants to become a chief himself one day
He thinks all chiefs must come from his village
He feels sorry for people who are not Coorgis

why.He wants to become a chief himself one d: This mixes the boy's pride with his own future dreams.
why.He thinks all chiefs must come from his: This wrongly thinks one man's success is a rule for all.
why.He feels sorry for people who are not Co: This adds a feeling of pity that the fact does not support.

activities.explanation: Right: General Cariappa, the first Chief of the Indian Army, was a Coorgi, so the boy shares that pride.

activities.prompt: A police officer stops many people for carrying guns. He sees a Kodavu man with a gun and lets him pass. Why does the officer let him pass?
options: Kodavus may carry firearms without a licence
The officer is too tired to check anyone
The gun belongs to the officer's own family
Kodavus pay the officer to look away

why.The officer is too tired to check anyone: This blames the officer's tiredness, not the special rule.
why.The gun belongs to the officer's own fam: This invents a family link that is not the reason.
why.Kodavus pay the officer to look away: This wrongly thinks a bribe is involved, not a legal right.

activities.explanation: Right: Kodavus are the only people in India allowed to carry firearms without a licence.

activities.prompt: A lazy boy visits Coorg. He sits by the river all day. On day three, he is climbing hills with a big smile. What happened to him?
options: He became a convert to high-energy adventure
He got bored and wanted to go back home
He was forced to climb by his strict parents
He forgot his way and climbed by mistake

why.He got bored and wanted to go back home: This reads boredom, but the boy is smiling and active.
why.He was forced to climb by his strict par: This thinks force caused it, but the change came from within.
why.He forgot his way and climbed by mistake: This thinks it was an accident, not a real change in him.

activities.explanation: Right: even laidback people become converts to high-energy adventure in Coorg.

lessons.title: Tea from Assam: Journey, Legends and Tea Garden

activities.prompt: Who really discovered tea, and why does no one know for sure?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Train Ride into Tea Country
activities.body: Pranjol is a youngster from Assam. He is Rajvir's classmate in Delhi. Pranjol's father manages a tea-garden in Upper Assam. So Pranjol invited Rajvir to visit his home during the summer vacation. On the way, the soft green paddy fields gave way to tea bushes. Rajvir was excited to learn all about tea.
keyPoints: Pranjol is from Assam and studies with Rajvir in Delhi.
Pranjol's father manages a tea-garden in Upper Assam.
Rajvir was invited for the summer vacation.
On the journey, paddy fields gave way to tea bushes.
activities.explanation: This lesson takes you on a train ride into the tea gardens of Assam.

activities.prompt: Rajvir is excited on the train, but Pranjol has a book and is not excited. Why do the two friends feel so different about the same tea gardens?
steps: Pranjol was born in Assam, so he has seen tea gardens many times before.
Because he has seen them often, the gardens feel normal to him, not new.
Rajvir lives in Delhi, so this is his first time seeing so many tea bushes.
So the same view feels boring to Pranjol but exciting to Rajvir, because it is new for one and old for the other.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Assam, the Land of Tea
activities.body: Assam has the largest concentration of plantations in the world. Against densely wooded hills, a sea of tea bushes stretched as far as the eye could see. Tea was first drunk in China as far back as 2700 BCE. The second-flush, or sprouting period, lasts from May to July and yields the best tea.
keyPoints: Assam has the largest concentration of plantations in the world.
A sea of tea bushes stretched as far as the eye could see.
Tea was first drunk in China in 2700 BCE.
The second-flush from May to July yields the best tea.
activities.explanation: Assam is a sea of tea bushes, and the best tea comes in the second-flush.

activities.prompt: Where is Pranjol from?
options: Assam
Delhi
China
Bengal
activities.explanation: Pranjol is a youngster from Assam. Well done!

activities.prompt: What did the soft green paddy fields give way to on the journey?
options: Tea bushes
Sandy deserts
Tall buildings
Mango orchards
activities.explanation: The paddy fields gave way to tea bushes as the train moved on.

activities.prompt: Pranjol invited Rajvir to visit his home during the summer ______.
activities.hint: It is the warm holiday time when school is closed.
activities.explanation: Rajvir went to Assam in the summer vacation. Lovely!

activities.prompt: Match each tea legend to what it says.
pairs: Always boiled water before drinking it
Cut off his eyelids during meditations
No one really knows who found it
activities.explanation: There are many legends about tea, and no one really knows who discovered it.

activities.prompt: Which period yields the best tea?
options: The second-flush, from May to July
The winter months, from December to January
The first rains, from March to April
activities.explanation: The second-flush is the sprouting period, and it yields the best tea.

activities.prompt: Put these moments from the journey in the order they happened.
items: Pranjol invited Rajvir to Assam for the summer vacation
The soft green paddy fields gave way to tea bushes
A sea of tea bushes stretched as far as the eye could see
Rajvir said over eighty crore cups of tea are drunk every day
activities.explanation: First the invitation, then the changing fields, then the sea of tea bushes, then Rajvir's tea fact. Great ordering!

activities.prompt: Rajvir keeps looking out of the train window. He says, 'Look, tea bushes everywhere!' Pranjol is reading his book and does not look up. Why does Pranjol not look up?
options: He is tired and wants to sleep on the train.
He has seen tea gardens many times, so they feel normal.
He does not like tea and does not care about it.
He is angry with Rajvir for talking too much.

why.He is tired and wants to sleep on the tr: Wrong: nothing shows he is tired; he is reading, not sleeping.
why.He does not like tea and does not care a: Wrong: he never says he dislikes tea; he is just used to the view.
why.He is angry with Rajvir for talking too: Wrong: he is not angry; he is simply busy with his book.

activities.explanation: Right: he grew up in Assam, so the gardens are not new or exciting for him.

activities.prompt: A boy in Delhi tells his friends, 'People drink more than eighty crore cups of tea every day.' His friends laugh and say, 'That cannot be true!' What does the boy's number really show?
options: Tea is a drink loved by people all over the world.
Tea is drunk only in India, not in other countries.
Tea is cheap, so poor people drink it the most.
Tea shops sell more tea in the morning than at night.

why.Tea is drunk only in India, not in other: Wrong: the number is for the whole world, so it cannot be only India.
why.Tea is cheap, so poor people drink it th: Wrong: the number tells how much tea is drunk, not its price.
why.Tea shops sell more tea in the morning t: Wrong: the number counts all cups in a day, not morning versus night.

activities.explanation: Right: such a huge number of cups means people everywhere drink tea daily.

activities.prompt: Rajvir looks out of the train. First he sees soft green paddy fields. After some time, he sees rows of tea bushes instead. What does this change show about the train journey?
options: The train is going backwards towards Delhi again.
The train has entered a place where tea grows.
The paddy fields were burnt and new plants came up.
The train has reached the end of its journey.

why.The train is going backwards towards Del: Wrong: the friends are travelling towards Assam, not back to Delhi.
why.The paddy fields were burnt and new plan: Wrong: nothing was burnt; one crop area simply gave way to another.
why.The train has reached the end of its jou: Wrong: seeing tea bushes means they are near the gardens, not that the trip is over.

activities.explanation: Right: paddy fields changing into tea bushes means the train has reached tea country.

activities.prompt: Rajvir reads that a Chinese emperor always boiled his water before drinking it. One day, some leaves fell into his boiling water. The water turned tasty and golden. Why is this a story about how tea was found?
options: It shows the emperor was a very careful cook.
It shows boiled water is always safe to drink.
It shows tea leaves were found by a lucky accident.
It shows the emperor liked golden things the most.

why.It shows the emperor was a very careful: Wrong: the story is not about cooking skill; the leaves fell by chance.
why.It shows boiled water is always safe to: Wrong: safe water is the reason he boiled it, not how tea was found.
why.It shows the emperor liked golden things: Wrong: the colour of the water is not the point; the new drink is.

activities.explanation: Right: leaves fell into the water by chance, and that chance drink became tea.

activities.prompt: A garden owner wants to pick leaves that will give the best tea. His helper says, 'Let us pick in March.' The owner shakes his head and waits. Why does the owner wait?
options: He wants to save money by picking later in the year.
He is waiting for the sprouting time that gives the best tea.
He thinks March leaves are too big to carry easily.
He wants the workers to rest for a few more months.

why.He wants to save money by picking later: Wrong: the reason is about quality of tea, not about saving money.
why.He thinks March leaves are too big to ca: Wrong: leaf size for carrying is not the reason for waiting.
why.He wants the workers to rest for a few m: Wrong: the workers' rest is not the point; the tea quality is.

activities.explanation: Right: the best tea comes from the second-flush sprouting time, from May to July, so he waits for it.
