chapters.title: Madam Rides the Bus
chapters.summary: In this chapter: valli and the bus outside her door; valli's wish and secret plan; valli boards the bus; the bus ride and the passengers.

lessons.title: Valli and the bus outside her door

activities.prompt: What could a little girl discover just by watching her street?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet Valli and her bus
activities.body: Valli is an eight-year-old girl who is very curious. Her favourite pastime is standing in her front doorway and watching the street outside. There are no playmates of her own age on her street, so watching gives her many new experiences. The most fascinating thing she sees is the bus that runs between her village and the nearest town.
keyPoints: Valli is eight years old and very curious.
She loves standing at her front doorway and watching the street.
The bus between her village and the town fascinates her the most.
activities.explanation: Valli's doorway becomes her window to the wide world outside.

activities.prompt: Valli has no friends to play with. Why does standing at her front door become her favourite pastime?
steps: Valli has no playmates of her own age, so she cannot play games with friends.
Because she has no friends, she needs another way to spend her time.
Her front door lets her watch the street, and the street gives her new experiences.
So watching the street from her doorway becomes her favourite pastime.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What does Valli love doing most?
options: Playing games with friends
Standing in her front doorway
Reading books in her room
Riding the bus to town
activities.explanation: Her favourite pastime is standing in her front doorway and watching the street. Well done!

activities.prompt: The bus passes through Valli's street every ______.
activities.hint: Think how often the bus comes by.
activities.explanation: The bus passes through her street each hour, once to town and once back.

activities.prompt: Why does the bus give Valli unending joy?
options: It is painted a bright colour
It carries new passengers each time
It drives very fast
It honks a loud horn
activities.explanation: The bus filled with new passengers is a source of unending joy for Valli.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what the lesson says about it.
activities.explanation: Each detail helps you picture Valli's world. Great matching!

activities.prompt: Put the bus journey in order, from first to last.
items: The bus starts in the village
It passes through Valli's street
It reaches the nearest town
It comes back to the village
activities.explanation: The bus goes once to town and once back, passing her street each hour.

activities.prompt: Valli has no friends of her age on her street. Every day she stands at her front door. She watches the street for a long time. Why does she stand there?
options: She is waiting for her mother to call her in.
Watching the street is her way of play and fun.
She is afraid to go out of the house.
She is waiting for the bus driver to wave at her.

why.She is waiting for her mother to call he: This thinks her standing depends on her mother, but the story says it is her favourite pastime.
This thinks fear keeps her inside, but the story never says she is afraid.
why.She is waiting for the bus driver to wav: This thinks she waits for one person, but she watches everything in the street.

activities.explanation: Right: with no playmates, watching the street gives her new experiences, so it becomes her pastime.

activities.prompt: A bus passes Valli's street every hour. It goes to town and then comes back. A bus has just gone to town. What will the next bus do?
options: It will go to town again.
It will come back from town.
It will stop running for the day.
It will go to a different village.

This forgets the bus goes to town and back, one after the other.
This thinks the bus stops, but it passes every hour.
This adds a new place, but the bus only goes between the village and the town.

activities.explanation: Right: the bus goes once to town and once back, so the next one comes back.

activities.prompt: Valli watches the street every day. She sees people, animals and the bus. Watching gives her many new experiences. What does this tell us about Valli?
options: She learns about the world by watching it.
She wants to sleep all day long.
She does not like the bus at all.
She is angry with the people outside.

This thinks watching is lazy, but the story says it gives her experiences.
This is the opposite of the story, because the bus fascinates her most.
This adds an angry feeling that the story never mentions.

activities.explanation: Right: watching gives her new experiences, so she learns from what she sees.

activities.prompt: Valli is very curious. A new bus comes each hour with new passengers. What will Valli most likely do when the bus comes?
options: She will run inside and hide from it.
She will watch the new people closely.
She will close her eyes and sleep.
She will ask the driver for money.

A curious child does not hide; hiding is what a scared child might do.
Closing her eyes stops her from seeing, and she loves to see new things.
This adds money, but her joy comes from watching, not from asking.

activities.explanation: Right: a curious child loves new things, so she will watch the new passengers.

lessons.sceneAlt: A poor rural Indian village street with simple huts along the side.
lessons.sceneCaption: A typical rural Indian village street, like the one Valli watches from her front doorway.

sceneCredit.text: India - Rural - 04 - typical street (2566361495) by McKay Savage from London, UK, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: McKay Savage from London, UK

lessons.title: Valli's wish and secret plan

activities.prompt: What secret wish made Valli's heart race every time the bus passed?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A tiny wish grows big
activities.body: A tiny wish crept into Valli's head and grew. She wanted to ride the bus, even if just once. Soon the wish became an overwhelming desire. She watched people getting on and off the bus. She listened to conversations and asked careful questions. Little by little, she made a secret plan for her very first bus ride.
keyPoints: A tiny wish crept into Valli's head and grew
She wanted to ride the bus even if just once
She watched people and asked careful questions to plan her trip
activities.explanation: Big dreams often start small, and Valli planned hers step by step.

activities.prompt: Valli wants to ride the bus. But she is a small girl with no one to help her. How can she make her plan work?
steps: Her wish grew into an overwhelming desire, so she could not just forget it.
She did not know the fare or the distance, so she listened to talks and asked discreet questions.
She learned the fare was thirty paise each way, so she knew she needed money for the ride back too.
So her secret plan worked because she quietly collected every fact she needed first.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did Valli want to do, even if just once?
options: Ride the bus
Visit the market
Swim in the river
Buy a new dress
activities.explanation: The lesson says she wanted to ride the bus, even if just once. A small wish that grew big!

activities.prompt: Valli learned that the town was ______ miles from her village.
activities.hint: Think of the number of miles mentioned in the lesson.
activities.explanation: The town was six miles from her village. Valli found this out by asking careful questions.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what Valli learned about it.
activities.explanation: Valli gathered every detail: the distance, the fare, the time and the return fare. Good detectives ask good questions!

activities.prompt: Put the steps of Valli's secret plan in the right order.
items: A tiny wish crept into her head and grew
She stared wistfully at people getting on or off the bus
She listened to conversations and asked discreet questions
She learned the distance, the fare and the time of the trip
activities.explanation: First the wish grew, then she watched, then she asked questions, and at last she knew all the details. That is how a plan is built!

activities.prompt: Valli pays thirty paise to go to town and thirty paise to come back. How much does the whole trip cost her?
options: Sixty paise
Forty-five paise
Thirty paise
Ninety paise
activities.explanation: Thirty paise one way plus another thirty paise for the return makes sixty paise. Valli saved every coin for this!

activities.prompt: Ravi stands near the gate every evening. He watches children get on the fair bus. He looks at them for a long time and sighs. What does Ravi most likely feel?
options: He wants to ride the bus too.
He is angry at the children.
He is very tired of standing.
He forgot something at his home.

Wrong. This confuses quiet longing with anger; he does nothing angry.
Wrong. This misses the feeling; the sigh comes from wanting, not tiredness.
Wrong. This adds a new problem; nothing in the scene says he forgot anything.

activities.explanation: Right. Staring wistfully at bus riders shows a longing to ride too.

activities.prompt: Sana wants to know the price of a toy. She feels shy to ask directly. She listens to other buyers and asks small careful questions. Which word tells how Sana asks?
options: She asks discreetly.
She asks rudely.
She asks loudly.
She asks sadly.

Wrong. Rude means hurting others; Sana is being careful, not rude.
Wrong. Loud questions would draw notice, the opposite of what she does.
Wrong. Sad tells a feeling, not the careful way she asks.

activities.explanation: Right. Careful, quiet questions that do not draw notice are discreet questions.

activities.prompt: Some boys play a slow, boring game. They call it 'pallu' and say it with a frown. What does the word 'pallu' show here?
options: It shows they dislike the game.
It shows they love the game.
It shows they made the game.
It shows they won the game.

Wrong. Loving words come with smiles, not frowns.
Wrong. Making a game says nothing about liking or disliking it.
Wrong. Winning is about the result, not the feeling in the word.

activities.explanation: Right. A word said with a frown works as slang showing disapproval.

activities.prompt: A bus goes to a town six miles from a village. The fare is thirty paise one way. You can return on the same bus. You ride to the town and come back. How much do you pay in all?
options: Sixty paise in all.
Thirty paise in all.
Ninety paise in all.
Forty-five paise in all.

Wrong. This pays only one way and forgets the return trip.
Wrong. This adds an extra trip that was never made.
Wrong. This mixes up the forty-five minutes of travel time with money.

activities.explanation: Right. Thirty paise to go plus thirty paise to return makes sixty paise.

activities.prompt: A tiny wish to ride a bus came into Asha's head. Day by day it grew bigger in her mind. Soon she could think of nothing else. What happened to her wish?
options: It became an overwhelming desire.
It slowly died away.
It stayed very small.
It was given by a friend.

Wrong. Dying away is the opposite of growing bigger.
Wrong. The wish clearly changed; it did not stay tiny.
Wrong. The wish grew inside her own head, not from a friend.

activities.explanation: Right. A wish that grows until it fills the mind becomes an overwhelming desire.

lessons.sceneAlt: A sheltered bus stop on a state highway in an Indian village.
lessons.sceneCaption: A sheltered bus stop in an Indian village, where Valli watched people getting on and off the bus.

sceneCredit.text: Taccode bus stop by Rohan Pinto, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Rohan Pinto

lessons.title: Valli boards the bus

activities.prompt: What happens when a determined little girl stops a bus all by herself?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Valli stops the bus
activities.body: One spring day, the afternoon bus was leaving the village. Valli wanted to get on it. She shouted in a small voice and raised her tiny hand like a command. The bus slowed down to a crawl. The conductor was a jolly man who loved a joke. He asked everyone to make way for madam and gave her a seat right up in front.
keyPoints: The afternoon bus was leaving the village on a spring day.
Valli stopped it with a small shout and a raised hand.
The jolly conductor gave her a front seat and called her madam.
activities.explanation: Valli was small, but she knew just how to stop a bus!

activities.prompt: Valli shouts to stop the bus and raises her hand. The bus is big and she is small. Why does the bus still stop for her?
steps: The bus is leaving the village, so the driver has not gone far yet.
Valli shouts in a loud way and raises her hand like a command, so the driver notices her at once.
Because the driver sees her clearly, he slows the bus down to a crawl.
So the bus stops not because Valli is big, but because her voice and hand show she really means it.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What was the bus doing when Valli saw it?
options: It was leaving the village
It was sleeping in the shed
It was washing in the river
It was racing a train
activities.explanation: The lesson says the afternoon bus was leaving the village. Well spotted!

activities.prompt: The conductor stuck his head out and told Valli to ______.
activities.hint: He wanted her to be quick.
activities.explanation: The conductor told her to hurry. He was in a playful mood!

activities.prompt: Why did the conductor ask everybody to make way for madam?
options: He was joking because he liked jokes
He was scared of Valli
The law said he must
Valli asked him to say it
activities.explanation: He was a jolly sort who liked joking, so he teased her kindly.

activities.prompt: Match each person or thing to what happened.
activities.explanation: Each one did its own little part in the story. Lovely matching!

activities.prompt: Put these events in the order they happened.
items: The afternoon bus was leaving the village
A small voice shouted to stop the bus
The bus slowed down to a crawl
The conductor told her to hurry
Valli showed the conductor some coins
activities.explanation: First the bus leaves, then Valli stops it, then she pays. You remembered the order!

activities.prompt: Valli said she could get on by herself. What does this show about her?
options: She was proud and independent
She was afraid of the conductor
She did not want a seat
She had no money for the fare
activities.explanation: She showed her coins and said she could manage alone. Valli liked doing things herself!

activities.prompt: A small girl stands by the road. She shouts and raises her hand high. The big bus slows down. How does the girl probably feel about herself?
options: She feels small and scared of the bus.
She feels sure she can stop the bus.
She feels sorry that she shouted loudly.
She feels lost because the bus is big.

Wrong: she raised her hand commandingly, so she is not acting scared.
Wrong: she shouted on purpose to stop the bus, not by mistake.
Wrong: she acts with command, so she does not feel lost.

activities.explanation: Right: a commanding hand and a loud shout show she is confident.

activities.prompt: A boy opens his hand before the shopkeeper. The shopkeeper sees the coins and smiles. Why did the boy open his hand?
options: To show he has money to pay.
To wave goodbye to the shopkeeper.
To hide the coins from the shopkeeper.
To ask the shopkeeper for more coins.

Wrong: opening a hand with coins is not a goodbye wave.
Wrong: an open hand shows coins, it does not hide them.
Wrong: she shows her own coins, she does not ask for more.

activities.explanation: Right: showing coins proves you can pay, just like Valli did.

activities.prompt: Valli says she can get on the bus by herself. Nobody lifts her up. What does this tell you about Valli?
options: She wants others to do things for her.
She is proud she can do things alone.
She is afraid to step up by herself.
She thinks getting on is very hard.

Wrong: she says the opposite, that she needs no help.
Wrong: if she were afraid, she would ask for help.
Wrong: she says it is easy enough to do alone.

activities.explanation: Right: saying she can do it alone shows pride in herself.

activities.prompt: The conductor calls Valli 'madam' and asks all to make way. He is really joking with her. How does Valli most likely feel?
options: She feels treated like a grown-up guest.
She feels angry at the silly old man.
She feels shy and hides her face away.
She feels sad that people laugh at her.

Wrong: the joke is friendly, so there is no reason for anger.
Wrong: she spoke boldly before, so she is not hiding now.
Wrong: the joke is kind, not mean, so she is not hurt.

activities.explanation: Right: being called madam and given a front seat makes her feel special.

lessons.sceneAlt: An express bus with its conductor standing on the footboard by the door.
lessons.sceneCaption: An express bus of the APSRTC with the conductor standing on footboard.

sceneCredit.text: An express bus of the APSRTC by Yathra Visheshangal, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Yathra Visheshangal

lessons.title: The bus ride and the passengers

activities.prompt: What did Valli see when she peeked over the bus window?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: All aboard!
activities.body: The conductor blew his whistle twice, and the bus moved with a roar. It was a new bus, gleaming white with green stripes. Inside, the overhead bars shone like silver, and a beautiful clock hung above the windshield. The seats were soft and luxurious. Valli devoured everything with her eyes. A canvas blind cut off the lower part of her window, so she stood on the seat and peered over it. The bus rolled along the bank of a canal, past palm trees, green fields and distant mountains.
keyPoints: The whistle blew twice and the bus roared off.
The bus was white with green stripes, with silver bars and a clock.
Valli stood on her seat to see over the canvas blind.
activities.explanation: Valli's first bus ride was full of new sights, and she did not want to miss a single one.

activities.prompt: Valli stands on her seat to look over the blind. Why does she take this risk instead of just sitting and waiting?
steps: The blind covers the lower part of the window, so sitting down she can only see a small strip, and that is not enough for her.
She devours everything with her eyes, so she is hungry to see the whole world outside, not just a piece of it.
Standing up lets her peer over the blind, so she can see the canal, the fields and the mountains fully.
So she stands because her strong wish to see everything is bigger than her worry about the conductor's rules.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A shining new bus
activities.prompt: What did the new bus look like?
options: Blue with yellow stars
Gleaming white with green stripes
Red with silver stripes
Green with white flowers
activities.explanation: The bus was new and painted gleaming white with green stripes. Well done!

activities.title: Above the windshield
activities.prompt: There was a beautiful ______ above the windshield.
activities.hint: It tells you the time.
activities.explanation: A beautiful clock sat above the windshield, keeping time for the journey.

activities.title: Inside and outside
activities.prompt: Match each thing with what the lesson says about it.
pairs: The bus went along its bank
activities.explanation: The bus was lovely inside, and the road beside the canal was lovely too.

activities.title: Why did she stand?
activities.prompt: Why did Valli stand on her seat?
options: She was tired of sitting down
She wanted to wave to the conductor
A canvas blind blocked the lower part of her window
She wanted to reach the overhead bars
activities.explanation: The blind hid the lower window, so standing up let her peer over it and see the world outside.

activities.title: The ride, step by step
activities.prompt: Put these moments of the ride in the order they happened.
items: The conductor blew his whistle twice
The bus moved with a roar
Valli devoured everything with her eyes
She stood on the seat and peered over the blind
The bus went along the bank of a canal
activities.explanation: First the whistle, then the roar, then Valli drank in every sight, stood up to see more, and off they went along the canal.

activities.title: Looking both ways
activities.prompt: Valli looked out on both sides of the bus. What could she see on each side?
options: Palm trees and mountains on one side, green fields on the other
Green fields on one side, a market on the other
Mountains on one side, a river on the other
Palm trees on one side, a town on the other
activities.explanation: Beyond the canal were palm trees, grassland and distant mountains, and on the other side, green fields everywhere.

activities.prompt: The bus roars and moves when the whistle blows twice. A boy says the whistle is like a key that starts the bus. What does he mean?
options: The whistle makes the driver start the bus.
The whistle tells people the bus is new.
The whistle opens the door of the bus.
The whistle warns the bus to stop.

Wrong: he is not talking about the bus being new, only about what makes it move.
Wrong: nothing about a door is said; a key that starts is not a key that opens.
Wrong: the bus moves, it does not stop, so the whistle cannot be a warning to stop.

activities.explanation: Right: the bus moves right after the whistle, so the whistle is the signal to start, like a key starts a car.

activities.prompt: The bus is gleaming white with green stripes, the bars shine like silver and the clock is beautiful. Valli drinks it all in with her eyes. How does she probably feel about the bus?
options: Bored, because she has seen such buses before.
Frightened, because the bus looks too grand.
Delighted, because everything looks so lovely.
Angry, because the bus is not her colour.

why.Bored, because she has seen such buses b: Wrong: someone who has seen it all before would not devour everything with her eyes.
why.Frightened, because the bus looks too gr: Wrong: nothing in the shiny, lovely bus would scare her; fear does not fit.
why.Angry, because the bus is not her colour: Wrong: she never says the colours are wrong; she enjoys looking, not complaining.

activities.explanation: Right: when everything looks new and beautiful, drinking it all in shows joy and wonder.

activities.prompt: The seats are soft and luxurious. A girl says, 'Sitting there must feel like sitting on a cloud.' What does she mean about the seats?
options: The seats are very hard to sit on.
The seats feel very soft and comfy.
The seats are high up in the air.
The seats are white like a cloud.

Wrong: a cloud is soft, so the girl is saying the opposite of hard.
Wrong: she is talking about how sitting feels, not how high the seat is.
Wrong: she means the feeling, not the colour of the seats.

activities.explanation: Right: 'like a cloud' is a picture for something soft and luxurious, which matches the seats.

activities.prompt: Valli stands on her seat and peers over the blind. The blind hides the lower window. What can we guess about why she does this?
options: She wants to see more than the blind lets her.
She wants to clean the window with her hands.
She wants to show the other people her dress.
She wants to hide from the man behind her.

why.She wants to clean the window with her h: Wrong: she is looking out, not cleaning; nothing about cleaning is in the story.
why.She wants to show the other people her d: Wrong: she is busy looking outside, not trying to be seen by others.
why.She wants to hide from the man behind he: Wrong: standing makes her easier to see, not harder, so hiding makes no sense.

activities.explanation: Right: the blind cuts off the lower window, so standing lets her look over it and see the whole view.

activities.prompt: An elderly man tells Valli not to stand and to sit down. Valli still wants to see over the blind. What is the man most likely feeling?
options: He is worried that standing is not safe.
He is angry because Valli is too noisy.
He is bored and wants a quiet bus.
He is jealous that Valli sees the view.

Wrong: Valli is looking, not shouting, so noise is not the problem.
Wrong: his words are about Valli standing, not about his own mood.
Wrong: nothing shows he wants the view; he is thinking about her safety.

activities.explanation: Right: grown-ups stop children from standing on moving buses because a moving bus can make them fall.

lessons.title: Valli's pride, the old woman, and the town

activities.prompt: Why does Valli refuse to be called a child or a madam?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Valli rides the bus like a grown-up
activities.body: Valli wants everyone to see her as a grown-up, not a child. When the conductor calls her a madam, she says she is not one and asks for her ticket. She pays her thirty paise like everyone else. She stands because she wants to, even though she might fall. An old woman sits beside her and asks if she is alone. Valli does not like the old woman at all.
keyPoints: Valli said nobody on the bus was a child.
She paid her thirty paise like everyone else.
The conductor called her a very grown-up madam.
An elderly woman sat beside her and asked if she was alone.
Valli found the old woman absolutely repulsive.
activities.explanation: Valli is proud of travelling alone, just like a grown-up.

activities.prompt: Valli says she is not a child, but she is only eight. Why does she keep saying this?
steps: Valli paid her fare like everyone else, so she feels equal to adults.
The conductor calls her a grown-up madam, so she gets the respect she wants.
But the old woman still treats her like a small child, so her pride is hurt.
So Valli says she is not a child because she wants to be seen as grown-up.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What did the conductor call Valli?
options: A very grown-up madam
A clever little child
A brave young boy
A quiet new passenger
activities.explanation: The conductor teased her kindly by calling her a very grown-up madam.

activities.prompt: Valli said she had paid her thirty ______ like everyone else.
activities.hint: It is the small money she gave for her ticket.
activities.explanation: She paid her thirty paise, the same as every other passenger.

activities.prompt: Valli told the conductor that she was eight years old.
activities.explanation: Yes, she said she was not a child and was eight years old.

activities.prompt: Why did Valli stand up again on the bus?
options: Because she wanted to
Because her seat was wet
Because the bus was full
Because the conductor asked her
activities.explanation: She stood again because she wanted to. It was her own proud choice.

activities.prompt: The conductor warned Valli she might fall. What did he say could happen then?
options: She might hurt herself
She might miss her stop
She might lose her ticket
She might feel dizzy
activities.explanation: He warned that she might fall and hurt herself if she kept standing.

activities.prompt: Put these events from the bus ride in the correct order.
items: The conductor called Valli a very grown-up madam
Valli said she was not a madam and asked for her ticket
The conductor punched a ticket and handed it to her
An elderly woman sat beside her and asked if she was alone
Valli said she was travelling alone
activities.explanation: First the teasing, then the ticket, then the old woman's questions.

activities.prompt: The conductor calls Valli a very grown-up madam. Valli says she is not a madam. What does this show about Valli?
options: She does not know the meaning of the word madam
She wants the ticket more than the joke
She is shy and cannot talk to strangers
She takes herself seriously and wants respect

why.She does not know the meaning of the wor: Wrong: she understands the word; she just refuses the title.
why.She wants the ticket more than the joke: Wrong: she asks for the ticket, but her words show pride, not hurry.
why.She is shy and cannot talk to strangers: Wrong: she talks confidently, so she is not shy.

activities.explanation: Right: she corrects the conductor because she wants to be taken seriously.

activities.prompt: Valli stands up again on the bus. The conductor warns she may fall and hurt herself. Valli still stands. What does this tell us?
options: She did not hear the conductor's warning at all
She is stubborn and does what she has decided
She wants to fall and get hurt on purpose
She is standing up to look for her mother

why.She did not hear the conductor's warning: Wrong: she heard it; she answers him, so she was listening.
why.She wants to fall and get hurt on purpos: Wrong: no child wants to get hurt; she just ignores the risk.
why.She is standing up to look for her mothe: Wrong: nothing in the story says she is looking for anyone.

activities.explanation: Right: she does what she wants even after a warning, showing her strong will.

activities.prompt: An old woman sits beside Valli and asks if she is alone. Valli finds the old woman repulsive. What does Valli most likely dislike?
options: The woman's looks and her way of treating her as small
The seat because it is too hard and dirty
The ticket because the conductor punched it wrongly
The bus because it is moving too fast

why.The seat because it is too hard and dirt: Wrong: her dislike is about the woman, not the seat.
why.The ticket because the conductor punched: Wrong: the ticket is already in her hand and fine.
why.The bus because it is moving too fast: Wrong: she loves the bus ride; that is why she is on it.

activities.explanation: Right: the woman looks unpleasant and treats Valli like a tiny child.

activities.prompt: The old woman asks if it is proper for such a young person to travel alone. Valli says she is travelling alone. What does Valli's short answer show?
options: She does not understand the old woman's question
She is too tired to speak more words
She does not want advice about how she should travel
She is hoping the old woman will travel with her

why.She does not understand the old woman's: Wrong: she understands it well; she answers it directly.
why.She is too tired to speak more words: Wrong: her short words come from pride, not tiredness.
why.She is hoping the old woman will travel: Wrong: she wants to be left alone, not joined.

activities.explanation: Right: she refuses to be told what is proper for a child.

activities.prompt: Valli says nobody on the bus is a child. She is eight years old herself. What is Valli really trying to prove?
options: That she is grown-up enough to travel by herself
That she is younger than all the other people
That she wants to sit with another child
That she forgot how old she really is

why.That she is younger than all the other p: Wrong: she is claiming to be older, not younger.
why.That she wants to sit with another child: Wrong: she has just said there is no child on the bus.
why.That she forgot how old she really is: Wrong: she knows her age well and states it proudly.

activities.explanation: Right: she wants others to see her as an independent grown-up person.

lessons.title: The town, return, dead cow, and home

activities.prompt: Why did one sad sight on the road spoil Valli's happiest day?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Valli's big day in town
activities.body: Valli had saved sixty paise for her bus ride. On the way, a young cow ran in front of the bus, and Valli laughed until there were tears in her eyes. In town, she saw glittering displays of clothes and other merchandise. She said she would go back on the same bus. But on the return, she saw the same cow lying dead by the roadside. That sad memory haunted her. The bus reached her village at three forty.
keyPoints: Valli saved sixty paise for her ride.
A live cow made her laugh; a dead cow made her sad.
The bus reached her village at three forty.
activities.explanation: A happy trip can hold one sad moment too.

activities.prompt: Valli laughed at a running cow on the way to town. On the way back, she saw a dead cow and could not forget it. Why did one cow make her happy and then sad?
steps: Valli laughed at the running cow because it looked full of life and joy.
On the way back, the same kind of cow lay dead, so the happy picture broke.
A mind remembers a sharp change from joy to sadness, so the dead cow stayed in her thoughts.
So the memory haunted her because it turned her best moment into a sad one.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: How much money had Valli saved in all?
options: Thirty paise
Sixty paise
Ninety paise
One rupee
activities.explanation: Well done! Valli saved a total of sixty paise for her trip.

activities.prompt: What ran in front of the bus on the way to town?
options: A young cow with its tail high
A dog with a stick
A goat with its head low
A young horse with a rider
activities.explanation: Yes! A young cow with its tail high ran in front of the bus.

activities.prompt: When the cow ran in front of the bus, the bus slowed to a ______.
activities.hint: Think of a word for moving very, very slowly.
activities.explanation: The bus slowed to a crawl so the cow could pass safely.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what happened.
pairs: Ran in front of the bus
Rushed past with a tremendous roar
Reached the village at three forty
activities.explanation: Each event was a step in Valli's big day.

activities.prompt: Put these events from Valli's day in the right order.
items: A young cow ran in front of the bus
A train rushed past the crossing gate
Valli saw glittering displays in the shops
Valli said she would return on the same bus
Valli saw the young cow lying dead by the roadside
activities.explanation: First the happy cow, then the town, and last the sad sight on the way home.

activities.prompt: Why did the dead cow haunt Valli so much?
options: She had laughed at that same cow when it was alive
She had wanted to buy that cow for her home
She had fed that cow some leaves that morning
She had seen that cow at the merry-go-round
activities.explanation: Think about it: the cow that made her laugh with joy was now lying dead. That change hurt her heart.

activities.prompt: Valli wanted to ride the merry-go-round very much. She did not spend her money on it. Why did she stop herself?
options: She was saving every paise for her bus ride.
She felt scared of fast rides like that.
She thought merry-go-rounds were boring.
A friend at home told her not to go.

Wrong. She wanted the ride, so fear was not the reason.
Wrong. She had a strong desire for it, so it was not boring to her.
Wrong. No friend stopped her; she stopped herself.

activities.explanation: Right. She saved sixty paise, so she gave up the ride to keep her money.

activities.prompt: A young cow ran in front of the bus. Its tail was high. The bus slowed to a crawl. Valli laughed until there were tears in her eyes. Why did she laugh?
options: The cow's joyful run looked funny to her.
She was crying about something very sad.
The driver shouted loudly at the slow cow.
She felt afraid when the bus slowed down.

Wrong. Tears from laughing are not tears of sadness.
why.The driver shouted loudly at the slow co: Wrong. The story does not say the driver shouted at all.
why.She felt afraid when the bus slowed down: Wrong. A slow bus is safe, so fear does not fit.

activities.explanation: Right. The lively cow made her so happy that she laughed till tears came.

activities.prompt: On the way to town, Valli saw a young cow running. She laughed a lot. On the way back, a young cow lay dead by the road. The memory haunted her. Why did the memory haunt her?
options: The happy sight had turned into a sad one.
She could not remember the way back home.
She was feeling hungry and very tired.
She wanted to see the town once again.

why.She could not remember the way back home: Wrong. She knew the way; the cow was the problem.
Wrong. Hunger and tiredness are not in the story.
Wrong. She said she was going back on the same bus.

activities.explanation: Right. The lively cow she loved became a dead cow, and that change hurt her.

activities.prompt: Valli's mother slept from about one to four. The bus reached her village at three forty. Why was this timing good for Valli?
options: She could slip home before her mother woke.
The bus ticket cost less money at that time.
The shops in the town were open then.
Her mother was busy cooking food then.

why.The bus ticket cost less money at that t: Wrong. Nothing in the story says tickets were cheaper then.
Wrong. She was coming home, not going to shops.
Wrong. Her mother was asleep, not cooking.

activities.explanation: Right. Three forty is before four, so her mother was still asleep.

activities.prompt: In town, Valli saw shining displays of clothes and other things. She said she was going back on the same bus. What does this show about her?
options: She had planned only a bus ride, not shopping.
She loved shopping more than the bus ride.
She felt lost and scared in the new town.
She had no money left for the ticket back.

why.She loved shopping more than the bus rid: Wrong. If she loved shopping, she would get down and buy things.
why.She felt lost and scared in the new town: Wrong. She spoke calmly about her return, so she was not scared.
why.She had no money left for the ticket bac: Wrong. She had saved sixty paise for her trip.

activities.explanation: Right. She only looked at the displays and stayed for the return bus.

lessons.title: Test practice
lessons.sceneAlt: A poor rural Indian village street with simple huts along the side.
lessons.sceneCaption: A typical rural Indian village street, like the one Valli watches from her front doorway.

sceneCredit.text: India - Rural - 04 - typical street (2566361495) by McKay Savage from London, UK, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: McKay Savage from London, UK

activities.context: Valli is an eight-year-old girl, very curious about the world. Her favourite pastime is standing in her front doorway, watching what happens in the street outside. There are no playmates of her own age on her street, but watching it gives her many new unusual experiences. The most fascinating thing is the bus between her village and the nearest town. It passes through her street each hour, going once to town and once back, and each time it is filled with new passengers, which is a source of unending joy for her. Her first bus journey takes her outside her village and makes her meet the mystery of life and death, where she sees the gap between knowing death and understanding it.
activities.prompt: If the bus stopped passing through Valli's street, what would most likely happen to her daily life?
options: She would lose her main source of joy and her window to new experiences
She would stop standing at her front doorway altogether
She would immediately make friends with children of her own age
She would lose interest in the mystery of life and death

why.She would stop standing at her front doo: Wrong: she watches the whole street, not only the bus, so she would still stand and watch.
why.She would immediately make friends with: Wrong: playmates cannot appear just because a bus stops; the street had none of her age.
why.She would lose interest in the mystery o: Wrong: her meeting with life and death came through her journey, not from the bus passing daily.

activities.explanation: Correct: the bus was her most fascinating sight and gave her unending joy, so losing it removes both.

activities.context: Valli is an eight-year-old girl, very curious about the world. Her favourite pastime is standing in her front doorway, watching what happens in the street outside. There are no playmates of her own age on her street, but watching it gives her many new unusual experiences. The most fascinating thing is the bus between her village and the nearest town. It passes through her street each hour, going once to town and once back, and each time it is filled with new passengers, which is a source of unending joy for her. Her first bus journey takes her outside her village and makes her meet the mystery of life and death, where she sees the gap between knowing death and understanding it.
activities.prompt: Why did watching the street give Valli so many new experiences when other children her age might not have gained as much?
options: Because she had no playmates, so all her attention went into careful watching
Because she was older and wiser than other children
Because her street was busier than most streets
Because her parents taught her what to notice

why.Because she was older and wiser than oth: Wrong: she is only eight; her age is not the reason for her sharp watching.
why.Because her street was busier than most: Wrong: nothing suggests her street was unusually busy; the point is her attention, not the street.
why.Because her parents taught her what to n: Wrong: her watching was her own curious habit, not something taught to her.

activities.explanation: Correct: with no playmates of her own age, watching became her whole pastime, so she noticed more.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The bus filled with new passengers was a source of unending joy for Valli.
Reason (R): The bus passed through her street each hour, going once to town and once back.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The hourly passing with fresh passengers each time is exactly what made the sight a lasting source of joy for her.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Valli's first bus journey took her deep into the nearest town.
Reason (R): Valli was very curious about the world outside.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The journey took her outside her village, not deep into the town, though her curiosity is truly stated.

activities.prompt: Explain why the bus became the most fascinating thing in Valli's life even though she had never travelled by it.
activities.answer: Valli was a curious eight-year-old with no playmates of her own age on her street, so standing in her front doorway and watching the street became her favourite pastime. This watching gave her many new unusual experiences, but the sight that fascinated her most was the bus between her village and the nearest town. It passed through her street each hour, going once to town and once back, and each time it was filled with new passengers. The ever-changing faces and the promise of a world outside her village made it a source of unending joy for her.
points: Mentions her curiosity and lack of playmates
Links doorway-watching to her new experiences
Notes the hourly bus to town and back with new passengers
Concludes that this made the bus her source of unending joy
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Every day Valli watched the bus stop near her lane. A tiny wish had crept into her head and grown until it became an overwhelming desire: she would ride that bus, even if just once. She stared wistfully at people getting on or off, their faces kindling her longings, dreams and hopes. When a friend described the town, she was too jealous to listen. So she listened carefully to conversations and asked discreet questions, learning that the town lay six miles away, the fare was thirty paise one way, the ride took forty-five minutes, and she could return on the same bus by paying another thirty paise.
activities.prompt: Valli has saved some coins. How much money must she set aside so that she can go to town and come back the same way?
options: Thirty paise, because one payment covers the whole journey
Sixty paise, because she must pay once while going and once while returning
Forty-five paise, because she pays for every minute of the ride
Ninety paise, because she pays separately for each mile of the route

why.Thirty paise, because one payment covers: Wrong: one payment only takes her one way, not back.
why.Forty-five paise, because she pays for e: Wrong: minutes measure the length of the ride, not the money to be paid.
why.Ninety paise, because she pays separatel: Wrong: the fare is not charged per mile; it is a fixed amount each way.

activities.explanation: Right: the fare is thirty paise each way, so going and returning costs twice that.

activities.context: Every day Valli watched the bus stop near her lane. A tiny wish had crept into her head and grown until it became an overwhelming desire: she would ride that bus, even if just once. She stared wistfully at people getting on or off, their faces kindling her longings, dreams and hopes. When a friend described the town, she was too jealous to listen. So she listened carefully to conversations and asked discreet questions, learning that the town lay six miles away, the fare was thirty paise one way, the ride took forty-five minutes, and she could return on the same bus by paying another thirty paise.
activities.prompt: Valli asks her questions quietly and carefully instead of announcing that she is planning a bus ride. What is the most likely reason for this?
options: She is afraid the fare will increase if many people start travelling
She does not actually want the information and is only being polite
She wants to keep her plan hidden until she is ready to carry it out
She hopes someone else will make the trip for her

why.She is afraid the fare will increase if: Wrong: nothing suggests the fare depends on how many people travel.
why.She does not actually want the informati: Wrong: she genuinely needs the details, which is why she gathers them so carefully.
why.She hopes someone else will make the tri: Wrong: her desire is to ride the bus herself, not to send anyone in her place.

activities.explanation: Right: discreet questions let her collect facts without revealing her secret plan.

activities.context: Every day Valli watched the bus stop near her lane. A tiny wish had crept into her head and grown until it became an overwhelming desire: she would ride that bus, even if just once. She stared wistfully at people getting on or off, their faces kindling her longings, dreams and hopes. When a friend described the town, she was too jealous to listen. So she listened carefully to conversations and asked discreet questions, learning that the town lay six miles away, the fare was thirty paise one way, the ride took forty-five minutes, and she could return on the same bus by paying another thirty paise.
activities.prompt: Suppose Valli had never stood watching the passengers get on and off the bus. What would most likely have happened to her wish?
options: It would have grown even faster, since she would have had more free time
It would have stayed a tiny wish instead of swelling into an overwhelming desire
It would have turned into anger towards the people who rode the bus
It would have made her stop speaking to friends who talked about the town

why.It would have grown even faster, since s: Wrong: free time alone would not feed the wish; it was the sight of travellers that fed it.
why.It would have turned into anger towards: Wrong: her feeling was longing and jealousy, not anger at the travellers.
why.It would have made her stop speaking to: Wrong: her jealousy showed only when a friend described the town, not because of watching the bus.

activities.explanation: Right: it was watching the passengers, whose faces kindled her longings, that made the tiny wish grow.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Valli's small wish slowly turned into an overwhelming desire to ride the bus.
Reason (R): She stared wistfully at people getting on or off the bus, and their faces kindled her longings, dreams and hopes.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Watching the passengers day after day is exactly what fed the tiny wish and made it grow overwhelming.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Valli knew she could make the return trip on the same bus by paying another thirty paise.
Reason (R): The town was six miles from her village, and the journey took forty-five minutes.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the distance and duration do not explain how she learned the return fare.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between Valli's first wish and the overwhelming desire it became, and how does the passage show this change?
activities.answer: At first, the wish was tiny: it simply crept into her head that she might ride the bus even once. As she kept staring wistfully at people getting on and off, and their faces kindled her longings, dreams and hopes, the wish grew stronger and became an overwhelming desire that ruled her thoughts. The change is shown in her behaviour: she could not tolerate a friend talking about the town, and she began listening to conversations and asking discreet questions to learn the distance, the fare and the time the trip took, preparing seriously for the journey.
points: Describes the wish at first as tiny and casual
Explains that watching passengers and their faces made the wish grow
Shows the desire became overwhelming and drove her actions
Cites her jealousy and her careful information-gathering as evidence of the change
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: One spring day, the afternoon bus was leaving the village when a small voice shouted to stop it. A tiny hand was raised commandingly, and the bus slowed to a crawl. The conductor stuck his head out and told her to hurry. Valli showed him some coins and said she could get on by herself. The jolly conductor gave her a seat right up in front and asked everybody to make way for madam. It was slack time, with few passengers.
activities.prompt: Why did the conductor play along and call Valli 'madam' instead of treating her like a small child?
options: Because he was bored during the slack time and wanted to amuse himself at her expense
Because she behaved like a confident grown-up, showing her coins and insisting on boarding alone
Because he wanted the other passengers to laugh at her and feel embarrassed
Because he believed she had boarded the wrong bus by mistake

why.Because he was bored during the slack ti: Wrong: the slack time gave him leisure, but his joking was a response to Valli, not boredom.
why.Because he wanted the other passengers t: Wrong: his teasing was good-natured, not meant to shame her before others.
why.Because he believed she had boarded the: Wrong: nothing suggests confusion about her bus; he simply responded to her grown-up manner.

activities.explanation: Correct: her commanding manner, coins and independence made him treat her with playful respect.

activities.context: One spring day, the afternoon bus was leaving the village when a small voice shouted to stop it. A tiny hand was raised commandingly, and the bus slowed to a crawl. The conductor stuck his head out and told her to hurry. Valli showed him some coins and said she could get on by herself. The jolly conductor gave her a seat right up in front and asked everybody to make way for madam. It was slack time, with few passengers.
activities.prompt: If the bus had been crowded instead of slack time, what would most likely have happened?
options: The conductor would still have kept the front seat empty for her
Valli would have had to pay a higher fare for the front seat
There would probably have been no free seat up front for the conductor to offer her
The bus would have waited longer at the village for her to board

why.The conductor would still have kept the: Wrong: with many passengers, the front seats would be taken; he could not reserve one.
why.Valli would have had to pay a higher far: Wrong: nothing in the situation links the fare to the seat or the crowd.
why.The bus would have waited longer at the: Wrong: the conductor actually told her to hurry, so a crowd would not make him wait longer.

activities.explanation: Correct: the easy seating came from the slack time; a full bus would remove that advantage.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Valli had to show the conductor some coins before getting on.
Reason (R): The conductor stuck his head out and told her to hurry.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but being told to hurry does not explain why she showed the coins.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Valli was given a seat right up in front of the bus.
Reason (R): The bus was crowded, so the conductor wanted to keep an eye on her.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because it was slack time with few passengers.

activities.prompt: Explain why the conductor's behaviour towards Valli was friendly and playful rather than strict.
activities.answer: The conductor was a jolly sort who liked joking, so teasing came naturally to him. When Valli showed her coins and declared that she could get on by herself, he did not scold her or brush her aside as a nuisance. Instead, he played along with her grown-up manner, giving her the best seat right up in front and asking everybody to make way for madam. The slack time of day, with few passengers on board, also left him free to be cheerful instead of hurried and stern.
points: His jolly, joking nature is the main reason
Valli's confidence and independence invited playful respect, not scolding
Calling her 'madam' shows he joined in her act of being grown-up
Slack time with few passengers gave him the leisure to be friendly
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Valli climbed into the new bus, painted gleaming white with green stripes, its overhead bars shining like silver and a beautiful clock above the windshield. The conductor blew his whistle twice, and the bus moved with a roar. Valli devoured everything with her eyes, but a canvas blind cut off the lower part of her window. Eager to see the canal, the palm trees and the green fields stretching to distant mountains, she stood on her seat and peered over the blind. An elderly man beside her frowned and told her not to stand and to sit down.
activities.prompt: Why did Valli stand on the seat instead of simply asking someone to raise the canvas blind?
options: She was so absorbed in drinking in the sights that she acted on impulse without thinking
She was too shy to speak to any of the passengers on the bus
She wanted to attract the conductor's attention for her fare
She believed the blind could not be moved at all by anyone

why.She was too shy to speak to any of the p: She had already interacted aboard the bus, so shyness does not fit.
why.She wanted to attract the conductor's at: The fare was not her concern at that moment; the view was.
why.She believed the blind could not be move: Nothing shows she thought the blind was fixed; she simply chose the quickest way to see over it.

activities.explanation: Her eagerness to devour everything with her eyes explains a quick, unthinking action.

activities.context: Valli climbed into the new bus, painted gleaming white with green stripes, its overhead bars shining like silver and a beautiful clock above the windshield. The conductor blew his whistle twice, and the bus moved with a roar. Valli devoured everything with her eyes, but a canvas blind cut off the lower part of her window. Eager to see the canal, the palm trees and the green fields stretching to distant mountains, she stood on her seat and peered over the blind. An elderly man beside her frowned and told her not to stand and to sit down.
activities.prompt: What should Valli do if she wants to enjoy the canal, the palm trees and the green fields without troubling the elderly man?
options: Sit down properly and look through the upper part of the window that the blind does not cover
Pull the canvas blind down completely so nothing distracts her
Change her seat to the one directly behind the driver
Wait until the bus reaches the mountains before looking out

why.Pull the canvas blind down completely so: Blocking the view defeats her own purpose of seeing the scenery.
why.Change her seat to the one directly behi: Changing seats is unnecessary and does not address the blind at all.
why.Wait until the bus reaches the mountains: The scenery she longs for is visible along the whole route, so waiting helps nothing.

activities.explanation: Only the lower part is covered, so sitting and looking above the blind satisfies both her wish and the man's.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Madam Rides the Bus

activities.prompt: Why did standing in her front doorway become Valli's favourite pastime?
options: Because there were no playmates of her own age on her street
Because her mother told her to stand there every day
Because she was waiting for the postman each morning
Because she was too shy to speak to anyone
activities.explanation: There were no playmates of her own age on her street, so watching it gave her many new unusual experiences. Well done if you remembered!

activities.prompt: The bus between Valli's village and the nearest town passed through her street each hour.
activities.explanation: The bus went once to town and once back, passing through her street each hour. That is why it fascinated her so much.

activities.prompt: Valli learned that a one-way ticket to town cost ______ paise.
activities.hint: Think of the small coins Valli saved for her trip.
activities.explanation: The fare was thirty paise one way, and she could return on the same bus by paying another thirty paise.

activities.prompt: Match each thing from Valli's journey with its detail.
activities.explanation: These small details made Valli's plan work, from saving coins to timing her trip. Great matching!

activities.prompt: Why did Valli stand on her seat to look out of the window?
options: Because the seats were too hard to sit on
Because a canvas blind cut off the lower part of her window
Because the conductor asked everyone to stand
Because she wanted the elderly man to see her
activities.explanation: A canvas blind cut off the lower part of the window, so she stood on the seat and peered over it. She devoured everything with her eyes!

activities.prompt: The conductor was a grumpy man who never joked with passengers.
activities.explanation: The conductor was a jolly sort who liked joking. He even asked everybody to make way for madam!

activities.prompt: Put these events from Valli's bus journey in the order they happened.
items: A young cow with its tail high ran in front of the bus
The bus slowed to a crawl
Valli laughed until there were tears in her eyes
A train rushed past the crossing gate with a tremendous roar
The bus reached her village at three forty
activities.explanation: First the cow made the bus slow down, then Valli laughed, then came the roaring train, and finally the bus reached home at three forty.

activities.prompt: Why did the memory of the dead cow haunt Valli on her way home?
options: Because she was afraid the cow would chase the bus
Because she saw the gap between knowing about death and understanding it
Because she wanted to take the cow home with her
Because the conductor scolded her about the cow
activities.explanation: The journey made her meet the mystery of life and death. She saw the gap between knowing death and understanding it. A deep thought for a brave traveller!

activities.prompt: By stifling her desire to ride the merry-go-round, Valli saved a total of ______ paise.
activities.hint: Add the fare for going and the fare for coming back.
activities.explanation: She resolutely stifled her wish to ride the merry-go-round and saved sixty paise, enough for both fares.

activities.prompt: In town, Valli enjoyed a happy ride on the merry-go-round before going home.
activities.explanation: She had stifled her strong desire to ride the merry-go-round so she could save her money. She said she was going back on the same bus.

chapters.summary: In this chapter: buddha's early life; enlightenment and first sermon; kisa gotami's search; kisa gotami's realization.

lessons.title: Buddha's Early Life

activities.prompt: Why did a wealthy prince leave his palace and family forever?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Prince Named Siddhartha
activities.body: Gautama Buddha began life as a prince named Siddhartha Gautama in northern India. At twelve, he was sent away to study the Hindu sacred scriptures. Four years later, he came home and married a princess. They had a son and lived like royalty for ten years. Until he was about twenty-five, he had been shielded from the world's sufferings. Then, while hunting, he saw a sick man, an aged man, a funeral and a monk begging. These sights moved him so much that he left at once to seek enlightenment about the sorrows he had seen.
keyPoints: Siddhartha Gautama was a prince in northern India.
He was shielded from suffering until about twenty-five.
Four sad sights moved him to leave and seek enlightenment.
activities.explanation: A protected prince saw real sorrow for the first time, and it changed his life.

activities.prompt: Ravi never leaves his house. His parents keep him inside. One day he walks out and sees a hungry dog crying. He starts crying too. Why does Ravi cry so much?
steps: Ravi stayed inside, so he never saw sad things before.
Because he never saw sad things, sad things feel new and very big to him.
So the dog's pain hits him hard, like a first shock.
So Ravi cries because he was kept away from pain, not because he is weak.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What was the Buddha's name when he was a prince?
options: Siddhartha Gautama
Gautama Siddhu
Siddhartha Kumar
activities.explanation: The lesson says he began life as a prince named Siddhartha Gautama. Well done!

activities.prompt: While out ______ one day, the Prince saw a sick man, an aged man, a funeral and a monk.
activities.hint: Think of the outdoor trip the Prince went on.
activities.explanation: It was while hunting that he came across the four sights. Lovely work!

activities.prompt: Siddhartha was sent away for schooling in the Hindu sacred scriptures at the age of twelve.
activities.explanation: Yes, at twelve he went away to study the sacred scriptures. Great memory!

activities.prompt: Why did the Prince leave his home?
options: To seek enlightenment about the sorrows he had seen
To become a soldier and fight for his kingdom
To travel to a faraway land for trade
activities.explanation: The sights of sorrow moved him to seek enlightenment. That is why he went out at once.

activities.prompt: Put the four sights in the order in which the Prince saw them.
items: a sick man
an aged man
a funeral procession
a monk begging for alms
activities.explanation: He saw the sick man, the aged man, the funeral, and finally the monk begging. Perfect order!

activities.prompt: Siddhartha was sent away at twelve and returned four years later to marry. About how old was he when he married?
options: Sixteen
Fourteen
Eighteen
activities.explanation: Twelve plus four years makes sixteen. You worked that out brilliantly!

activities.prompt: Meena stayed in her room all week. She saw no sad news. Then she saw a hurt bird outside. She could not stop thinking about it. Why did the bird upset her so much?
options: She was shielded from sad things for a long time.
She wanted the bird to fly into her room.
She was too tired from staying in her room.
She thought the bird came to visit her.

why.She wanted the bird to fly into her room: Wrong: she thinks the bird is a gift, which misses the feeling of shock.
why.She was too tired from staying in her ro: Wrong: she blames tiredness, but the real cause is never seeing pain before.
Wrong: she makes up a happy reason and misses the shock of first seeing pain.

activities.explanation: Right: being kept away from pain makes pain feel new and very strong.

activities.prompt: Siddhartha saw a sick man, an old man, and a funeral. These sights made him sad. Then he saw a monk begging for alms. This last sight gave him hope. Why did the monk give him hope?
options: The monk showed a way to face all the sorrows.
The monk looked rich and could give him money.
The monk told him to go back home at once.
The monk was younger and stronger than him.

why.The monk looked rich and could give him: Wrong: he thinks hope comes from money, but the monk was begging for alms.
why.The monk told him to go back home at onc: Wrong: he thinks the monk sent him home, but the monk made him leave.
why.The monk was younger and stronger than h: Wrong: he focuses on looks, not on the monk's calm way of life.

activities.explanation: Right: the monk showed a path, so Siddhartha left to seek enlightenment.

activities.prompt: A mother covers her son's eyes during a sad movie scene. She shields him from the sad part. What does 'shields' mean here?
options: She keeps the sad part away from him.
She makes the sad part last longer.
She shows him the sad part twice.
She records the sad part for later.

Wrong: she thinks shielding makes pain bigger, which is the opposite.
Wrong: she thinks shielding means showing more, not hiding.
Wrong: she thinks it is about saving something, not protecting a person.

activities.explanation: Right: to shield is to protect someone from seeing pain.

activities.prompt: Siddhartha saw the monk begging for alms. He went out into the world at once. He did not wait or pack anything. What does this show about his feelings?
options: The sight was so strong he could not stay.
He was in a hurry to meet his old friends.
He forgot to take his things from the palace.
He wanted to finish his hunt very quickly.

why.He was in a hurry to meet his old friend: Wrong: he thinks friends pulled him out, but the monk's sight did.
why.He forgot to take his things from the pa: Wrong: he thinks it was forgetfulness, not a strong inner pull.
why.He wanted to finish his hunt very quickl: Wrong: he mixes up the hunt with the moment of leaving.

activities.explanation: Right: he was so moved that he left at once to seek enlightenment.

activities.prompt: Siddhartha had a son and lived ten years as royalty. He had comfort and a family. Still, he left it all. What does this show?
options: The sorrows he saw mattered more than comfort.
He did not love his son or his wife.
He was angry with the royal family.
He wanted to become a hunter again.

Wrong: leaving does not mean no love; it means a bigger pull inside.
Wrong: he thinks anger caused the leaving, but sorrow did.
Wrong: he mixes up the hunting trip with his search for enlightenment.

activities.explanation: Right: the sorrows moved him so much that even comfort could not keep him.

lessons.title: Enlightenment and First Sermon

activities.prompt: What would make someone sit under a tree until wisdom came?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Wise Man Under the Tree
activities.body: A seeker wandered for seven years, looking for answers. At last he sat down under a peepal tree. He made a vow: he would not rise until enlightenment came. After seven days, it came! He named the tree the Bodhi Tree, the Tree of Wisdom. He became known as the Buddha, the Awakened One. Then he travelled to Benares and preached his first sermon.
keyPoints: He wandered for seven years before he sat under the peepal tree.
He vowed to stay until enlightenment came, and it came after seven days.
He renamed the tree the Bodhi Tree, or Tree of Wisdom.
He became known as the Buddha, the Awakened or the Enlightened.
His first sermon was preached at Benares.
activities.explanation: Wisdom came to him because he did not give up, and then he shared it with others.

activities.prompt: Ravi's friend says, 'I will not eat until I finish my hard drawing.' He sits for many days. Why does he do this?
steps: Ravi's friend made a strong promise to himself, so he will not stop early.
He keeps sitting because finishing the drawing matters more to him than food.
A person who makes such a vow shows he wants something very deeply.
So the friend is not being silly; he is showing strong will until his goal comes.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Under which tree did the seeker sit down?
options: A peepal tree
A mango tree
A banyan tree
A neem tree
activities.explanation: The lesson says he sat down under a peepal tree. Later he gave it a new name.

activities.prompt: He was enlightened after ______ days of sitting under the tree.
activities.hint: It is the same word as the number of years he wandered.
activities.explanation: He waited with a strong vow, and after seven days enlightenment came.

activities.prompt: Why did people begin to call him the Buddha?
options: Because he was enlightened
Because he owned the tree
Because he lived in Benares
Because he wrote a book
activities.explanation: Buddha means the Awakened or the Enlightened. He earned the name after his great wisdom came.

activities.prompt: Match each thing with what the lesson says about it.
activities.explanation: Each pair comes straight from the lesson. Well done if you matched them all!

activities.prompt: Put these events from the lesson in the right order.
items: He sat down under a peepal tree
He vowed to stay until enlightenment came
He was enlightened after seven days
He renamed the tree the Bodhi Tree
He preached his first sermon at Benares
activities.explanation: First he sat and made his vow. Then wisdom came, the tree got its new name, and at last he taught others.

activities.prompt: Why was Benares a special place for the first sermon?
options: It was the most holy dipping place on the Ganges
It was the biggest market in the land
It was where he first saw the tree
It was the nearest town to his home
activities.explanation: Benares was the most holy of the dipping places on the River Ganges. A fitting place for a first sermon!

activities.prompt: A girl sits under a tree and says, 'I will not get up until I understand this maths problem.' She sits there for many hours. What does her promise show about her?
options: She is scared of the tree
She is very determined to reach her goal
She is too lazy to walk home
She loves sitting more than learning

why.She is scared of the tree: This mixes the place with her reason; the tree is not what she fears.
why.She is too lazy to walk home: This thinks staying means laziness, but she is working hard.
why.She loves sitting more than learning: This mixes loving the seat with wanting the answer.

activities.explanation: Right: a vow to stay until the goal comes shows strong determination.

activities.prompt: A man sits under one tree for seven days. On the last day, he suddenly understands something deep. After that, he gives that tree a new name. Why does he give it a new name?
options: He wants to forget the old name of the tree
He wants the tree to grow taller and stronger
He wants to mark the special change that happened there
He wants other people to stay away from the tree

why.He wants to forget the old name of the t: This thinks the name change is about forgetting, not about remembering.
why.He wants the tree to grow taller and str: This mixes naming a tree with changing how a tree grows.
why.He wants other people to stay away from: This adds a wish to keep people away, which is not his reason.

activities.explanation: Right: the new name marks the special wisdom that came to him there.

activities.prompt: A teacher learns a big secret after years of hard work. The very next day, she calls her students and starts explaining it to them. What does this show about her?
options: She wants to keep the secret only for herself
She wants to share her new understanding with others
She wants the students to feel jealous of her
She wants to test if the students are listening

why.She wants to keep the secret only for he: This is the opposite of her action; keeping it would mean telling no one.
why.She wants the students to feel jealous o: This adds a jealous feeling that her action does not show.
why.She wants to test if the students are li: This mixes teaching with testing; she is giving, not checking.

activities.explanation: Right: teaching others right away shows she wants to share what she learned.

activities.prompt: People start calling a wise man 'the Awakened One'. Before this, he was just a searcher like others. When do people most likely start using this new name for him?
options: Before he starts his long search for answers
While he is still walking from village to village
After his understanding finally comes to him
Only when he sits down under the tree

why.Before he starts his long search for ans: This is too early; before the search he has not found anything yet.
why.While he is still walking from village t: This is still too early; during the search he is looking, not finding.
why.Only when he sits down under the tree: Sitting down is the start of waiting, not the moment of waking.

activities.explanation: Right: 'Awakened' fits only after his understanding finally comes.

activities.prompt: A speaker wants many holy-minded people to hear his first important talk. He picks the holiest riverside bathing place in the land. What does his choice of place show?
options: He wants to swim and enjoy the river water
He wants to hide his talk from most people
He wants to speak where holy people already gather
He wants to show that rivers are not important

why.He wants to swim and enjoy the river wat: This mixes the holy place with fun; his aim is the talk, not swimming.
why.He wants to hide his talk from most peop: A famous holy place would bring people, not hide him from them.
why.He wants to show that rivers are not imp: He chose a holy river spot, so he does not think rivers are unimportant.

activities.explanation: Right: the holiest spot is where holy-minded people are already found.
