lessons.title: Kisa Gotami's Search

activities.prompt: Can a single mustard seed bring a broken heart back to life?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Kisa Gotami's Search
activities.body: Kisa Gotami's only son died. In her grief, she carried him to her neighbours and asked for medicine. A man sent her to the Buddha. The Buddha asked for a handful of mustard-seed. But it had to come from a house where no one had ever lost a child, husband, parent or friend. She found no such house. Slowly, she saw that death comes to every family.
keyPoints: Kisa Gotami's only son died, and she looked for medicine to cure him.
The Buddha asked her to bring mustard-seed from a house where no one had died.
No house was free from loss, so she understood that death comes to all.
activities.explanation: Her search for medicine became a search that taught her about loss.

activities.prompt: Kisa Gotami knocks on many doors for mustard-seed. Every family says no. Why does she come back with empty hands but a changed heart?
steps: She needs seed from a house where death never came, because the Buddha set that rule.
Each family has lost someone, so each house fails her test, because death visits every home.
Her empty hands show the rule cannot be met, because no such house exists anywhere.
So the seed was never the real medicine; seeing shared sorrow everywhere was the cure for her grief.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Sad Thing Happened
activities.prompt: What happened to Kisa Gotami's son?
options: He fell ill and recovered.
He died.
He went away to a far town.
activities.explanation: Her only son died, and this filled her heart with grief.

activities.title: What the People Said
activities.prompt: What did the people say when Kisa Gotami asked for medicine?
options: They said she had lost her senses and the boy was dead.
They said they would fetch a doctor at once.
They gave her the medicine she wanted.
activities.explanation: The people knew the boy was dead, so they said she had lost her senses.

activities.title: The Buddha's Request
activities.prompt: The Buddha asked Kisa Gotami to bring him a handful of ______.
activities.hint: It is a tiny seed used in cooking.
activities.explanation: The Buddha asked for a handful of mustard-seed. It sounded easy to find.

activities.title: Who Said What
activities.prompt: Match each person to what they did in the story.
pairs: Asked for medicine for her son
Told her to go to the Buddha
Asked for a handful of mustard-seed
Said she had lost her senses
activities.explanation: Each person played a part in her long search.

activities.title: House After House
activities.prompt: Kisa Gotami went from house to house looking for the mustard-seed. What did she find?
options: Every house gave her the seed at once.
No house had been spared the loss of a beloved one.
Only one house had never known any loss.
activities.explanation: There was no house where some beloved one had not died. Loss touches every family.

activities.title: Put the Story in Order
activities.prompt: Put these events from the story in the right order.
items: Kisa Gotami's only son died.
She asked her neighbours for medicine.
A man told her to go to the Buddha.
The Buddha asked for mustard-seed from a house where no one had died.
She found no house free from loss.
activities.explanation: First came her loss, then her search, then the Buddha's task, and last her great understanding.

activities.prompt: Kisa Gotami carries her dead son from door to door. She keeps asking for medicine. What does this show about her?
options: She cannot accept that her son has died.
She wants the neighbours to feel sorry for her.
She is angry with the doctors of her town.
She is too tired to stay at home alone.

why.She wants the neighbours to feel sorry f: Wrong: this reads her walk as a wish for pity, not as denial of death.
why.She is angry with the doctors of her tow: Wrong: this blames doctors, but she never blames anyone in the story.
Wrong: this makes it about tiredness, missing her real hope of curing him.

activities.explanation: Right: asking medicine for a dead child shows her mind refuses the truth of death.

activities.prompt: The neighbours tell Kisa Gotami that she has lost her senses. How do the neighbours most likely feel when they say this?
options: Sad for her, because they know the boy is truly gone.
Jealous of her, because her son was loved by all.
Afraid of her, because she may harm their houses.
Bored with her, because she visits them every day.

why.Jealous of her, because her son was love: Wrong: this adds jealousy, which the story never shows in the neighbours.
why.Afraid of her, because she may harm thei: Wrong: this turns their words into fear, but they speak to help her.
why.Bored with her, because she visits them: Wrong: this makes them tired of her, yet they answer her kindly.

activities.explanation: Right: they state the hard truth because they care and see her pain.

activities.prompt: The Buddha asks for a handful of mustard-seed. But he adds one condition about the house it comes from. Why does he add this condition?
options: He wants her to see that every family has lost someone.
He wants to test if she can walk long distances daily.
He wants to check if mustard-seed is rare in the town.
He wants her to make new friends in the neighbourhood.

why.He wants to test if she can walk long di: Wrong: this reads the task as a walking test, missing its real lesson.
why.He wants to check if mustard-seed is rar: Wrong: this thinks he needs the seed itself, but the seed is only a reason to search.
why.He wants her to make new friends in the: Wrong: this turns the search into social visits, not a lesson about loss.

activities.explanation: Right: the impossible condition makes her learn that death touches every home.

activities.prompt: At every house, people tell Kisa Gotami that the living are few but the dead are many. What does this line really mean?
options: Death has come to almost every family at some time.
More people die each year than babies are born.
People should stop living because death wins in the end.
Only a few rich families can escape death with medicine.

why.More people die each year than babies ar: Wrong: this turns the line into a counting fact about births and deaths.
why.People should stop living because death: Wrong: this twists it into giving up on life, which the story never says.
why.Only a few rich families can escape deat: Wrong: this adds money and medicine, ideas not in the line at all.

activities.explanation: Right: it means loss is common, so no house is free from sorrow.

activities.prompt: Kisa Gotami returns to the Buddha with no mustard-seed. She has knocked at every house. What has she really gained on her search?
options: She now knows her sorrow is shared by every family.
She now knows which neighbours hide their mustard-seed.
She now knows the shortest road to reach the Buddha.
She now knows the names of all the sick people in town.

why.She now knows which neighbours hide thei: Wrong: this thinks the search was about finding seed, missing the lesson.
why.She now knows the shortest road to reach: Wrong: this makes it a lesson in roads, not in the truth about death.
why.She now knows the names of all the sick: Wrong: this invents a list of sick people, which she never made.

activities.explanation: Right: every house had a loss, so she sees her grief is not hers alone.

activities.prompt: A girl reads that Kisa Gotami asked each house about a son, daughter, father or mother who had died. The girl says, 'Kisa Gotami wanted to write a list of names.' What mistake is the girl making?
options: She misses that the question was a test for the seed rule.
She misses that Kisa Gotami wanted to learn each family's name.
She misses that Kisa Gotami was too shy to ask for seed.
She misses that the families refused to speak to strangers.

why.She misses that Kisa Gotami wanted to le: Wrong: this repeats the girl's own mistake of seeing a name list.
why.She misses that Kisa Gotami was too shy: Wrong: this adds shyness, but Kisa Gotami asked boldly at every door.
why.She misses that the families refused to: Wrong: this blames the families, though they answered her with pity.

activities.explanation: Right: the question checked if the house could give the mustard-seed.

lessons.title: Kisa Gotami's Realization

activities.prompt: Can watching city lights change how we feel about losing someone?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What Kisa Gotami Understood
activities.body: Kisa Gotami sat by the roadside, tired and without hope. She watched the lights of the city flicker up and go out. Soon darkness covered everything. Then she saw the truth: human lives flicker up and go out too. Death comes to all. She felt sorry for her selfish grief and found a path of hope.
keyPoints: Kisa Gotami was weary and hopeless at the wayside.
The city lights flickered up and were extinguished again.
She saw that human lives flicker up and are extinguished too.
Death is common to all, and selfishness must be given up.
activities.explanation: Watching the lights helped Kisa Gotami understand the truth about life and death.

activities.prompt: Kisa Gotami sat by the road at night. She watched the city lights come on and then go out. Why did this make her feel less selfish about her grief?
steps: She was weary and hopeless, so she stopped and watched the lights of the city.
Each light flickered up and was extinguished again, until darkness reigned everywhere.
She saw that the lights were like the lives of men, which flicker up and are extinguished again.
So she understood that death is common to all, and she saw how selfish she was in her grief.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Where She Sat
activities.prompt: Where did Kisa Gotami sit down when she felt weary and hopeless?
options: In a market full of people
At the wayside watching the city lights
Under a tree in a dark forest
On the roof of her house
activities.explanation: She sat at the wayside and watched the lights of the city.

activities.title: Her Own Thought
activities.prompt: Kisa Gotami thought, "How ______ am I in my grief!"
activities.hint: She saw that her sorrow was only about herself.
activities.explanation: She felt sorry that her grief had made her think only of herself.

activities.title: What Did the Lights Remind Her Of?
activities.prompt: The city lights flickered up and went out. What did this make Kisa Gotami think about?
options: The stars that shine at night
Lamps that must be filled with oil
Human lives that flicker up and are extinguished
Birds that fly home in the evening
activities.explanation: She saw that human lives are like the lights: they flicker up and are extinguished again.

activities.title: Match the Ideas
activities.prompt: Match each idea from Kisa Gotami's words with its meaning.
pairs: Give up thinking only of yourself
The way a light or a life shines and ends
activities.explanation: These are the special words Kisa Gotami used when she spoke about life and death.

activities.title: The Path of Hope
activities.prompt: Kisa Gotami said there is a path that leads to immortality for those who surrender all ______.
activities.hint: It is the same fault she saw in her own grief.
activities.explanation: The path leads to immortality only for the one who has surrendered all selfishness.

activities.title: Her Journey of Understanding
activities.prompt: Put the steps of Kisa Gotami's realization in the order they happened.
items: She sat at the wayside, weary and hopeless.
She watched the lights of the city flicker up and go out.
Darkness of the night reigned everywhere.
She saw that human lives flicker up and are extinguished too.
She realized death is common to all and gave up her selfish grief.
activities.explanation: First she sat and watched, then the lights went out, and at last she understood the truth about death.

activities.prompt: The city lights flickered up one by one. Then they were extinguished again. At last darkness reigned everywhere. What do the lights make Kisa Gotami think about?
options: Lives flicker up and are extinguished again.
The city should buy better lamps.
The night is dark and frightening.
Morning always comes after the night.

This mistake reads the lights as a real problem about lamps, not a picture.
This mistake focuses on fear of the dark, not on what the lights mean.
This mistake brings in hope of morning, which the story does not say.

activities.explanation: Right: she compares each short-lived light with a short human life.

activities.prompt: Kisa Gotami thought about her own grief. Then she said, 'How selfish am I in my grief!' What did she see about herself?
options: She saw she loved her son too much.
She saw she did not grieve at all.
She saw she thought only of her own pain.
She saw she was angry with her neighbours.

This mistake confuses deep love with thinking only of oneself.
This mistake thinks 'selfish' means she felt no grief, which is not true.
why.She saw she was angry with her neighbour: This mistake mixes grief with anger at other people.

activities.explanation: Right: she saw her grief made her think only of herself, not of others.

activities.prompt: Kisa Gotami spoke of a valley of desolation. In this valley, people lose the ones they love. What does 'desolation' mean here?
options: Great sadness and emptiness.
A dry sandy desert place.
A place full of tall houses.
A happy green field in spring.

This mistake guesses from the word 'valley' instead of the feeling in it.
This mistake thinks of a real place with buildings, not a picture of sorrow.
This mistake picks the opposite feeling, because the valley is sad, not happy.

activities.explanation: Right: a valley of desolation is a picture of deep sorrow and loss.

lessons.title: Buddha's Sermon

activities.prompt: Why did the Buddha say grieving can't bring peace?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What the Buddha Taught
activities.body: In this lesson, the Buddha speaks to people who are sad about death. He says that the life of mortals is troubled, brief, and combined with pain. Everyone, young or old, wise or foolish, must face death one day. The world is afflicted with death and decay. But the Buddha also shows a way forward. The wise do not grieve, because they know the terms of the world. If we let go of crying and complaining, we can find peace of mind.
keyPoints: Life is troubled, brief, and combined with pain.
All are subject to death, both young and old.
The wise do not grieve, knowing the terms of the world.
activities.explanation: The Buddha explains death calmly and shows how to find peace.

activities.prompt: Riya's grandfather dies. She cries all night and stops eating. Her mother says crying is making her body weak too. Why does the Buddha say her crying cannot bring her grandfather back or give her peace?
steps: Death comes to everyone, so no one can stop it, not even family.
Crying cannot change this rule of the world, so it cannot bring him back.
While she cries, her own body suffers more pain and gets weaker.
So peace comes only when she removes grief from her heart, like pulling out an arrow.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: The Arrow of Grief
activities.body: The Buddha asks: can weeping bring peace of mind? No. Not from weeping nor grieving will anyone obtain peace of mind. In fact, pain will be greater and the body will suffer. So he gives advice. He who seeks peace should draw out the arrow of lamentation, complaint, and grief. When the arrow is drawn out and a person becomes composed, peace of mind follows. One who overcomes all sorrow becomes free from sorrow and is blessed.
keyPoints: Weeping and grieving do not bring peace of mind.
Draw out the arrow of lamentation, complaint, and grief.
One who overcomes all sorrow becomes free from sorrow and blessed.
activities.explanation: Grief is like an arrow; removing it brings peace.

activities.title: Life of Mortals
activities.prompt: According to the Buddha, what is the life of mortals like?
options: Long, easy and full of joy
Troubled, brief and combined with pain
Quiet, slow and free of worry
Rich, bright and full of gifts
activities.explanation: The Buddha said life is troubled, brief, and combined with pain. Well done for remembering!

activities.title: Earthen Vessels
activities.prompt: As earthen vessels made by a ______ end in being broken, so is the life of mortals.
activities.hint: Think of the person who shapes clay pots with his hands.
activities.explanation: Pots made by a potter break in the end, and the Buddha says mortal life is the same.

activities.title: Ripe Fruits
activities.prompt: The Buddha says that as ripe fruits are in danger of falling, so mortals are always in danger of death.
activities.explanation: Yes! Ripe fruits may fall at any moment, just as death may come to anyone.

activities.title: Who Must Face Death?
activities.prompt: Who falls into the power of death, according to the Buddha?
options: Only fools and the young
Only the old and unwise
Both young and adult, both fools and wise
Only those who live far away
activities.explanation: The Buddha says all fall into the power of death. No one is left out.

activities.title: Pictures from the Sermon
activities.prompt: Match each picture from the sermon with what it teaches.
pairs: Lament as mortals are carried off
activities.explanation: Each picture helps us understand death and how the wise respond to it.

activities.title: The Path to Peace
activities.prompt: Put these steps from the Buddha's teaching in the correct order.
items: Draw out the arrow of lamentation, complaint, and grief
Become composed
Obtain peace of mind
Overcome all sorrow
Become free from sorrow and be blessed
activities.explanation: First draw out the arrow, then become composed, gain peace, overcome sorrow, and finally be blessed.

activities.prompt: A mango is fully ripe on the tree. A storm is coming tonight. What will most likely happen to the mango?
options: It will hang on the tree for many more months.
It will fall from the tree very soon.
It will become green and hard again.
It will turn into a new fruit.

why.It will hang on the tree for many more m: Wrong: a child forgets that ripe things do not stay long.
Wrong: a child thinks things can go backwards, but ripeness cannot undo itself.
Wrong: a child confuses fruits with seeds and thinks fruits make new fruits directly.

activities.explanation: Right: ripe fruits are in danger of falling, like humans are in danger of death.

activities.prompt: A potter makes twenty clay pots for a fair. On the way, the cart shakes hard. What will happen to the pots?
options: They will all reach the fair safely.
They will turn into metal pots.
Some or all will break on the way.
They will become stronger from the shaking.

Wrong: a child hopes for the best and forgets how weak clay is.
Wrong: a child mixes up materials, thinking things change into stronger things.
why.They will become stronger from the shaki: Wrong: a child thinks shaking makes things strong, but clay pots are fragile.

activities.explanation: Right: earthen vessels end in being broken, just like human life ends in death.

activities.prompt: A school cricket team has a young boy of twelve and a wise old coach of sixty. A match is fixed for next year. What does the lesson say about both of them?
options: Only the old coach can be harmed by death.
Both the boy and the coach can die.
The wise coach is safe because he is clever.
The young boy is safe because he is strong.

why.Only the old coach can be harmed by deat: Wrong: a child thinks death only touches old people.
why.The wise coach is safe because he is cle: Wrong: a child thinks wisdom can protect a person from death.
why.The young boy is safe because he is stro: Wrong: a child thinks being young and strong keeps death away.

activities.explanation: Right: both young and adult, fools and wise, all fall into the power of death.

activities.prompt: Meena's pet dog dies. Her uncle sits beside her all night and cries louder than Meena. The dog does not come back. What is the uncle's crying doing to the uncle?
options: It is bringing the dog back slowly.
It is giving him peace of mind.
It is making his own body suffer more.
It is saving the dog from death.

Wrong: a child believes crying hard enough can undo death.
Wrong: a child mixes up crying with real peace of mind.
Wrong: a child thinks grief has power to change what has already happened.

activities.explanation: Right: weeping and grieving do not bring peace; pain grows and the body suffers.

activities.prompt: Two neighbours lose their old fathers in the same week. One cries for months and falls sick. The other feels sad but stays calm and healthy. What does the calm neighbour know?
options: He knows crying longer will bring his father back.
He knows the terms of the world, so he does not grieve.
He knows his father was not a good person.
He knows he will never lose anyone he loves.

why.He knows crying longer will bring his fa: Wrong: a child still believes grief can undo death.
why.He knows his father was not a good perso: Wrong: a child wrongly links calmness with loving the dead person less.
why.He knows he will never lose anyone he lo: Wrong: a child thinks calm people believe death will never touch their family.

activities.explanation: Right: the wise do not grieve because they know the terms of the world.

lessons.title: Grief and Love

activities.prompt: Why does losing someone we love hurt so much?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: What is grief?
activities.body: Grief is a big, natural feeling that comes with any loss or big change. Martha lost her husband of twenty-six years to cancer. Anya cries in her room and does not feel like eating. Sadness is the most common feeling in grief, but people may also feel anger or guilt. All these feelings are normal.
keyPoints: Grief is a natural feeling that comes with loss or big change.
Sadness is the most common feeling of grief, and it is not always shown by crying.
Anger and guilt can also come with grief.
activities.explanation: Grief touches everyone after a loss, and every feeling it brings is natural.

activities.prompt: Ravi's grandfather died last week. Ravi has not cried at all. But he feels heavy inside and keeps saying, 'I should have called him more often.' His friend says, 'You are not grieving, because you never cried.' Is Ravi grieving or not?
steps: Grief is a natural feeling after any loss or big change, so losing a grandfather can surely cause it.
Sadness is the most common feeling in grief, but it does not have to come out as crying, so Ravi's dry eyes do not prove anything.
Ravi keeps blaming himself for not calling enough, and this kind of self-blame is guilt, a known part of grief.
So Ravi is grieving; his grief is just showing as heavy sadness and guilt, not as tears.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: A talk about yellow hair
activities.body: The poem in this lesson is a conversation between a young man and a young woman. He says a young man thrown into despair will not love her for herself alone. She says she can dye her hair brown, black, or carrot. Then young men may love her for herself alone. But an old religious man said only God could love her for herself alone.
keyPoints: The poem is a conversation between a young man and a young woman.
The young woman says she can dye her hair brown, black, or carrot.
An old religious man said only God could love her for herself alone.
activities.explanation: The poem asks a big question: can anyone love us for ourselves alone?

activities.prompt: Your classmate moves to a new city and feels very low. What is this feeling called?
options: Joy
Grief
Pride
Courage
activities.explanation: Grief is natural to all types of loss or significant change, and moving away is a big change.

activities.prompt: Martha lost her husband of ______ years to cancer.
activities.hint: Look at how long Martha and her husband were married.
activities.explanation: Martha was married for twenty-six years before she lost her husband to cancer.

activities.prompt: Anya does not feel like eating and spends days in her room crying. Which feeling from the lesson does this show most clearly?
options: Sadness
Anger
Fear
Happiness
activities.explanation: Sadness is the most common feeling of grief, and crying shows it here.

activities.prompt: Match each feeling of grief with what the lesson says about it.
pairs: The most common feeling of grief
One of the most confusing feelings for a survivor
May make people feel they were not kind enough
activities.explanation: Grief brings many feelings. Each one is natural, even the confusing ones like anger.

activities.prompt: Put the young woman's plan in order, from first step to last.
items: She says she can get a hair-dye.
She can set such colour there.
She can make her hair brown, black, or carrot.
Young men in despair may then love her for herself alone.
activities.explanation: First she gets the dye, then sets the colour, then changes her hair, and only then may young men love her for herself alone.

activities.prompt: According to the old religious man, who alone could love the young woman for herself alone?
options: A young man in despair
Her family
Only God
The young man in the poem
activities.explanation: The old religious man said he had found a text proving that only God could love her for herself alone.

activities.prompt: Meera's father died last month. She smiles and cooks food for the family. She never cries. What is Meera most likely feeling inside?
options: She has already forgotten her father
She is sad but does not cry
She is angry at her father
She feels nothing at all now

why.She has already forgotten her father: Wrong: this thinks no tears means no love or memory.
why.She is angry at her father: Wrong: this confuses sadness with anger, another feeling of grief.
why.She feels nothing at all now: Wrong: this thinks grief always looks the same in everyone.

activities.explanation: Right: sadness is the most common feeling of grief, and it need not show as crying.

activities.prompt: Sona's mother died last week. Her friend gently says, 'Please eat something.' Sona shouts, 'Leave me alone!' Why does Sona shout at her friend?
options: She hates her friend now
Anger is a confusing part of grief
The food smelled bad to her
She wants to find new friends

why.She hates her friend now: Wrong: this thinks one angry word ends a real friendship.
why.The food smelled bad to her: Wrong: this looks at the food, not at Sona's pain.
why.She wants to find new friends: Wrong: this misses that her anger comes from grief, not friendship.

activities.explanation: Right: anger is one of the most confusing feelings for a survivor of loss.

activities.prompt: Dev's dog died, and he feels deep sadness. Ria moved to a new city, and she feels deep sadness too. What does this show?
options: Only death can cause grief
Grief comes from any loss or big change
Ria is too weak to be happy
Dev and Ria are just very tired

why.Only death can cause grief: Wrong: this thinks grief has only one cause, death.
why.Ria is too weak to be happy: Wrong: this blames Ria instead of seeing a normal feeling.
why.Dev and Ria are just very tired: Wrong: this calls a deep emotion simple tiredness.

activities.explanation: Right: grief is natural to all types of loss or significant change.

activities.prompt: In the poem, the young woman says she can dye her hair. She says brown, black, or carrot. Why does she say this?
options: She wants to look like her friends
She wants love for herself, not her hair
She thinks yellow hair is unlucky
She works in a big hair shop

why.She wants to look like her friends: Wrong: this misses her real wish about being loved.
why.She thinks yellow hair is unlucky: Wrong: this adds a superstition the poem never says.
why.She works in a big hair shop: Wrong: this turns her words into a job, not a wish.

activities.explanation: Right: she says young men may then love her for herself alone, not her yellow hair.

activities.prompt: In the poem, some men love the girl's yellow hair. The young man says they will not love her for herself. What is he really worried about?
options: Her hair will fall out soon
Men may love her hair, not her
She will never find any friend
Hair dye is bad for hair

why.Her hair will fall out soon: Wrong: this worries about hair health, not real love.
why.She will never find any friend: Wrong: this invents a fear about friends that he never shows.
why.Hair dye is bad for hair: Wrong: this turns his warning into advice about dye.

activities.explanation: Right: he says a man in despair will not love her for herself alone.

activities.prompt: An old religious man found a holy text. It says only God could love her for herself alone. What does this imply?
options: The young woman is a bad person
The young man must dye his hair too
Perfect human love may be very hard
Old men never read holy books

why.The young woman is a bad person: Wrong: this wrongly turns the text into an insult.
why.The young man must dye his hair too: Wrong: this mixes up the man's words with the woman's dye.
why.Old men never read holy books: Wrong: this mocks the old man instead of reading his point.

activities.explanation: Right: if only God can love her for herself alone, such love is very hard for people.

lessons.title: Test practice
lessons.sceneAlt: A statue of young Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha as a child, in the Lumbini Development Zone in Nepal.
lessons.sceneCaption: Statue of young Siddhartha Gautama at Lumbini, Nepal, the traditionally recognized birthplace of the Buddha.

activities.context: Siddhartha Gautama began life as a prince in northern India. At twelve, he was sent away for schooling in the Hindu sacred scriptures, and four years later he returned home to marry a princess. They had a son and lived for ten years as royalty. All this while, the Prince had been shielded from the world's sufferings. One day, while out hunting, he came across a sick man, an aged man, a funeral procession, and finally a monk begging for alms.
activities.prompt: The monk begging for alms was the last sight Siddhartha saw that day. What did he most likely do immediately afterwards?
options: He ordered his servants to keep him even more protected from such sights in future
He went out into the world at once to seek enlightenment about the sorrows he had witnessed
He returned to the palace and discussed the sights with his wife and son
He waited several years before deciding what to do about what he had seen

why.He ordered his servants to keep him even: Wrong: he wanted to understand suffering, not hide from it further
why.He returned to the palace and discussed: Wrong: there is no suggestion he consulted his family; the sights moved him to act himself
why.He waited several years before deciding: Wrong: he was moved to go out into the world at once, not after a delay

activities.explanation: Correct: the sights moved him so much that he left immediately to seek enlightenment

activities.context: Siddhartha Gautama began life as a prince in northern India. At twelve, he was sent away for schooling in the Hindu sacred scriptures, and four years later he returned home to marry a princess. They had a son and lived for ten years as royalty. All this while, the Prince had been shielded from the world's sufferings. One day, while out hunting, he came across a sick man, an aged man, a funeral procession, and finally a monk begging for alms.
activities.prompt: Why did these ordinary sights affect Siddhartha so deeply?
options: Because his schooling in the sacred scriptures had taught him nothing about them
Because his wife and son had never allowed him to leave the palace before
Because he had been shielded from the world's sufferings until that day
Because as a hunter he felt guilty about the animals he had killed

why.Because his schooling in the sacred scri: Wrong: the passage blames his sheltered life, not the quality of his schooling
why.Because his wife and son had never allow: Wrong: his family is not said to have kept him confined; he had lived freely as royalty
why.Because as a hunter he felt guilty about: Wrong: his feelings arose from the four sights, not from guilt about hunting

activities.explanation: Correct: having never known sickness, age, death or renunciation, he saw them for the first time

activities.context: Siddhartha Gautama began life as a prince in northern India. At twelve, he was sent away for schooling in the Hindu sacred scriptures, and four years later he returned home to marry a princess. They had a son and lived for ten years as royalty. All this while, the Prince had been shielded from the world's sufferings. One day, while out hunting, he came across a sick man, an aged man, a funeral procession, and finally a monk begging for alms.
activities.prompt: Suppose Siddhartha had never gone hunting that day. Which outcome fits the passage best?
options: He would have continued living as royalty, still unaware of the world's sufferings
He would have met the sick man and the monk at the palace gates instead
He would have left home years earlier because of his scripture studies
He would have sent his son out to seek enlightenment in his place

why.He would have met the sick man and the m: Wrong: the sights were encountered while hunting, not at the palace
why.He would have left home years earlier be: Wrong: his schooling ended with his return home and marriage, not with leaving
why.He would have sent his son out to seek e: Wrong: nothing in the facts suggests his son would take up such a search

activities.explanation: Correct: it was the hunting trip that exposed him to suffering; without it, his sheltered royal life would have continued

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Siddhartha lived as royalty for ten years after his marriage.
Reason (R): He wanted those ten years to forget the sorrows he had witnessed on his hunting trip.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because he saw the sorrows only after those ten years of royal life.

activities.prompt: Explain why the four sights moved Siddhartha so deeply, even though sickness, old age and death were common in the world around him.
activities.answer: Siddhartha had been shielded from the world's sufferings for about twenty-five years. As a prince, he was sent at twelve to study the Hindu sacred scriptures, returned home to marry a princess, had a son, and lived for ten years as royalty. Such a protected life meant he had never truly faced sickness, old age, death or renunciation. So when he came across a sick man, an aged man, a funeral procession and a monk begging for alms while hunting, each sight revealed a sorrow he had never known. Deeply moved, he went out into the world at once to seek enlightenment about them.
points: Mentions that he had been shielded from the world's sufferings
Refers to his protected royal life (schooling, marriage, son, ten years as royalty)
Links each of the four sights to a sorrow he was seeing for the first time
Concludes that this is why he left at once to seek enlightenment
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Meera was preparing a class talk on the Buddha. She knew he wandered for seven years, then sat down under a peepal tree and vowed to stay there until enlightenment came. After seven days, he was enlightened. He renamed the tree the Bodhi Tree, or Tree of Wisdom, and began to teach and share his new understandings. Later, at Benares, the most holy of the dipping places on the River Ganges, he preached his first sermon, which has been preserved.
activities.prompt: A classmate asks Meera why the tree received a new name. What should she answer?
options: Because it was under that tree that he gained wisdom, so he marked the spot by calling it the Tree of Wisdom
Because it was the oldest tree in the forest and already sacred to villagers
Because the tree was planted at Benares after his first sermon there
Because he rested under it each night during his seven years of wandering

why.Because it was the oldest tree in the fo: No fact says the tree was old or already sacred; this invents a reason.
why.Because the tree was planted at Benares: The tree and Benares are separate events; the sermon was not preached there.
why.Because he rested under it each night du: The vow to stay was made at the tree after wandering, not during it.

activities.explanation: Correct: the renaming followed directly from his enlightenment under it, and Bodhi means wisdom.

activities.context: Meera was preparing a class talk on the Buddha. She knew he wandered for seven years, then sat down under a peepal tree and vowed to stay there until enlightenment came. After seven days, he was enlightened. He renamed the tree the Bodhi Tree, or Tree of Wisdom, and began to teach and share his new understandings. Later, at Benares, the most holy of the dipping places on the River Ganges, he preached his first sermon, which has been preserved.
activities.prompt: Meera wonders what would most likely have happened if enlightenment had not come after seven days. Based on the story, what is the best answer?
options: He would have kept his vow and remained seated under the tree, waiting
He would have travelled to Benares and begun preaching there instead
He would have renamed the tree anyway and started teaching his ideas
He would have declared himself the Awakened One without enlightenment

why.He would have travelled to Benares and b: Benares came only after enlightenment and teaching had begun.
why.He would have renamed the tree anyway an: The renaming and teaching happened only because enlightenment came.
why.He would have declared himself the Awake: The name Awakened or Enlightened was a result of enlightenment, not a claim made before it.

activities.explanation: Correct: he had vowed to stay until enlightenment came, so he would not leave without it.

activities.context: Meera was preparing a class talk on the Buddha. She knew he wandered for seven years, then sat down under a peepal tree and vowed to stay there until enlightenment came. After seven days, he was enlightened. He renamed the tree the Bodhi Tree, or Tree of Wisdom, and began to teach and share his new understandings. Later, at Benares, the most holy of the dipping places on the River Ganges, he preached his first sermon, which has been preserved.
activities.prompt: Meera's teacher says the place of the first sermon was significant. What should Meera explain to the class?
options: Benares was chosen because pilgrims already gathered there to dip in the Ganges, making it the holiest such place
Benares was chosen because it was where he had spent his seven years of wandering
Benares was chosen because the Bodhi Tree stood there and people came to see it
Benares was chosen because it was the only city where sermons could be preserved

why.Benares was chosen because it was where: The wandering happened before he sat under the tree, not at Benares.
why.Benares was chosen because the Bodhi Tre: The Bodhi Tree was where he was enlightened, not where he preached first.
why.Benares was chosen because it was the on: The sermon was preserved, but nothing says preservation depended on the city.

activities.explanation: Correct: its importance lay in being the most holy of the dipping places on the River Ganges.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The Buddha began to teach soon after he was enlightened under the tree.
Reason (R): He wanted to share his new understandings with others.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the desire to share his new understandings directly explains why he began to teach.

activities.prompt: Explain why the peepal tree came to be called the Bodhi Tree.
activities.answer: The tree was an ordinary peepal tree until the man sat down beneath it, vowing to stay there until enlightenment came. After seven days, he was enlightened at that very spot. Because the tree was the place where he gained wisdom, he renamed it the Bodhi Tree, or Tree of Wisdom. The new name marks the tree's special role in his transformation: under its shade he stopped searching and became the Enlightened One, ready to teach others what he had understood.
points: Mentions the vow to stay under the peepal tree until enlightenment came
States that enlightenment came after seven days at that spot
Links the name Bodhi or Tree of Wisdom to the wisdom gained there
Connects the renaming to his becoming the Enlightened One
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Kisa Gotami's only son died, and she could not accept it. Carrying his body, she went to every neighbour asking for medicine to bring him back. The people told her she had lost her senses, for the boy was already dead. Then a man directed her to Sakyamuni, the Buddha. The Buddha agreed to help, but asked for a handful of mustard-seed from a house where no child, husband, parent or friend had ever died. She went from door to door, but in every house someone beloved had died.
activities.prompt: Kisa Gotami keeps knocking on doors, but every family she meets has lost someone. What is the most likely result of her search?
options: She will find a house untouched by death and get the seed.
She will slowly realise that loss is common to every family.
She will stop searching because the neighbours refuse to speak to her.
She will bring back seeds from many houses and mix them.

why.She will find a house untouched by death: Wrong: the story states no such house exists, so this cannot happen.
why.She will stop searching because the neig: Wrong: the neighbours pity her and answer her questions, so they do not refuse to speak.
why.She will bring back seeds from many hous: Wrong: the Buddha asked for seed from one special house, not many, so mixing seeds is not her aim.

activities.explanation: Correct: visiting house after house and hearing of death everywhere leads her to see death is universal.

activities.context: Kisa Gotami's only son died, and she could not accept it. Carrying his body, she went to every neighbour asking for medicine to bring him back. The people told her she had lost her senses, for the boy was already dead. Then a man directed her to Sakyamuni, the Buddha. The Buddha agreed to help, but asked for a handful of mustard-seed from a house where no child, husband, parent or friend had ever died. She went from door to door, but in every house someone beloved had died.
activities.prompt: Suppose a kind neighbour offers her mustard-seed from his kitchen, forgetting that his old father died there last year. What should Kisa Gotami do?
options: Accept it quickly, since the seed itself is what cures her son.
Refuse it, because the house does not meet the Buddha's condition.
Ask the neighbour to visit the Buddha and explain on her behalf.
Take the seed but tell the Buddha she found it easily.

why.Accept it quickly, since the seed itself: Wrong: the seed matters only with its condition; a seed from a house touched by death defeats the purpose.
why.Ask the neighbour to visit the Buddha an: Wrong: sending someone else does not satisfy the condition; the seed must come from the right kind of house.
why.Take the seed but tell the Buddha she fo: Wrong: hiding the truth would break the condition and defeat the purpose of her search.

activities.explanation: Correct: the Buddha's condition was a house where no child, husband, parent or friend had died, and this house fails it.

activities.context: Kisa Gotami's only son died, and she could not accept it. Carrying his body, she went to every neighbour asking for medicine to bring him back. The people told her she had lost her senses, for the boy was already dead. Then a man directed her to Sakyamuni, the Buddha. The Buddha agreed to help, but asked for a handful of mustard-seed from a house where no child, husband, parent or friend had ever died. She went from door to door, but in every house someone beloved had died.
activities.prompt: At many houses people tell her, 'The living are few but the dead are many.' Why do they say this to her?
options: They are counting the people of the town and reporting the numbers.
They are warning her that the Buddha's medicine is dangerous.
They are showing her that nearly every family has known such loss.
They are complaining that their neighbours die too young.

why.They are counting the people of the town: Wrong: they are not giving statistics; they are speaking from their own experience of loss.
why.They are warning her that the Buddha's m: Wrong: nothing suggests danger; they pity her and speak of their own dead.
why.They are complaining that their neighbou: Wrong: they are not complaining about early deaths; they are pointing to loss as a shared human experience.

activities.explanation: Correct: their words mean death has visited almost every household, which is exactly why she finds no qualifying house.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Kisa Gotami returned without a single handful of mustard-seed.
Reason (R): In every house she visited, some beloved person had died at some time.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Since no house was free of loss, she could never obtain the seed that met the Buddha's condition.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The neighbours refused to give Kisa Gotami any medicine for her son.
Reason (R): The neighbours believed that medicine could bring a dead boy back to life.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The neighbours did turn her away, but because they said the boy was dead and she had lost her senses, not because they trusted medicine.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between what Kisa Gotami asked her neighbours for at first and what the Buddha asked her to find?
activities.answer: At first Kisa Gotami asked her neighbours for medicine to cure her son, hoping to bring him back from death. The neighbours said she had lost her senses, since the boy was already dead. The Buddha, however, did not give her medicine at all; he asked her to find mustard-seed from a house where no one had lost a child, husband, parent or friend. The difference is that her request tried to escape death, while the Buddha's request made her face death. Her search for a cure became a search for understanding, and that understanding was the real answer.
points: She wanted medicine to reverse her son's death.
The Buddha asked for a conditional mustard-seed, not a cure.
The impossible condition turned her outward search inward.
One sought to defeat death; the other taught acceptance of it.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: After losing her only child, Meera wandered from door to door until, weary and hopeless, she sat down at the wayside as evening fell. She watched the lights of the city as they flickered up, then went out one by one, until the darkness of the night reigned everywhere. Sitting alone in that darkness, she began to think about what the dying lights might be telling her about people and about her own grief.
activities.prompt: Why does Meera most likely keep watching the lights instead of going home?
options: The flickering and dying lights remind her of how human lives rise and end
She is waiting for a neighbour to come and comfort her
She wants to count exactly how many lights go out
She is afraid to walk home in the dark

why.She is waiting for a neighbour to come a: Wrong: nothing in the situation suggests she expects anyone; her mind is on the lights themselves
why.She wants to count exactly how many ligh: Wrong: counting is not her concern; the pattern of flickering and dying is what holds her
why.She is afraid to walk home in the dark: Wrong: fear of the dark is not shown; she sits calmly and thinks, not trembles

activities.explanation: Correct: the lights going out mirror lives that flicker up and are extinguished, which is what she is beginning to grasp

activities.context: After losing her only child, Meera wandered from door to door until, weary and hopeless, she sat down at the wayside as evening fell. She watched the lights of the city as they flickered up, then went out one by one, until the darkness of the night reigned everywhere. Sitting alone in that darkness, she began to think about what the dying lights might be telling her about people and about her own grief.
activities.prompt: If Meera finally whispers, 'How selfish am I in my grief!', what change has happened inside her?
options: She has stopped thinking only of her own loss and sees that everyone must face death
She has decided that her neighbours were right to refuse her request
She has concluded that grieving itself is a waste of time and must be dropped at once
She has promised never to feel sorrow again for any reason

why.She has decided that her neighbours were: Wrong: her realisation is about death and selfishness, not about judging her neighbours
why.She has concluded that grieving itself i: Wrong: she does not reject grief itself; she sees through the selfishness within it
why.She has promised never to feel sorrow ag: Wrong: sorrow is not banned; only the self-centred way of carrying it is seen through

activities.explanation: Correct: calling her grief selfish means she now sees death as common to all, not her burden alone

boss.title: Chapter challenge: The Sermon at Benares

activities.prompt: Siddhartha lived safely as a prince. Why did he leave his home one day?
options: He wanted to hunt more animals in the forest.
He was sent away for schooling in the scriptures.
Seeing sickness, old age, death and a monk moved him to seek enlightenment.
He wished to marry a princess from another land.
activities.explanation: While hunting, he saw a sick man, an aged man, a funeral and a monk begging. These sights moved him to go out and seek enlightenment about the sorrows he had seen.

activities.prompt: The Buddha asked Kisa Gotami to bring a handful of rice from any house she chose.
activities.explanation: He asked for a handful of mustard-seed, not rice. It had to come from a house where no one had ever lost a child, husband, parent or friend.

activities.prompt: The Buddha preached his first sermon at ______, the most holy of the dipping places on the River Ganges.
activities.hint: It is the name of a holy city.
activities.explanation: Benares was the most holy of the dipping places on the River Ganges, and the Buddha's first sermon was preached there.

activities.prompt: Match each thing from the lesson with what it means.
pairs: holy dipping place on the Ganges
from a house where no one had died
activities.explanation: Each of these carries a special meaning in the lesson. The peepal tree was renamed the Bodhi Tree, or Tree of Wisdom, after enlightenment came.

activities.prompt: In the poem, the old religious man found a text to prove that only one being could love the young woman for herself alone. Who was it?
options: A young man in despair
God
Her neighbours
The man who dyed her hair
activities.explanation: The old religious man said his text proved that only God could love her for herself alone, and not her yellow hair.

activities.prompt: The Buddha says earthen vessels made by a potter end in being broken. What do the broken vessels stand for?
options: The sorrow of Kisa Gotami
The wisdom of the wise
The potter's skill in the market
The life of mortals
activities.explanation: Just as every pot ends in being broken, the life of mortals also ends in death. Both ripe fruits and broken vessels teach the same truth.

activities.prompt: The Buddha taught that weeping and grieving will bring a person peace of mind.
activities.explanation: Not from weeping nor grieving will anyone obtain peace of mind. Instead, pain grows greater and the body suffers.

activities.prompt: The Buddha said that he who seeks peace should draw out the ______ of lamentation, complaint and grief.
activities.hint: It is a sharp thing that wounds, and it must be pulled out.
activities.explanation: He who draws out this arrow and becomes composed will obtain peace of mind. Overcoming sorrow makes a person free from sorrow and blessed.

activities.prompt: Put the events of Kisa Gotami's story in the order they happened.
items: Her only son died, and she carried him to her neighbours asking for medicine.
A man told her to go to Sakyamuni, the Buddha.
The Buddha asked for mustard-seed from a house where no one had died.
She went from house to house, but every family had lost someone they loved.
Watching the city lights go out, she realised death is common to all.
activities.explanation: Her search for medicine led her to the Buddha, and his mustard-seed task showed her that the dead are many. Like the city lights, lives flicker up and are extinguished again.

activities.prompt: Match each feeling with what the lesson says about it.
pairs: a natural emotion to loss or big change
the most common feeling, not always shown by crying
one of the most confusing feelings for a survivor
believing you were not kind or caring enough
activities.explanation: Grief comes in many feelings, and each one is natural. Knowing this can help you be gentle with yourself, just as Kisa Gotami learned to let her grief go.

chapters.summary: In this chapter: before you read: proposal and a russian wedding; the proposal: introduction and characters; lomov comes to propose; natalya and the oxen meadows quarrel begins.

lessons.title: Before You Read: Proposal and A Russian Wedding

activities.prompt: Why would a groom have to pay money just to see his bride?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Words to Know Before You Read
activities.body: The word 'proposal' has more than one meaning. It can be a plan or a suggestion. It can also mean asking someone to marry you. In this lesson you will also meet a Russian wedding. A Russian wedding sounds grand, but the article says it is very simple. You will learn about rings, cars, stairs and a happy groom.
keyPoints: 'Proposal' can mean a plan, a suggestion or a scheme.
'Proposal' can also mean asking someone to marry you.
A Russian wedding is very simple, says the article.
activities.explanation: Knowing these two ideas will help you enjoy both texts.

activities.prompt: Priya reads a card from her friend. It says: 'I have a proposal. Let us plant a garden together.' Priya wonders what 'proposal' means here. Is it about marriage?
steps: The friend is talking about planting a garden, not about love or a ring.
So the word 'proposal' here cannot mean asking someone to marry.
A proposal can also mean a plan or suggestion for doing something.
So here 'proposal' means a plan to plant a garden together.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Your friend says, "Here is my proposal for the class picnic." What does 'proposal' mean here?
options: A suggestion or plan
A marriage request
A wedding car
activities.explanation: Well done! A proposal can be a plan or a scheme for doing something.

activities.prompt: A Russian wedding lasts for ______ days.
activities.hint: Think of the number of days, not hours.
activities.explanation: Right! A Russian wedding lasts two days, and some last even longer.

activities.prompt: Match each wedding word with its meaning from the lesson.
pairs: the man who climbs the stairs
activities.explanation: Great matching! These words will appear again in the lesson.

activities.prompt: The groom must answer a question at each landing. What happens if he guesses wrong?
options: He must pay cash to move ahead
He must climb down and start again
He must sing a song for the bride
activities.explanation: Correct! A wrong guess costs him cash before he can go up.

activities.prompt: Put the groom's journey in the right order.
items: The groom arrives and sees the stairs to his bride.
At each landing, he must answer a question.
If he guesses wrong, he must pay cash.
At last, he reaches his bride.
activities.explanation: Perfect order! Each question is a small test on his way up.

activities.prompt: Some Russian weddings last even longer than two days. How long can they last?
options: As long as a week
As long as a month
As long as a day
activities.explanation: Yes! Some weddings last as long as a whole week.

activities.prompt: Aman kneels in front of Leela. He holds a small ring. He asks her to marry him. What is Aman making?
options: A proposal of marriage
A proposal of a picnic
A proposal of a game
A proposal of a journey

why.A proposal of a picnic: Wrong: he thinks proposal always means a plan, not marriage.
why.A proposal of a game: Wrong: he thinks proposal always means a plan, not marriage.
why.A proposal of a journey: Wrong: he thinks proposal always means a plan, not marriage.

activities.explanation: Right: asking someone to marry you is one meaning of 'proposal'.

activities.prompt: Nina is going to a Russian wedding. She packs clothes for many days. Some weddings last as long as a week. Why does Nina pack so many clothes?
options: The wedding may go on for many days
The wedding may be very cold outside
The wedding may need many new gifts
The wedding may have many long dances

why.The wedding may be very cold outside: Wrong: she thinks packing depends on weather, not wedding length.
why.The wedding may need many new gifts: Wrong: she thinks packing is about gifts, not the long wedding.
why.The wedding may have many long dances: Wrong: she thinks packing is about dancing, not the long wedding.

activities.explanation: Right: a Russian wedding can last two days or even a week.

activities.prompt: A groom climbs stairs to reach his bride. At each landing, a guard asks him a question. A wrong answer costs him cash. Why does the groom carry money with him?
options: He may need to pay to climb ahead
He may need to buy a new ring
He may need to pay for the cars
He may need to tip the bride's family

why.He may need to buy a new ring: Wrong: he mixes up the ring with the stair game payment.
why.He may need to pay for the cars: Wrong: he mixes up the cars with the stair game payment.
why.He may need to tip the bride's family: Wrong: he thinks the money is a gift, not a penalty.

activities.explanation: Right: a wrong answer means he must pay cash to move ahead.

activities.prompt: Misha sees many cars driving together to a wedding. The cars go in one long line. This is a needed part of the ceremony. What is this line of cars?
options: A wedding procession of cars
A wedding race of cars
A wedding parade of prizes
A wedding queue of guests

why.A wedding race of cars: Wrong: he thinks the cars are competing, not celebrating.
why.A wedding parade of prizes: Wrong: he thinks the cars carry prizes, not the wedding party.
why.A wedding queue of guests: Wrong: he thinks the cars are waiting in line, not moving together.

activities.explanation: Right: a procession of several cars is a necessary part of the ceremony.

lessons.sceneCaption: A Russian wedding ceremony, showing how weddings are celebrated in Russia.

lessons.title: The Proposal: Introduction and Characters

activities.prompt: What happens when a marriage proposal turns into a quarrel?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Meet the Play
activities.body: Today you will meet a funny play called 'The Proposal'. It was first named 'A Marriage Proposal'. Anton Chekhov, a Russian story writer and dramatist, wrote it in 1888–89. It is a one-act play and a farce, which means a silly, fast story that makes you laugh. It shows rich families who want ties with other rich families, because marriages made good economic sense to them.
keyPoints: The play was first called 'A Marriage Proposal'.
Anton Chekhov, a Russian writer, wrote it in 1888–89.
It is a one-act play and a farce.
Rich families wanted marriages that made good economic sense.
activities.explanation: Keep these four ideas in mind as you play on.

activities.prompt: Your neighbour visits your house. He talks and talks about your dog and your fields. He never says why he came. Why does he keep forgetting his real reason?
steps: Lomov is a wealthy neighbour who comes to ask for Natalya's hand, so he has one big reason to visit.
All three people are quarrelsome, so small fights start easily between them.
They quarrel over petty issues, so the fights pull their minds away from the real talk.
So the proposal is in danger of being forgotten, because quarrelling keeps pushing it aside.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who wrote 'The Proposal'?
options: Anton Chekhov
William Shakespeare
Ruskin Bond
Charles Dickens
activities.explanation: Chekhov was a Russian short story writer and dramatist. Well done!

activities.prompt: What kind of play is 'The Proposal'?
options: A one-act farce
A long tragedy
A musical drama
A silent film
activities.explanation: It is a one-act play and a farce, so it is short and silly on purpose.

activities.prompt: Lomov comes to seek the hand of Chubukov's daughter, ______.
activities.hint: She is twenty-five years old.
activities.explanation: Lomov visits to ask for Natalya's hand in marriage.

activities.prompt: Match each person to what the lesson says about them.
activities.explanation: Lomov is hearty but suspicious; Chubukov is a landowner; Natalya is his daughter.

activities.prompt: Why is Lomov's proposal in danger of being forgotten?
options: The three keep quarrelling over petty issues
Natalya refuses to meet Lomov
Chubukov loses all his money
Lomov forgets the way to the house
activities.explanation: All three are quarrelsome people. Their petty quarrels push the proposal aside.

activities.prompt: Put these events from the lesson in the right order.
items: Chekhov writes the play in 1888–89
Lomov visits his long-time neighbour Chubukov
Lomov seeks the hand of Natalya
The three quarrel over petty issues
The proposal is in danger of being forgotten
activities.explanation: First the play was written, then Lomov visits, asks for Natalya, quarrels begin, and the proposal nearly slips away.

activities.prompt: A play is called 'A Marriage Proposal'. Later the title becomes 'The Proposal'. The new title is shorter. Why might a writer pick a shorter title?
options: Because the shorter title is easier to say and remember
Because the writer wanted to hide that marriage happens
Because the play is really about buying a big shop
Because the shorter title costs less money to print

why.Because the writer wanted to hide that m: Wrong: this thinks a title must hide the story, but titles usually show it.
why.Because the play is really about buying: Wrong: this mixes the play up with a story about shops, which it is not.
why.Because the shorter title costs less mon: Wrong: this thinks titles are about printing money, not about readers.

activities.explanation: Right: a short title is simple and easy to remember, so it works well.

activities.prompt: A play has only one act. It must finish its whole story very fast. A farce makes us laugh at silly, mixed-up events. Lomov comes to propose but keeps fighting instead. What will the audience most likely feel?
options: Sad, because Lomov will never get married at all
Amused, because the proposal keeps getting lost in silly fights
Scared, because the fights may turn into real danger
Bored, because nothing at all happens in the play

why.Sad, because Lomov will never get marrie: Wrong: this thinks a farce ends sadly, but a farce is meant to be funny.
why.Scared, because the fights may turn into: Wrong: this thinks petty quarrels are truly dangerous, but they are only funny fights.
why.Bored, because nothing at all happens in: Wrong: this thinks one act means nothing happens, but a lot happens very fast.

activities.explanation: Right: a farce makes us laugh, and the proposal getting lost in fights is the silly mix-up.

activities.prompt: Chekhov wrote short stories and plays in Russia. A friend asks him to write a funny play about marriage. Chekhov knows both story-writing and play-writing well. Why is he a good choice for this job?
options: Because he is rich and can pay for the play himself
Because he can tell a story and shape it as a play
Because he has acted in many plays on big stages
Because he is young and will work for very little money

why.Because he is rich and can pay for the p: Wrong: this thinks money makes a writer good, but skill matters more.
why.Because he has acted in many plays on bi: Wrong: this confuses writing plays with acting in them.
why.Because he is young and will work for ve: Wrong: this thinks a low price makes a writer the best choice.

activities.explanation: Right: he is a short story writer and a dramatist, so he has both skills.

activities.prompt: Two rich families want their children to marry. Both families have plenty of money. The parents ask: will this marriage make good economic sense? What do the parents care about most?
options: Whether the two young people truly love each other
Whether the marriage will join wealth with wealth
Whether the children are old enough to marry
Whether the neighbours will like the wedding party

why.Whether the two young people truly love: Wrong: this thinks love comes first, but the parents ask about economic sense.
why.Whether the children are old enough to m: Wrong: this thinks age is the main worry, but the question is about money sense.
why.Whether the neighbours will like the wed: Wrong: this thinks the party and neighbours matter most to the parents.

activities.explanation: Right: wealthy families seek ties with other wealthy families, so joining wealth matters most.

activities.prompt: Lomov is large and hearty, so he looks strong and friendly. But he is also very suspicious, so he doubts people easily. At a party, a neighbour says his dog is better than Lomov's dog. What will Lomov most likely do?
options: Laugh loudly and quickly change the whole topic
Quietly walk away without saying a single word
Start a quarrel over the dog with the neighbour
Kindly agree that the neighbour's dog is better

why.Laugh loudly and quickly change the whol: Wrong: this thinks his hearty side always wins, but suspicion makes him doubt and fight.
why.Quietly walk away without saying a singl: Wrong: this thinks he avoids fights, but quarrelsome people jump into them.
why.Kindly agree that the neighbour's dog is: Wrong: this thinks he gives in easily, but suspicion stops him from agreeing.

activities.explanation: Right: he is suspicious and quarrelsome, so a small dog talk turns into a quarrel.

activities.prompt: Chubukov is a landowner with a daughter named Natalya. Lomov, a long-time wealthy neighbour, comes to his house. Lomov starts talking about land and dogs, and they begin to quarrel. What is in danger of being forgotten?
options: The money Chubukov owes to Lomov
The real reason why Lomov came today
The name of Lomov's big farm nearby
The time when Chubukov must eat dinner

why.The money Chubukov owes to Lomov: Wrong: this invents a debt, but the danger is about the proposal, not money owed.
why.The name of Lomov's big farm nearby: Wrong: this thinks the farm name matters, but the real reason is the proposal.
why.The time when Chubukov must eat dinner: Wrong: this thinks dinner time is the worry, but the proposal is what may be lost.

activities.explanation: Right: Lomov came to seek Natalya's hand, and the quarrelling pushes that aside.

lessons.sceneAlt: A portrait photograph of the Russian writer Anton Pavlovich Chekhov.
lessons.sceneCaption: Anton Pavlovich Chekhov, the Russian writer of the play.

sceneCredit.creator: Unknown author Unknown author

lessons.title: Lomov Comes to Propose

activities.prompt: Why is a nervous visitor in white gloves hiding his real reason for visiting?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: A Visit with a Secret
activities.body: Lomov walks into Chubukov's drawing-room. He looks very grand in a dress-jacket and white gloves. Chubukov greets him warmly, but inside he has a worry. He thinks Lomov may have come to borrow money! Really, Lomov has a sweet request: he wants to marry Natalya Stepanovna, Chubukov's daughter.
keyPoints: The scene is a drawing-room in Chubukov's house.
Lomov wears a dress-jacket and white gloves.
Chubukov secretly fears Lomov wants to borrow money.
Lomov's real wish is to ask for Natalya's hand in marriage.
activities.explanation: A grand visit, a secret worry and a happy surprise — that is how this scene begins.

activities.prompt: Lomov puts on a dress-jacket and white gloves just to visit his neighbour. Why would a person dress up so much for a simple visit?
steps: People usually wear fancy clothes only when a day feels very special to them.
Lomov is going to ask for Natalya's hand in marriage, which is a huge step in his life.
So the fancy clothes show that, for Lomov, this visit is not a small chat but a big event.
His dress-jacket and white gloves are really his nervous way of showing the visit matters.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Where Are We?
activities.prompt: Where does this scene take place?
options: In a drawing-room
In a market square
In a school hall
In a garden shed
activities.explanation: The lesson tells us the scene is set in a drawing-room in Chubukov's house.

activities.title: Dressed for the Day
activities.prompt: What is Lomov wearing when he enters?
options: A dress-jacket and white gloves
An old coat and torn shoes
A nightshirt and a cap
A school uniform and a hat
activities.explanation: Lomov enters wearing a dress-jacket and white gloves. He has dressed with care!

activities.title: Lomov's Request
activities.prompt: Lomov says he has come to trouble Chubukov with a ______.
activities.hint: It is something you politely ask for.
activities.explanation: Lomov says he has come to trouble Chubukov with a request. That request turns out to be a marriage proposal!

activities.title: Who Said What?
activities.prompt: Match each person to what the lesson tells us about them.
pairs: Asks for Natalya's hand in marriage
The daughter whose hand is asked for
The name Chubukov uses for Lomov
activities.explanation: Lomov is also called Ivan Vassilevitch, and Natalya Stepanovna is the daughter he hopes to marry.

activities.title: A Joyful Answer
activities.prompt: When Lomov asks for Natalya's hand, how does Chubukov react?
options: He joyfully asks Lomov to say it again
He angrily sends Lomov out of the house
He quietly asks Lomov to borrow money
He sadly says he has no daughter
activities.explanation: Chubukov is overjoyed. He asks Lomov to say it again and says he has been hoping for it for a long time.

activities.title: Put the Visit in Order
activities.prompt: Put these moments from the scene in the order they happen.
items: Lomov enters in a dress-jacket and white gloves
Chubukov rises and greets him gladly
Chubukov secretly suspects Lomov wants to borrow money
Lomov speaks of a request he has come to make
Lomov asks for Natalya's hand in marriage
activities.explanation: First comes the entrance, then the greeting, then the secret doubt, then the mention of a request, and last the big question itself.

activities.prompt: Lomov wears a dress-jacket and white gloves. He is only visiting a neighbour's house. What does his fancy dress most likely show?
options: He thinks this visit is a very big day for him.
He is going to a party after the visit.
He wants to look richer than his neighbour.
He forgot to change his work clothes.

Wrong: this treats the clothes as normal party wear, missing the special reason.
why.He wants to look richer than his neighbo: Wrong: this reads the clothes as showing off, but the story gives no such sign.
Wrong: this treats it as an accident, but he chose these clothes on purpose.

activities.explanation: Right: people dress up when an event feels huge, and asking for marriage is huge.

activities.prompt: Chubukov asks why Lomov is so formal. Secretly, he thinks Lomov wants to borrow money. Why does Chubukov ask this question?
options: He wants to guess the real reason for the visit.
He wants to teach Lomov how to dress well.
He wants Lomov to leave the house quickly.
He wants to borrow money from Lomov himself.

why.He wants to teach Lomov how to dress wel: Wrong: this takes the words at face value and misses his hidden suspicion.
why.He wants Lomov to leave the house quickl: Wrong: nothing shows he wants Lomov to go; he greets him warmly.
why.He wants to borrow money from Lomov hims: Wrong: this flips the roles; Chubukov fears lending, not borrowing.

activities.explanation: Right: his secret doubt shows he is fishing for the true purpose behind the formality.

activities.prompt: Lomov first says he came only to see Chubukov. Then he says he has a request to make. Why does he speak this way?
options: He feels nervous about asking his big question.
He forgot the real reason he came today.
He wants to hide that he likes Chubukov.
He is angry with Chubukov about something.

Wrong: he clearly knows his request; he just delays saying it.
Wrong: the visit is friendly; nothing suggests he dislikes Chubukov.
why.He is angry with Chubukov about somethin: Wrong: anger would show in his words, but his words are polite.

activities.explanation: Right: easing in with small talk before a scary request shows nervousness.

activities.prompt: Lomov asks for Natalya's hand in marriage. Chubukov joyfully asks him to say it again. What does Chubukov's wish to hear it again show?
options: He is so happy he can hardly believe it.
He did not hear the words the first time.
He wants Lomov to change his request.
He is angry that Lomov asked at all.

why.He did not hear the words the first time: Wrong: this takes the words literally and misses the joy in them.
Wrong: he is happy, so he does not want the request changed.
Wrong: 'joyfully' is the opposite of anger.

activities.explanation: Right: joy plus asking again shows delighted disbelief at wonderful news.

activities.prompt: Chubukov says he always loved Lomov like his own son. He says this right after the marriage request. What is Chubukov really saying?
options: He happily accepts Lomov into his family.
He wants Lomov to live in his house now.
He thinks Lomov looks like his real son.
He wishes Lomov had visited him more often.

Wrong: this takes the words as a housing plan, not a feeling.
Wrong: 'like my own son' is about love, not looks.
why.He wishes Lomov had visited him more oft: Wrong: the line is about love, not complaints about visits.

activities.explanation: Right: 'like my own son' plus joy means Lomov is welcomed as family.

activities.prompt: Chubukov rises from his seat to meet Lomov. He says he is extremely glad to see him. Yet he secretly suspects a money request. What do these actions together show?
options: He stays polite to guests even while doubting them.
He likes Lomov more than his own family.
He has already guessed the marriage request.
He is afraid that Lomov will hit him.

Wrong: 'like his own son' comes later; here doubt and warmth sit together.
why.He has already guessed the marriage requ: Wrong: if he knew, he would not suspect a money request.
Wrong: nothing shows fear; his welcome is friendly, not scared.

activities.explanation: Right: warm welcome plus hidden doubt shows polite manners with private worry.

lessons.sceneCaption: A watercolour of a grand Russian drawing-room, like the setting in Chubukov's house where Lomov arrives.
