lessons.title: Natalya and the Oxen Meadows Quarrel Begins

activities.prompt: Why does a marriage proposal suddenly turn into an argument about land?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Lomov comes to speak to Natalya
activities.body: Lomov visits Natalya. He thinks she is an excellent housekeeper, not bad-looking and well-educated. He is 35 and calls it a critical age, so he wants a quiet and regular life. He has made up his mind to ask her to hear him out. But when he mentions his Oxen Meadows, Natalya says they are hers, not his. A quarrel begins.
keyPoints: Lomov thinks Natalya is an excellent housekeeper, not bad-looking and well-educated.
Lomov is 35, a critical age, and wants a quiet and regular life.
Lomov says his Oxen Meadows touch Natalya's birchwoods, but Natalya says they are hers.
activities.explanation: A visit that should be happy turns into a quarrel about a piece of land.

activities.prompt: Lomov comes to Natalya's house wearing a formal dress jacket on a hot day. Why does he dress up so much just to visit a neighbour?
steps: Lomov wants to ask Natalya to marry him, so this is not a normal visit.
Because it is a special request, he wants to look serious and respectful.
He is also nervous, since he is 35 and calls it a critical age.
So the fancy jacket shows he has come for something big, not just to talk.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: How Lomov feels
activities.body: Lomov is not a calm man. He suffers from palpitations, which means his heart beats fast and hard. He gets upset easily. He says his lips are trembling and his right eyebrow twitches. He also says he ought to lead a quiet and regular life. So a quarrel about land makes him feel worse very quickly.
keyPoints: Lomov suffers from palpitations and gets upset easily.
Lomov says his lips are trembling and his right eyebrow twitches.
Lomov says he ought to lead a quiet and regular life.
activities.explanation: Lomov's body shows his worry: trembling lips and a twitching eyebrow.

activities.title: Why has Lomov come?
activities.prompt: Lomov has made up his mind to do something. What is it?
options: To sell his Oxen Meadows to Natalya
To ask Natalya to hear him out
To help Natalya dry her peas
To buy Natalya's birchwoods
activities.explanation: Lomov says he has made up his mind to ask Natalya to hear him out. Well done!

activities.title: Natalya says sorry
activities.prompt: Natalya apologises for her apron and neglige. Why?
options: Because they are old and torn
Because they are wet from the rain
Because they are shelling peas for drying
activities.explanation: Natalya says they are shelling peas for drying, so she is dressed like that. Good thinking!

activities.title: Lomov's age
activities.prompt: Lomov says he is already 35, and he calls it a critical age.
activities.explanation: Yes, Lomov says he is 35 and calls it a critical age.

activities.title: What do the Meadows touch?
activities.prompt: Lomov says his Oxen Meadows touch Natalya's ______.
activities.hint: It is a kind of tree that Natalya owns.
activities.explanation: Lomov says his Oxen Meadows touch Natalya's birchwoods. Lovely work!

activities.title: Who said what?
activities.prompt: Match each person or thing to what the lesson tells us.
pairs: gave free use of the Meadows
told her a merchant had come
activities.explanation: Each person has their own words in the lesson. Super matching!

activities.title: Put the visit in order
activities.prompt: Put these things in the order they happen in the lesson.
items: Lomov thinks Natalya is an excellent housekeeper, not bad-looking and well-educated.
Lomov makes up his mind to ask Natalya to hear him out.
Lomov says his Oxen Meadows touch Natalya's birchwoods.
Natalya says the Oxen Meadows are theirs, not Lomov's.
The quarrel about the Meadows begins.
activities.explanation: First Lomov's kind thoughts, then his request, then the Meadows, then the quarrel. Perfect order!

activities.prompt: A boy is choosing a wife. He makes a list: she cooks well, she looks fine, she reads a lot. He never writes 'I love her'. What does the list show about him?
options: He is thinking with his head, not his heart
He does not really want to marry anyone
He cares only about how she looks
He is too shy to meet her family

why.He does not really want to marry anyone: This reads the list as dislike, but the list is full of good points.
why.He cares only about how she looks: Looks is only one of three points, so this misses the other two.
why.He is too shy to meet her family: Nothing in the list is about shyness or meeting the family.

activities.explanation: Right: he picks practical reasons, so he is using his head, not his heart.

activities.prompt: A man says: 'I am 35. That is a critical age. I should live a quiet and regular life.' He is talking about getting married. Why does he call his age critical?
options: He feels time is running out to settle down
He thinks 35 is too young to marry
He wants to wait ten more years first
He believes quiet life means staying single

why.He thinks 35 is too young to marry: He says critical, not too young, so this flips his meaning.
why.He wants to wait ten more years first: He is hurrying because of his age, not planning to wait.
why.He believes quiet life means staying sin: He wants a quiet life through marriage, not by staying single.

activities.explanation: Right: 'critical age' means he feels he must marry soon and settle down.

activities.prompt: Before a big talk, a man says: 'My lips are trembling and my right eyebrow twitches. My heart beats too fast.' He still walks into the room. What does this show about him?
options: He is nervous but goes on anyway
He is angry with the people inside
He is ill and should be in bed
He is bored and wants to leave soon

why.He is angry with the people inside: Anger was not mentioned; the signs given are all signs of nerves.
why.He is ill and should be in bed: He feels unwell from nerves, but he chooses to go in, not to bed.
why.He is bored and wants to leave soon: Boredom looks calm and slow, not trembling and a fast heart.

activities.explanation: Right: shaking lips and a fast heart show nerves, yet he still goes in.

activities.prompt: A guest arrives. A girl is in an old apron, picking peas with her father. She says sorry for her clothes and explains they are drying peas. What does her sorry tell you about her?
options: She cares about looking proper before guests
She is angry that the guest came now
She wants the guest to help pick peas
She forgot she was wearing an apron

why.She is angry that the guest came now: If she were angry, she would not say sorry or explain politely.
why.She wants the guest to help pick peas: She is explaining her clothes, not asking the guest to work.
why.She forgot she was wearing an apron: She noticed the apron herself, so she did not forget it.

activities.explanation: Right: saying sorry for old clothes shows she cares about looking proper.

activities.prompt: A girl says: 'We cut a whole field yesterday. I fear the hay may rot if it is not collected.' She keeps looking at the sky while talking. Why does she keep looking up?
options: She is worried rain will spoil the hay
She is looking for birds in the sky
She is checking how late it is
She is waiting for more workers to come

why.She is looking for birds in the sky: Birds were never mentioned; her fear was about the hay.
why.She is checking how late it is: Time is not her worry; rotting hay is her worry.
why.She is waiting for more workers to come: Her words are about weather and hay, not about workers.

activities.explanation: Right: she fears the hay may rot, and rain is what rots cut hay.

activities.prompt: Two neighbours argue about a field. One says: 'My aunt's grandmother let your family use it free, forever. But that never made it yours.' What is he trying to prove?
options: Kindness in the past was not a sale
His aunt's grandmother was a bad judge
The other family should pay rent now
The field really belongs to both families

why.His aunt's grandmother was a bad judge: He blames no one's judgement; he only explains the old favour.
why.The other family should pay rent now: He is arguing about who owns it, not asking for rent.
why.The field really belongs to both familie: He says it is his, so sharing it is not his claim.

activities.explanation: Right: free use forever was a favour, not a transfer of ownership.

lessons.sceneAlt: A nineteenth-century Russian painting showing a matchmaking visit, like the proposal scene between Lomov and Natalya.
lessons.sceneCaption: Pavel Fedotov's painting 'The Major's Marriage Proposal' shows a matchmaking visit in a Russian home, like Lomov's visit.

sceneCredit.text: Pavel Fedotov - Сватовство майора - Google Art Project by Pavel Fedotov, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons
sceneCredit.creator: Pavel Fedotov

lessons.title: The Oxen Meadows Quarrel Grows and Chubukov Joins

activities.prompt: How fast can a friendly visit turn into a shouting match?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: The Quarrel Gets Louder
activities.body: Natalya says her mowers will reach the Meadows that very day. Lomov clutches his heart and says the Meadows are his. Chubukov joins in and says the Meadows belong to his family. The two men trade harsh names. Chubukov even bans Lomov from his house. Then he lets slip why Lomov came: to propose to Natalya.
keyPoints: Natalya says her mowers will be in the Meadows that day.
Chubukov joins the quarrel and sides with Natalya.
Chubukov reveals Lomov came to propose to Natalya.
activities.explanation: A small talk about land turns into a big family quarrel.

activities.prompt: Natalya and Lomov fight about the Meadows. Then Chubukov shouts that Lomov came to propose. Natalya falls into a chair and wails. Why does she cry so suddenly?
steps: Natalya was fighting about land, so she felt angry, not loving.
She did not know Lomov came to propose, so she drove him away.
When she hears the truth, she sees she lost what she wanted.
So her wailing shows regret, because anger made her lose Lomov.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Who says the mowers will be in the Meadows that very day?
options: Lomov
Chubukov
Natalya
activities.explanation: Well done! Natalya is the one who speaks about the mowers.

activities.prompt: Natalya asks Lomov not to shout and to ______ himself.
activities.hint: It means to hold yourself back and stay calm.
activities.explanation: Natalya wants Lomov to restrain himself and stop shouting. Good spotting!

activities.prompt: When Chubukov joins the quarrel, what does he say about the Meadows?
options: He says they are Lomov's.
He says they are nobody's.
He says they are theirs.
activities.explanation: Chubukov takes Natalya's side and claims the Meadows are theirs.

activities.prompt: Match each speaker to what they say about the other family.
activities.explanation: Both families fling harsh words. Spotting who said what helps you follow the quarrel.

activities.prompt: At the height of the quarrel, what does Chubukov tell Lomov?
options: Never set foot in his house again
Never speak to Natalya again
Never touch the Meadows again
activities.explanation: Chubukov is so angry that he bans Lomov from his house.

activities.prompt: Put these events from the quarrel in the order they happen.
items: Natalya says her mowers will be in the Meadows that day.
Lomov clutches at his heart and claims the Meadows.
Chubukov says the Meadows are theirs.
Chubukov calls Lomov a pettifogger.
Natalya wails for them to bring Lomov back.
activities.explanation: The quarrel grows step by step, from mowers to harsh names to tears. You followed it perfectly!

activities.prompt: Natalya was shouting at Lomov about the Meadows. Then she hears he came to propose. She falls into a chair and wails. What does she most likely feel?
options: She is happy because the fight is over now.
She is sorry because her anger pushed Lomov away.
She is scared because Chubukov shouted at her.
She is tired because the argument lasted too long.

why.She is happy because the fight is over n: She cannot be happy; she just learned she lost something she wanted.
why.She is scared because Chubukov shouted a: Chubukov told her the news, not shouted at her, so fear is the wrong feeling.
why.She is tired because the argument lasted: Tiredness does not make a person fall into a chair and wail.

activities.explanation: Right. She sees her shouting drove away the man who came to propose.

activities.prompt: Chubukov is fighting with Lomov about the Meadows. Suddenly he says Lomov came to propose to Natalya. Why does Chubukov say this now?
options: He wants to hurt Lomov by ending the secret.
He wants to help Lomov marry Natalya quickly.
He wants to show he remembers old family stories.
He wants to change the topic to something happy.

why.He wants to help Lomov marry Natalya qui: If he wanted to help, he would say it kindly, not during a fight.
why.He wants to show he remembers old family: The secret is news about today, not an old family story.
why.He wants to change the topic to somethin: He is still fighting about the Meadows, so he is not changing the topic.

activities.explanation: Right. He is angry, so he throws out the secret to wound Lomov.

activities.prompt: Lomov hears the mowers will come to the Meadows that very day. He says he will 'give it to them in the neck'. What does he mean?
options: He will give the mowers a gift for their necks.
He will punish the mowers for coming to the Meadows.
He will tie a cloth around his own neck.
He will ask the mowers to bend their necks down.

why.He will give the mowers a gift for their: He is angry, not friendly, so a gift makes no sense here.
His own neck is not part of this angry threat at all.
why.He will ask the mowers to bend their nec: He is threatening them, not politely asking them to do anything.

activities.explanation: Right. The angry words mean he will attack or punish them.

activities.prompt: Lomov clutches his heart and shouts about the Meadows. Natalya says, 'Don't shout. Restrain yourself.' Why does Natalya say this?
options: She wants the fight to stay calm and continue.
She wants Lomov to leave the house at once.
She wants Lomov to shout even louder than before.
She wants Chubukov to answer instead of Lomov.

why.She wants Lomov to leave the house at on: She is still arguing with him, so she does not want him to leave.
why.She wants Lomov to shout even louder tha: Asking him to restrain himself means less shouting, not more.
why.She wants Chubukov to answer instead of: She speaks to Lomov directly, so she is not calling Chubukov in.

activities.explanation: Right. She asks him to hold back his shouting, so the talk can go on.

activities.prompt: Natalya wails and asks them to bring Lomov back. What will most likely happen next?
options: The family will try hard to call Lomov back.
The family will burn all the papers about Meadows.
Lomov will come back with more mowers to fight.
Chubukov will refuse to speak to Natalya again.

why.The family will burn all the papers abou: The papers were never the real problem, so burning them helps nothing.
why.Lomov will come back with more mowers to: Lomov left upset, so bringing more mowers is not what anyone wants now.
why.Chubukov will refuse to speak to Natalya: Chubukov revealed the proposal, so he knows Natalya wants Lomov back.

activities.explanation: Right. Her wailing shows she wants him back, so they will try to fetch him.

lessons.title: The Dog Quarrel and the Engagement

activities.prompt: Can two people argue about dogs and still get engaged?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Two Dogs, One Big Argument
activities.body: Lomov and Natalya begin to quarrel again about their dogs. Lomov's dog is Guess, and Natalya's dog is Squeezer. Lomov says his heart is beating awfully. Chubukov joins in and praises Squeezer. At last, Chubukov puts Lomov's hand into Natalya's hand. She says she is willing, and they kiss. But even at the end, Natalya still says Guess is worse than Squeezer!
keyPoints: Lomov's dog is Guess and Natalya's dog is Squeezer.
Chubukov puts Lomov's hand into Natalya's hand to end the quarrel.
Even after the engagement, Natalya says Guess is worse than Squeezer.
activities.explanation: The quarrel about dogs goes on right up to the happy end.

activities.prompt: Lomov and Natalya fight about dogs even after they agree to marry. Why do they keep arguing?
steps: They agree to marry, so the big problem is solved.
But they still argue about Guess and Squeezer right away.
This shows the quarrel matters more to them than being right or calm.
So they argue out of habit, not because they are truly angry.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Who Owns the Meadows?
activities.prompt: Natalya says they were heated, but what does she admit about Oxen Meadows?
options: They really are Lomov's.
They really are Chubukov's.
They belong to nobody at all.
activities.explanation: Well done! Natalya admits that Oxen Meadows really are Lomov's.

activities.title: How Lomov Feels
activities.prompt: Lomov says his heart is beating awfully and his eyebrows are twitching.
activities.explanation: Yes, that is just what Lomov says. Poor Lomov is very worried!

activities.title: The Price of Squeezer
activities.prompt: Natalya says her papa gave ______ roubles for Squeezer.
activities.hint: It is less than what Lomov paid for Guess.
activities.explanation: Good memory! Natalya says her papa gave 85 roubles for Squeezer.

activities.title: Who Said What About the Dogs?
activities.prompt: Match each person or dog to what the lesson says.
pairs: Called the best dog in the district
Says Guess is old and short in the muzzle
Says Squeezer is overshot and a bad hunter
activities.explanation: Great matching! Each person has strong words about the other dog.

activities.title: How the Engagement Happened
activities.prompt: Put these things in the order they happen in the lesson.
items: Lomov says his heart is beating awfully.
Chubukov puts Lomov's hand into Natalya's hand.
Natalya says she is willing.
They kiss, and Lomov says it is very nice.
Natalya still says Guess is worse than Squeezer.
activities.explanation: Perfect order! The quarrel calms down, the hands join, and still the dog argument continues.

activities.title: What Happens at the Very End?
activities.prompt: Even after the engagement, what does Natalya keep saying?
options: That Guess is worse than Squeezer.
That Squeezer is worse than Guess.
That both dogs are equally good.
activities.explanation: Yes! Even at the happy end, Natalya still says Guess is worse than Squeezer. The quarrel never truly stops.

activities.prompt: Natalya says Oxen Meadows are Lomov's. Earlier she fought hard over them. How does she probably feel now?
options: She wants peace more than winning the land.
She still thinks the land belongs to her family.
She is hiding her anger and will fight again.
She forgot the quarrel because it was long ago.

why.She still thinks the land belongs to her: This thinks she still holds her old belief, but she gave it up.
why.She is hiding her anger and will fight a: Nothing shows a plan to fight again in her words.
why.She forgot the quarrel because it was lo: She remembers the quarrel; she even calls it heated.

activities.explanation: Right. Giving up the claim shows she now wants peace.

activities.prompt: Lomov says his heart beats awfully and his eyebrows twitch. He says this while talking to Natalya. What does this tell us?
options: He is too weak to stay and talk.
His body shows how upset he feels inside.
He is lying to make Natalya feel sorry.
He is excited about the dogs only.

He stays and keeps talking, so he is not leaving.
He does not ask for pity; he reports his own state.
The signs are about his body, not the dogs.

activities.explanation: Right. His body signs show his inner stress.

activities.prompt: Lomov paid 125 roubles for Guess. Natalya's papa paid 85 for Squeezer. Natalya still says Squeezer is better. Why does she say this?
options: She does not know the two prices.
She wants her family's dog to sound best.
She thinks a lower price means a better dog.
She is only joking with Lomov.

She knows the prices; she names the 85 herself.
why.She thinks a lower price means a better: She never says price decides quality in that way.
Her claim is serious, not a joke.

activities.explanation: Right. Family pride makes her defend her own dog.

activities.prompt: Chubukov calls Squeezer the best dog in the district. He also says Guess is old and short in the muzzle. What is he really doing?
options: He is giving fair facts about both dogs.
He is helping Lomov choose a new dog.
He is taking his daughter's side in the quarrel.
He is testing if Lomov knows dogs well.

His praise and blame are one-sided, not fair.
He never talks about buying or choosing a dog.
He is not testing anyone's knowledge here.

activities.explanation: Right. He backs Natalya by praising her dog and blaming Lomov's.

activities.prompt: Lomov says Squeezer is overshot and a bad hunter. Natalya's papa calls Squeezer the best dog around. What does this clash show?
options: One of them has never seen Squeezer.
Each person judges the dog to win the quarrel.
The word 'hunter' means different things to them.
Squeezer changed a lot between the two talks.

Both speak with sure knowledge of the same dog.
why.The word 'hunter' means different things: They disagree about the dog, not the word's meaning.
why.Squeezer changed a lot between the two t: The dog did not change; the speakers' sides differ.

activities.explanation: Right. Each side praises its own dog to win.

activities.prompt: Chubukov puts Lomov's hand into Natalya's hand. They kiss. Lomov says it is very nice. What does his words show?
options: He is happy the quarrel is over at last.
He wants to start a new quarrel soon.
He feels shy and cannot speak more.
He is only repeating what others say.

He speaks kindly, not with a plan to fight.
He does speak, so shyness is not the point.
His words are his own feeling, not a copy.

activities.explanation: Right. Calling it nice shows relief and joy after the fight.

lessons.sceneAlt: A Russian wedding ceremony taking place in Russia.
lessons.sceneCaption: A Russian wedding ceremony, showing how weddings are celebrated in Russia.

activities.context: Nikolai has just made a special proposal to Anna, and she has said yes. Their families begin the planning: rings are arranged, a dress is chosen for the bride, cars are booked, and a reception is prepared. On the wedding day, the procession of several cars sets off. Nikolai faces the stairs to Anna's flat, knowing that at every landing a question waits, and a wrong guess will cost him money before he can climb higher.
activities.prompt: Nikolai reaches the second landing but gives a wrong answer to the question asked there. What is he most likely to do next?
options: Hand over some money so that he may continue climbing
Turn back home and call off the whole wedding
Wait on the stairs until Anna comes down to help him
Ask the wedding guests to answer the question for him

why.Turn back home and call off the whole we: Wrong: nothing in the custom ends the wedding over one wrong answer.
why.Wait on the stairs until Anna comes down: Wrong: the custom expects the groom himself to get past each landing.
why.Ask the wedding guests to answer the que: Wrong: the questions are put to the groom, not to the guests.

activities.explanation: Correct: a wrong guess is settled by paying cash before he can move ahead.

activities.context: Nikolai has just made a special proposal to Anna, and she has said yes. Their families begin the planning: rings are arranged, a dress is chosen for the bride, cars are booked, and a reception is prepared. On the wedding day, the procession of several cars sets off. Nikolai faces the stairs to Anna's flat, knowing that at every landing a question waits, and a wrong guess will cost him money before he can climb higher.
activities.prompt: Anna's family is worried because in earlier times one side alone paid for the reception. Under today's practice, what should the two families expect?
options: The bride's family pays everything, as was always done
The groom's family pays everything to show its generosity
The two families divide the cost between them
The reception is dropped from the plans to save money

why.The bride's family pays everything, as w: Wrong: that was the older practice, not the present one.
why.The groom's family pays everything to sh: Wrong: the custom never placed the whole burden on the groom's side.
why.The reception is dropped from the plans: Wrong: the reception remains part of the planning; only the payment has changed.

activities.explanation: Correct: nowadays the expenses are usually shared by both families.

activities.context: Nikolai has just made a special proposal to Anna, and she has said yes. Their families begin the planning: rings are arranged, a dress is chosen for the bride, cars are booked, and a reception is prepared. On the wedding day, the procession of several cars sets off. Nikolai faces the stairs to Anna's flat, knowing that at every landing a question waits, and a wrong guess will cost him money before he can climb higher.
activities.prompt: Nikolai tells a friend, "I made my proposal last month." In which sense is he using the word here?
options: A scheme he drew up for organising the cars
An offer of a possible plan for the reception
The act of asking Anna to marry him
A suggestion he gave about the bride's dress

why.A scheme he drew up for organising the c: Wrong: a scheme for cars would be a plan, not what a groom offers his bride.
why.An offer of a possible plan for the rece: Wrong: an offer of a possible plan concerns actions, not marriage.
why.A suggestion he gave about the bride's d: Wrong: a suggestion about a dress is a plan-type meaning, not the marriage one.

activities.explanation: Correct: asking for someone's hand in marriage is one meaning of the word, and it fits a groom.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): A Russian wedding may extend over several days.
Reason (R): Some Russian weddings continue for as long as a week.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the fact that some weddings last a week explains why a wedding may run beyond two days.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): In earlier times, the groom's family paid for the reception.
Reason (R): Nowadays the bride's and groom's families usually share the wedding expenses.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because it was the bride's family that paid earlier, while the reason about sharing expenses today is true.

activities.prompt: Explain why a groom in a Russian wedding would be wise to carry some money with him on the wedding day.
activities.answer: In a Russian wedding, the groom must climb several stairs to reach his bride, and at each landing he is asked a question. Only a correct answer allows him to go up. If he guesses wrong, he has to pay cash before he can move ahead. Since he cannot be sure of answering every question correctly, carrying money ensures that a wrong guess will not stop him from reaching his bride and continuing the ceremony.
points: Mentions the climb up several stairs to reach the bride
States that a question must be answered at each landing
Explains that a wrong guess means paying cash to move ahead
Concludes that money keeps the groom from being held up
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A wealthy landowner visits his long-time wealthy neighbour to ask for the hand of the neighbour's twenty-five-year-old daughter. The father is happy, since a tie between two well-off households is exactly what families like his encourage. But the visitor, though large and hearty, is very suspicious, and both men are quarrelsome. Soon they are arguing over petty issues, and the daughter joins in. The real purpose of the visit keeps getting pushed aside as the arguing grows.
activities.prompt: If the three of them continue arguing over petty issues, what is most likely to happen to the visitor's real purpose?
options: It will be forgotten amidst the quarrelling.
It will be accepted at once because the families are old friends.
It will be decided by the daughter without any discussion.
It will become easier to raise once the arguing dies down on its own.

why.It will be accepted at once because the: Wrong: being old neighbours does not stop the quarrelling; the play shows friendship does not prevent petty arguments.
why.It will be decided by the daughter witho: Wrong: the daughter joins the quarrels rather than settling matters calmly on her own.
why.It will become easier to raise once the: Wrong: nothing suggests the arguing will stop by itself; the pattern in the play is that quarrels continue and crowd out the proposal.

activities.explanation: Correct: the passage shows the purpose being pushed aside, and the play tells us the proposal is in danger of being forgotten amidst the quarrelling.

activities.context: A wealthy landowner visits his long-time wealthy neighbour to ask for the hand of the neighbour's twenty-five-year-old daughter. The father is happy, since a tie between two well-off households is exactly what families like his encourage. But the visitor, though large and hearty, is very suspicious, and both men are quarrelsome. Soon they are arguing over petty issues, and the daughter joins in. The real purpose of the visit keeps getting pushed aside as the arguing grows.
activities.prompt: Why do the two families welcome this match?
options: Because marriages that made good economic sense were encouraged between wealthy families.
Because the daughter had refused every other offer in the neighbourhood.
Because the two men wanted to end a long-standing dispute between them.
Because the visitor was poor and needed the father's land.

why.Because the daughter had refused every o: Wrong: nothing in the lesson says anything about other offers or the daughter refusing anyone.
why.Because the two men wanted to end a long: Wrong: the lesson gives no dispute between the families; they are long-time neighbours.
why.Because the visitor was poor and needed: Wrong: this reverses the facts, since Lomov is himself a wealthy landowner.

activities.explanation: Correct: the play tells us wealthy families sought ties with other wealthy families and encouraged marriages that made good economic sense.

activities.context: A wealthy landowner visits his long-time wealthy neighbour to ask for the hand of the neighbour's twenty-five-year-old daughter. The father is happy, since a tie between two well-off households is exactly what families like his encourage. But the visitor, though large and hearty, is very suspicious, and both men are quarrelsome. Soon they are arguing over petty issues, and the daughter joins in. The real purpose of the visit keeps getting pushed aside as the arguing grows.
activities.prompt: What should the visitor do to make sure his purpose succeeds?
options: State his proposal clearly and refuse to be drawn into petty quarrels.
Win every argument first so that the neighbour will respect him.
Stay silent and hope the father guesses why he has come.
Pull the daughter into each quarrel so that she takes his side.

why.Win every argument first so that the nei: Wrong: trying to win arguments feeds the quarrelling that endangers the proposal.
why.Stay silent and hope the father guesses: Wrong: silence will not help, since the others are quarrelsome and the purpose is already being pushed aside.
why.Pull the daughter into each quarrel so t: Wrong: the daughter is quarrelsome too, so drawing her in would deepen the quarrels, not end them.

activities.explanation: Correct: since the proposal is in danger of being forgotten amidst the quarrelling, keeping to the purpose and avoiding petty quarrels is the sensible course.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The proposal Lomov has come to make is in danger of being forgotten amidst the quarrelling.
Reason (R): All three characters are quarrelsome people who quarrel over petty issues.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the constant petty quarrelling is exactly what keeps pushing the proposal aside, so R explains A.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The play is a farce.
Reason (R): It was written by Anton Chekhov, a Russian short story writer and dramatist.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, but the author's nationality and profession do not explain why the play is a farce.

activities.prompt: Explain why a marriage between Lomov and Natalya would be considered a good match by their families.
activities.answer: In the world of the play, wealthy families sought ties with other wealthy families, and they encouraged marriages that made good economic sense. Lomov is a long-time wealthy neighbour of Chubukov, and both men are landowners, so both households are well-off. A marriage between Lomov and Natalya would join two wealthy neighbouring landowning families, strengthening the tie between them and making sound economic sense. This is exactly the kind of marriage such families encouraged, which is why Lomov comes to seek Natalya's hand.
points: Wealthy families sought ties with other wealthy families.
Such families encouraged marriages that made good economic sense.
Lomov is a long-time wealthy neighbour of Chubukov, and Chubukov is a landowner.
The union would therefore join two well-off landowning households.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: In the drawing-room of Chubukov's house, Lomov enters in a dress-jacket and white gloves. Chubukov rises to meet him, saying he is extremely glad to see Ivan Vassilevitch, and asks why Lomov is so formal in his get-up. Secretly Chubukov suspects a visit to borrow money. But Lomov says he has come only to see Chubukov, to trouble him with a request: the hand of Natalya Stepanovna in marriage. Chubukov joyfully asks him to say it again.
activities.prompt: Arjun arrives at Mr. Rao's house in a suit and tie. Mr. Rao welcomes him warmly, jokes about the formal clothes, and privately guesses Arjun wants a loan. Nervously, Arjun says he has a request. Why did Mr. Rao privately guess that money was involved?
options: Because Arjun's formal clothes and vague mention of a request made him look like someone about to ask a favour
Because Arjun avoided greeting Mr. Rao politely at the door
Because Arjun directly told Mr. Rao he needed a loan for his business
Because Mr. Rao had already decided not to lend money to anyone that month

why.Because Arjun avoided greeting Mr. Rao p: Wrong: the case says Rao welcomed him warmly, so there was no cold or rude greeting to go on.
why.Because Arjun directly told Mr. Rao he n: Wrong: Arjun never stated a loan; he only spoke nervously of a request, like Lomov did.
why.Because Mr. Rao had already decided not: Wrong: nothing in the case says Rao had made any decision about lending; the guess came from Arjun's appearance and manner.

activities.explanation: Correct: the formal get-up plus talk of a 'request' is exactly the cue that made Chubukov suspect borrowing.

activities.context: In the drawing-room of Chubukov's house, Lomov enters in a dress-jacket and white gloves. Chubukov rises to meet him, saying he is extremely glad to see Ivan Vassilevitch, and asks why Lomov is so formal in his get-up. Secretly Chubukov suspects a visit to borrow money. But Lomov says he has come only to see Chubukov, to trouble him with a request: the hand of Natalya Stepanovna in marriage. Chubukov joyfully asks him to say it again.
activities.prompt: Arjun then asks to marry Mr. Rao's daughter, and Rao, delighted, asks him to repeat it. What will Mr. Rao most likely do immediately after this?
options: Quietly work out how much money he could afford to lend Arjun
Ask Arjun to come back on a less formal occasion
Say joyfully that he has hoped for this for a long time and treat Arjun like his own son
Show Arjun out because the visit has wasted his evening

why.Quietly work out how much money he could: Wrong: the money suspicion dissolves the moment the real request is revealed, so lending is no longer on his mind.
why.Ask Arjun to come back on a less formal: Wrong: there is nothing in the visit to object to; the formality that puzzled him has now been explained happily.
why.Show Arjun out because the visit has was: Wrong: the visit turned out to be welcome news, not a waste of time, so turning Arjun out makes no sense.

activities.explanation: Correct: this mirrors Chubukov's reaction — joy, asking to hear it again, and claiming long-held hope and fatherly love.

activities.context: In the drawing-room of Chubukov's house, Lomov enters in a dress-jacket and white gloves. Chubukov rises to meet him, saying he is extremely glad to see Ivan Vassilevitch, and asks why Lomov is so formal in his get-up. Secretly Chubukov suspects a visit to borrow money. But Lomov says he has come only to see Chubukov, to trouble him with a request: the hand of Natalya Stepanovna in marriage. Chubukov joyfully asks him to say it again.
activities.prompt: Suppose Arjun had arrived in everyday clothes instead of a suit and tie. What would most likely have been different in the visit?
options: Arjun's request would have turned from marriage into a business favour
Mr. Rao would have been less quick to suspect that money was the reason for the visit
Mr. Rao would have refused to let Arjun into the house at all
Arjun would have been unable to state his request clearly

why.Arjun's request would have turned from m: Wrong: the clothes do not change the purpose of the visit; the request itself stays the same.
why.Mr. Rao would have refused to let Arjun: Wrong: a warm host who rises to greet a visitor would not bar the door over clothing.
why.Arjun would have been unable to state hi: Wrong: nervousness about stating a request comes from the visitor, not from what he is wearing.

activities.explanation: Correct: it was the unusual formality that triggered the money guess, so ordinary clothes would remove that trigger.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Chubukov secretly thinks Lomov may have come to borrow money.
Reason (R): Lomov arrives unusually formally dressed and speaks of troubling Chubukov with a request.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The formal get-up and the vague talk of a request are exactly what make Chubukov imagine an unwelcome money favour.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Lomov has actually come to borrow money from Chubukov.
Reason (R): Chubukov secretly suspects that Lomov has come to borrow money.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Chubukov's suspicion is genuine but mistaken, since Lomov's real purpose is asking for Natalya Stepanovna's hand in marriage.

activities.prompt: Explain why Chubukov's guess that Lomov has come to borrow money is understandable, and why it turns out to be wrong.
activities.answer: Chubukov's guess is understandable because Lomov arrives unusually formally dressed, in a dress-jacket and white gloves, and speaks vaguely about troubling Chubukov with a request. Formal clothes and a hesitant request naturally suggest someone about to ask a favour such as a loan. The guess is wrong because Lomov says he has come only to see Chubukov, and his real request is not money at all: he asks for the hand of Natalya Stepanovna in marriage, a request that fills Chubukov with joy.
points: Formal dress-jacket and white gloves plus a vague 'request' explain the suspicion
Lomov states he has come only to see Chubukov
The real request is Natalya Stepanovna's hand in marriage
Chubukov's joyful reaction shows the suspicion was mistaken
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: The Proposal

activities.prompt: The title word 'proposal' has more than one meaning. Which meaning fits this play best?
options: A plan for building a house
A scheme to sell some land
Asking for someone's hand in marriage
A suggestion about a new job
activities.explanation: A proposal can be a suggestion or an offer, but in this play it means asking someone to marry you. Well done for spotting the right sense!

activities.prompt: A Russian wedding lasts for two days, and some weddings last as long as a week.
activities.explanation: The lesson says a Russian wedding lasts two days, and some go on for a whole week. That is a long celebration!

activities.prompt: As the groom climbs the stairs, at each landing he must answer a ______ before he is allowed to go up.
activities.hint: The people on the landing test him before he may pass.
activities.explanation: At each landing the groom must answer a question to be allowed to go up. If he guesses wrong, he must pay cash to move ahead!

activities.prompt: The play we read was not always called 'The Proposal'. What was its original title?
options: A Marriage Proposal
Oxen Meadows
The Quarrelsome Neighbour
A Wedding in Russia
activities.explanation: The play was first called 'A Marriage Proposal'. Chekhov later gave it the shorter title we know.

activities.prompt: Match each person or pet to the right description.
pairs: a wealthy neighbour who comes to propose
a landowner and father of Natalya
Lomov's dog, who has gone lame
the dog Chubukov calls the best in the district
activities.explanation: Lomov visits Chubukov to ask for Natalya's hand, and even the two dogs join the quarrel. Great matching!

activities.prompt: Put these events from the play in the order they happen.
items: Lomov enters wearing a dress-jacket and white gloves
Chubukov secretly suspects Lomov has come to borrow money
Lomov asks for the hand of Natalya in marriage
Lomov and Natalya quarrel over Oxen Meadows
Chubukov puts Lomov's hand into his daughter's hand
activities.explanation: The visit begins politely, the proposal is nearly lost in quarrels, yet it ends with joined hands. You traced the whole play!

activities.prompt: Lomov says he paid 85 roubles for his dog Guess.
activities.explanation: Lomov says he gave Mironov 125 roubles for Guess. It was Natalya who spoke of 85 roubles, for Squeezer.

activities.prompt: Why does Lomov feel he must marry now rather than wait?
options: He is already 35 and wants a quiet, regular life
He wishes to win the quarrel over the Meadows
Chubukov has ordered him to marry at once
His dog Guess needs a new home to live in
activities.explanation: Lomov says he is already 35, a critical age, and ought to lead a quiet and regular life. His nerves push him on too!

activities.prompt: In the heat of the quarrel, Chubukov angrily calls Lomov a ______.
activities.hint: An unkind name for someone who argues over small matters.
activities.explanation: Chubukov calls Lomov a pettifogger during their quarrel. The two neighbours say many unkind things before calming down.

activities.prompt: The proposal is accepted and the couple kiss. What does Natalya still say at the very end?
options: That the wedding should last a whole week
That Oxen Meadows truly belong to her family
That Lomov must never set foot in the house
That Guess is worse than Squeezer
activities.explanation: Even after saying she is willing and kissing Lomov, Natalya still claims Guess is worse than Squeezer. The quarrelsome fun never quite stops!
